TAXMANN ADVISORY AND RESEARCH TEAM (INCOME TAX)

Despite the COVID-19 pandemic, the Year 2021 has been busy for the Courts and Tribunals. Several significant rulings were delivered onInternational Taxation and Transfer Pricing matters, including the Supreme Court's landmark ruling on the treatment of sum received on the sale of software.In this article, we have shortlisted key 15 rulings related to International Taxation, and Transfer Pricing reported at taxmann.com during the year 2021.

1. Sum received by a non-resident for sale of computer software through EULAs not taxable as royalty : SC

Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd . v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC)

The Supreme Court of India held that as per the definition of royalties contained in Article 12 of the DTAAs, it is clear that there is no obligation under section 195 to deduct tax at source on payments towards software purchase. This is because the distribution agreements or EULAs of such software do not create any interest or right in such distributors/end-users, which would amount to the use of or right to use any copyright.

The provisions of section 9(1)(vi), along with Explanations 2 and 4 thereof, which deal with royalty, couldn't also be applied as the same is not more beneficial to the assessees in comparison to the provision contained in DTAAs.

Accordingly, amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for the resale/use of the computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, was not the payment of royalty for the use of copyright in the computer software.

2. Indian tax authorities cannot grant a refund of taxes paid in foreign jurisdictions: Mumbai ITAT

Bank of India v. Asstt.CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 155 (Mum. - Trib.)

The Mumbai Tribunal held that the tax credit schemes, as evident from the international tax literature and model convention commentaries, do not envisage any situation in which the excess foreign tax credit can result in a tax refund to the taxpayers from the exchequer of residence jurisdictions.

All the methods of eliminating double taxation, i.e., exemption method, credit method or hybrid method, restrict the liability to tax in the source jurisdiction. The relief sought in the instant case goes well beyond that and would result in a refund of taxes by India, and what is being termed as a refund is not even paid to the Indian exchequer.

Wherever tax credits exceed the tax liability, at best a carry forward or back of excess tax credit can be given when permitted by the domestic law, or at best when not restricted by the domestic law.

3. A non-resident is liable to tax in all years in which its project exceeding threshold limit for the creation of PE falls : AAR

Tiong Woon Project & Contracting (P.) Ltd., In re [2021] 124 taxmann.com 549 (AAR - Mumbai)

Applicant executed a project between 06-01-2011 to 30-01-2012 comprising nearly 13 months. The project was continued for a period of 85 days in the previous year 2010-11 and 306 days in the previous year 2011-12.

Before the Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR), the applicant took the view that no taxable income accrues or arises in India from its activities of execution of 'installation project' in the previous year 2010-11 since the duration of the project was only 85 days. The taxable income arises in the previous year 2011-12, where the duration of the project was 306 days resulting in the creation of permanent establishment (PE) in India in terms of Article 5 of DTAA between India and Singapore.

The revenue argued that article 5 clearly states that an installation project constitutes a PE if it continues for a period of 183 days in any fiscal year. That article refers to any fiscal year and not every or relevant fiscal year.

Attention is also invited to Article 15 of the DTAA, which deals with dependent personal services. The article mandates that the recipient should be present in the other State for a period or periods not exceeding in aggregate 183 days in the relevant fiscal year to escape taxation. Thus, it is emphasized that the phrase 'any fiscal year' in article 5 indicates that a PE is constituted if the whole duration of the project, which may be spread over more than one fiscal year, includes 183 days or above in any fiscal year.

Thus, it was held that the applicant's income is taxable in India as business profit in both the previous year's 2010-11 and 2011-12.

man 477 (Kar.) (HC)

Similar view was also taken by Hon'ble Delhi Bench of ITAT in the case of Micro Soft Corporation ITA No: 1392 of 2005 (Delhi). It is also pertinent to examine what rights the manufacturer of a software has in respect of sueing the user over infringement of the copyright of a software. This analysis would also help in understanding of the rights on transfer to the user of the license in respect of a copyrighted article. 2.1 At this juncture, three Explanations have been inserted 4,5 and 6 to section 9(1)(vi) retrospectively from 01-06-1976. The explanations read as under:

"Explanation 4 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Explanation 5 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not–

(a)

the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b)

such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c)

the ocation of such right, property or information is in India.

Explanation 6 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the expression "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-lining of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret."

On comparing Explanation 4 with Article 12(2) of OECD MC it is evident that the term "used or right to use" is succeeded by the word "a computer software" in the former and the word "copyright" in the later. It is also being discussed among the scholarly circles whether Explanation4 is amplifying the scope of Explanation2 or is it creating another dimension of the substantive provision. Is it legally acceptable in respect of a new Explanation providing an expanded meaning of term "royalty" which was already defined in Explanation 2 of section 9(1)(vi) ? If it amounts to altering the meaning of "royalty" can it be retrospective through an Explanation. It is well understood that the meaning of "royalty" under the Act is wider than the meaning provided under OECD MC. The gap is further widened by this new Explanation4.

2.2. Explanation 5 seeks to clarify that the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer or not would not make difference in deciding whether particular payment is "royalty". In the same manner, whether the payer used such right, property or information directly or not and whether the location of such right, property or information is in India or not would not make difference in deciding whether the payment is "royalty" or not. However, Hon'ble Delhi High Court while deciding the case of Ericsson A.B., (supra) has held that for the purpose of section 9(1) (v), (vi), (vii) it is not required to go into explanation to Sec.9 (2) of the Act, if the payment does not fall into any of the categories covered by (v), (vi) and (vii).

In view of the same, it is possible to argue that once sale of computer software is not covered by Explanation 2, so as to be treated as "royalty" than the new Explanation 5 would not have any bearing on such a transaction. It is also interesting to note that Explanations4 and 5 refer to the rights in respect of right, property or information leaving aside other terms such as "patent, process, invention etc," as mentioned in Explanation 2.

2.3 The newly inserted Explanations 4 and 5 would not bring finality for interpreting the term "royalty" either under the treaty law or under the post amended domestic law.

2.4 Explanation 6 has been inserted to neutralize the judgment of Asia Satellite Telecommunications Co. Ltd. v. DIT [2011] 332 ITR 340/197 Taxman 263/9 taxmann.com 168(Delhi), thereby providing the term "process" includes transmission by satellite, cable, optic fiber, any other similar technology whether or not such process is secret, whether or not the satellite etc are under the control of the customers. The amendment is widening the scope of the term "royalty".

CASE STUDY 3: Transfer of Bundled Intellectual Property – Web-based business model

3.1 Introduction - The traditional notion of software has been a company hiring engineers who sit in a building writing code to create a software program used for a specific purpose and such program once developed is sent to customers in the tangible form of CD’s or DVD’s. This model equated well with the assembly line manufacturing process and an age-old model of tangible products.

However, the above is not how a majority of software is developed nowadays; the Internet has brought forth new business model – both business to business (B2B) & business to consumer (B2C) models.

Today there exists "web" companies which are valued at billions of dollars whose "crown jewels" are usually the intangible intellectual property they own or their patented business models or their proprietary technology web-service platforms. Examples of such web companies are Google, Facebook, eBay5 2 etc.

3.2 A simple web-based business model - In this case study we take a web-based business model related to the online advertising market (also called SEM – Search Engine Marketing), one of the fastest growing markets in the world. This is similar to the case study presented in Elizabeth King’s case study on Replication of Internet-Based Business Model52.

Search engines like Google5 3 derive most of their income from such markets which allow advertisers to bid on keywords in an auction-model on their technology platforms; when users search for the keywords which have been bid upon they are shown text ads sorted in the descending order of their bid. Such a market gave rise to a host of web companies who provide service to advertisers to efficiently and optimally bid on millions of companies – they are essentially providing SEM solutions to online advertisers.

We consider a USA company, USCo, which provides SEM i.e. Search Engine Marketing solutions using its unique and patented algorithmic techniques for efficient and optimal bidding; in simple terms the company takes control of advertisers online campaigns of its clients and bids on keywords in the online advertisement marketplaces offered by search engines like Google Adwords54 . USCo’s clients are typically two-fold: companies who wants to advertise online to boost traffic to its website and sales of its products & services, advertising agencies who provide full-service to their clients and provide both offline (TV, newspapers etc.) & online advertising solutions for clients.

USCo has a successful and established business model and handles over $500 million in advertising spend on the various search engines. Parts of USCo’s business model are patented. Further, USCo has developed proprietary software for its internal usage – to process, analyze & model the huge amount of data it churns daily. USCo has also developed online marketing & solicitation tools which it uses to market to, obtain, test and sign-up clients.

Now an Indian company, lets call it IndCo, wants to replicate USCo’s business model in India. Towards this the top management gets training in USCo and on doing so provides the USCo’s business model of online advertising solutions to clients & ad agencies in India.

To summarize:

1.USCo transfers the intellectual property of its proprietary software modified to suit local conditions.

2.USCo also provides the right to use of its marketing and solicitation online tools to IndCo, again these pages have to be modified slightly for local conditions.

3.USCo will perform routine service, maintenance and upgrades on the proprietary software given to IndCo.

4.USCo will provide legal and financial planning and advisory services to IndCo.

5.IndCo has been issued the rights to use USCo’s trademark and name in the Indian market.

3.3 International taxation issues - The above model is akin to a business format franchise 70. The key question is what are the arm’s length services fees payable by IndCo to USCo?

The resale and cost-plus methods presuppose a particular division of labour that is not characteristic of the USCo and IndCo. The profit-comparison methods would require quasi-comparable companies in the same startup stage and would probably yield no residual profits to USCo.

Introduction

Technology has always been at the cutting edge of the significant transformation that is taking place in the market place today. Mobile technology, analytics, cloud computing and wearables have emerged as new forms of technology, and even several traditional companies have started to add capabilities in these areas to cater to the growing customer preferences. In this digital revolution, leading the pack is the e-commerce segment, which is driving rapid growth of domestic IT-ITeS industry and is attracting unprecedented levels of global interest, funding and talent. Owing to such rapid revolution and growth, India ranks third in start-ups formed in the technology industry globally.

Keeping in pace with the growth in this industry, the controversies surrounding taxation of digital transactions are also ever on the rise. Governments and tax administrators of many countries are constantly evaluating the tax implications arising on operations of such entities, since transactions of the e-commerce players raises several contentious tax issues due to absence of national boundaries, physical presence of goods and non-requirement of physical delivery. In India, there are innumerable tax issues faced by the technology industry and in the ensuing paragraphs we have discussed the populist ones.

1. Withholding tax issues on cross border payments involving software

Transactions in the technology industry such as payments for purchase or usage of software, payments for online advertising, app stores, cloud computing are under the tax radar. Such transactions could involve:

-

Transfer of rights in a property (such as right to alter or reproduce work or issue copies of the work);

-

Few transactions could involve payment for services such as access / subscription to databases, standardised applications, e-library, online games, music, news etc.; and

-

Certain transactions could be a combination of both transfer of property rights and services. For e.g. customised software or configurable computing resources such as networks, servers, storage, applications along with services made available to the users through the internet.

The taxation and the related withholding tax implications on such payments to non-residents would be based on the characterisation of such income (business income or royalty or fees for technical services) under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("the Act") read with the beneficial provisions of the tax treaty. Non-resident tax payers in several instances were seeking to characterise their income from such transactions as business income and offer the same to tax in India only where such income was attributable to a permanent establishment ("PE") in India. Hence, in order to curb such mischief, in the garb of a clarification, the Government brought in a retrospective amendment in the Act to widen the scope of definition of "Royalty". The amended definition of "Royalty" seeks to include transfer of any right to use a software including the granting of a license, irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred. This amendment significantly targets transactions involving payments for shrink-wrap or embedded software.

The issue of taxation of cross border software licensing transactions including payments towards access to databases, online applications etc. have been a significant bone of contention between the Indian Revenue authorities and the tax payers over the last decade.

Some of the key illustrative factors considered relevant by the Courts for determining the characterisation of income are listed below:

Nature of rights granted to the payee - Whether rights in the property is transferred or mere right of usage of property is conferred;

Nature of software - Customised vis-à-vis standardised software;

Whether the payment is towards the use or right to use a copyrighted article or a copyright in the article.

Degree of possession and control of the server / database / application;

Recourse to the service provider for the further requirement of any services;

Whether any specific configuration is carried out for the payee?

Whether any information is made available to the payee and right of further commercial exploitation is conferred on the payee?

Whether the payment is made for right other that right in the intellectual property?

Determination of taxability of transactions should be based on a holistic evaluation of the intention of the parties involved and the primary purpose for which the payment is being made. Issues on taxability of software payments along with taxation aspects of e-commerce transactions were extensively researched and opined upon by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development ("OECD") - Technical Advisory Group almost two decades back. However, India differed on most of the views of the OECD on this issue and currently maintains an enhanced observer status to the OECD. The views expressed by India are in variance with most of the developed countries on characterisation of income on software payments. The current action plans initiated by the OECD under the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting ("BEPS") also do not deal with such issues adding to the woes of the technology industry players.

Till now, the Tribunals have been holding that packaged software being ‘goods’, there was no need for the importer to deduct tax at source and that the payment towards procurement of the packaged software cannot be considered as ‘royalty’. However, this latest decision from the Karnataka High Court would supersede such Tribunals’ decisions, at least, for importers in Karnataka. 2.2 The facts of the case, in brief: Certain importers of software licenses had taken a view that the payments made for software imports would not attract the provisions of section 195 of the Income-tax Act, necessitating the deduction of tax at source, since such payments would not constitute taxable income in the nature of royalty or scientific work, in the hands of the non-resident, in terms of section 9(1)(vi) read with the DTAA. The First and Second Appellate Authorities had upheld the importers’ contention that when the payments would be for acquiring a right to use a copyright and not the copyright itself it would not get treated as royalty payments in terms of the DTAAs and, hence, there was no need for deducting tax at source under section 195. The Tribunal had also upheld the importers’ contention that the import of software licenses would be in the nature of a transaction involving import of goods, in the light of the precedents set by the various Courts including the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the TCS case. The revenue contended that software is a ‘scientific work’ and payments for import of software would be covered under section 9(1)(vi) of the Act and that the importer cannot contend that the payment made by him would not constitute income in the hands of the non-resident recipient and that, the importer is duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195.

2.3 The gist of the judgment: In a sweeping judgment, which is perhaps the first judgment from a High Court on the contentious issue related to the applicability of section 195 on software imports, the Karnataka High Court has rejected, in toto, the decisions of the Bangalore Tribunal in various similar judgments and has held that the importer was duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195 for import of software licenses, based almost exclusively, on the Apex Court’s judgment in Transmission Corporation of AP Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 105 Taxman 742. The High Court’s judgment in leads to the premise that the obligation to deduct tax at source under section 195 has nothing to do, with the actual liability of the non-resident to tax under the provisions of the Act, including the quantum thereof. The importer could take recourse to the provisions of section 195(2) if he is of the view that only a part of the payment made by him would bear the character of income in the hands of the non-resident.

2.4 The implications arising out of this judgment: Due to this ruling of the Karnataka High Court, all overseas payments will now be subject to withholding tax, whether or not the income is taxable. Not only is this in dramatic contrast to previous High Court’s decisions, it is also a judgment that will lead to higher cost of business, increased uncertainty and may be even more litigation—at Least for a while.

The law itself as it reads, which is section 195, specifically says that it is a sum which is chargeable to tax under the Income-tax Act on which tax has to be deducted at source, if that payment, of course, is being made to a non-resident. Based on that, for example, the Rajasthan High Court in the SBI case has taken a view that if income is exempt under provisions of the Indian Income-tax Act, one does not need to withhold tax at source at all when the payment is being made to non-resident of such an exempt income.

But now, a judgment by the Karnataka High Court has turned this established principle.

•In terms of this judgment, the importer has only two options before him, vis-à-vis the payments to be effected to the non-resident, viz. either to deduct tax at source under section 195 or to make an application to the Department under section 195(2). In terms of the judgment, this principle would apply equally to import of goods or to import of services or for transactions involving import of goods and services as in the case of a works contract.

•It would look like that importer cannot get into issues related to the applicability of section 9(1) or to the provisions of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA) for purposes of discharging his liability under section 195. In other words, in terms of this judgment, the provisions of section 195 are quite draconian, requiring the resident payer to deduct tax at source without getting into issues related to the taxation of the receipts, in the hands of the non-resident.

’ - Generally, the term ‘income’ in case of commercial activities is used in the sense of ‘profit from business’ or ‘gains from profession’, i.e. net amount after deducting allowable expenses. However, this is not the only sense in which the term ‘income’ has been understood or used either in Income Tax Act or in DTAA.

The word ‘income’ is often used in two senses, i.e. either gross amount received or net amount after deducting expenses. 12.5 DTAA applies to ‘gross receipts’ in many cases - In DTAA, ‘income’ is often understood as ‘gross receipts’ and not ‘net income’. Articles 7 and 8 of DTA agreement specifically speak about ‘business profits’. However, Article 12 speaks about ‘gross amount of royalties and fees for technical services’, Article 10 of DTA agreement speaks about ‘gross dividend’ and Article 11 speaks about ‘gross interest’.

12.6 Restrictions on tax on royalties and technical services - Article 12 of Convention with USA states that ‘Royalties and fees for ‘included services’ (term used for ‘technical services’) arising in a Contracting State and paid to a resident of the other Contracting State may be taxed in that other State’. Such royalties and fees for ‘included services’ may also be taxed in the Contracting State in which they arise and according to the laws of that State; but such tax on gross amount cannot exceed 15% of ‘gross amount’. [similar provision in Article 13 of DTA agreement with UK]. [‘Included services’ mean technical services].

In case of China and some other countries, the tax is 10%.

It may be noted that this amount is already collected as TDS under Income Tax provisions.

Can additional amount be collected as ‘service tax’ on royalties and technical services? - The amount of tax that can be collected under DTAA is already collected by Government of India under income tax provisions. The question is whether some additional amount can be collected as ‘service tax’ on royalty and technical services? Article 2(2) of Convention very clearly states that the convention applies to any identical or substantially similar taxes which are imposed after convention.

Charging service tax on gross amount of technical services provided by non-resident seems to be nothing but additional tax by different name.

Collecting the tax from service receiver means doing something indirectly which you cannot do directly, as effect of both is same.

12.7 Services provided by person who has no place of business in India - Article 7 of the convention with USA reads as follows, ‘The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to (a) that permanent establishment ; (b) sales in the other State of goods or merchandise of the same or similar kind as those sold through that permanent establishment ; or (c) other business activities carried on in the other State of the same or similar kind as those effected through that permanent establishment’.

Article 7(1) of Convention with UK reads as follows, ‘The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is directly or indirectly attributable to that permanent establishment’. [identical provision in Convention with China and many other countries].

Charging service tax on service provided by non-resident amounts to tax on ‘profits’ - Charging service tax on services provided by person who has no place of business in India means indirectly taxing ‘profits’ of non-resident. What cannot be directly, can as well not be done indirectly. As explained above, only the liability of payment of service tax has been shifted to service receiver in respect of services received from a non-resident. It may be noted that a person providing service abroad cannot charge ‘service tax’ in his invoice to the service receiver.

For example, if Income Tax Act provides that amounts paid for services to non-resident will not be allowable as ‘expenditure’ under Income Tax Act, it will amount to imposing a tax on services provided by non-resident. This would be the easiest way of getting over restrictions placed under DTA agreements.

Delhi High Court observed that the language of the India-Finland DTAA differed from amended section 9(1)(vi) and retrospective amendment could not be read into the treaty.

In November 2013, the Madras High Court, in the case of Verizon Communications Singapore (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 70, ruled that the amount paid by Indian companies to a foreign company for dedicated broadband services constituted "royalty" and ought to be taxed in India under the Income-tax Act as well as the India Singapore treaty. IBM and Sonata have now approached the Apex Court for determining whether packaged software can be taxed as royalty under DTAAs. It appears that only the verdict of the Supreme Court will put this debate to rest.

B. TRANSFER PRICING

Though transfer pricing is a relatively new area of law, we have all recently witnessed 2 high profile cases before the Bombay High Court that thrust the subject into limelight. Till a couple of years ago, only tax professionals dealing with international tax management/compliance of MNCs were concerned with the nuances of transfer pricing. However, there has been a noticeable change in this trend, with the print and electronic media reporting extensively on these cases. Suddenly, transfer pricing has become a topic of interest not only with most tax professionals but with the general public as well. The fact that transfer pricing has less to do with tax and more to do with market dynamics and economics definitely has a role to play in this development. But another, more important reason, for the increased interest in transfer pricing is the fact that most economies have started showing decreased tolerance to the practices adopted by MNCs for shifting profits to low tax jurisdictions, thereby depriving the "source countries" of their legitimate revenue. The vigour with which OECD is driving its Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) Action Plan and the frequency with which this problem is being discussed at international forums indicates the increasing concern of tax base erosion. Before I elaborate more on BEPS, I want to touch upon a few important issues that are currently in focus.

I. Vodafone II and Vodafone III before Bombay High Court

It seems that any litigation involving 'Vodafone' can never be a low-key affair. If foreign investors complained of flip flops on indirect share transfers in 2012, subjecting share issue transactions to transfer pricing provisions left them 'Shell Shocked' in 2013.

In a detailed judgment of 239 pages, the Bombay High Court cleared the air on some important procedural aspects in the realm of transfer pricing, including the powers of the AO, TPO and DRP. In this case popularly termed as "Vodafone II", the High Court clarified that the AO is not only bound by the TPO's decision in respect of ALP computation, but is also bound by the TPO's decision as regards the character of the transaction i.e. whether or not the transaction is an 'international transaction.' The High Court also held that the powers of the DRP are wide enough to consider all questions of fact/law raised before it. The DRP's power to 'confirm' a transfer pricing adjustment would also include the power 'not to confirm' the same, thereby empowering it to annul the variations as well.

Maintenance of branch outside India

10. Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012 reads as follows - An establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

This Explanation has been given to definition of 'service'. In fact, this Explanation has nothing to do with definition of 'service' and is at a wrong place.

However, this Explanation is creating lot of difficulties (may be mainly because it has been placed at a wrong place). This Explanation is being interpreted to mean that HO in India and branch outside India are two different 'persons'. Hence, if the HO in India remits money to maintain branch outside India, it will be treated as 'import of service' i.e. branch outside India is providing service to Head Office in India.

Really, 'shall be treated as establishment of different persons' does not mean 'shall be treated as two different persons'.

Thus, Branch/office in India and branch/office of same business entity outside India will be treated as different 'establishments' and not 'different persons'.

A branch received service from its other branch outside India will not be subject to service tax under reverse charge mechanism as 'import of service', as they are not different persons.

Similarly, a branch in India cannot 'export' service to its branch outside India.

Royalties in general means the payment made to the owners of certain types of rights by those who are permitted by the owners to exercise the rights. The term originated from the fact that in Great Britain for centuries gold and silver mines were the property of the Crown and such 'royal' metals could be mined only if a payment ("Royalty") were made to the Crown.

Royalties thus reflect usage-based payments made by one party (the "licensee") to another (the "licensor") for ongoing use of intangible or tangible assets. Intangible assets are defined as identifiable non-monetary assets that cannot be seen, touched or physically measured, which are created through time and/or effort and that are identifiable as a separate asset. There are two primary forms of intangibles - legal intangibles (such as trade secrets (e.g., customer lists), copyrights, patents, trademarks, and goodwill) and competitive intangibles (such as knowledge activities (know-how, knowledge, collaboration activities, leverage activities, and structural activities). Royalties can be determined as a percentage of gross or net sales derived from use of the asset or a fixed price per unit sold. Further, there also exist other modes and metrics of compensation.

The cross border transactions have given rise to tax controversies, which are pending adjudications before the Tribunals and Courts in India.

The first leg of the controversy relates to the taxability of the foreign entity, granting the rights. When the user of the right, property or information is resident in one country say India and pays royalties to the owner thereof who is resident in another country say the USA, the amount paid by the user is generally subject to withholding tax in India, the source country. The basic challenge, which is pending before courts relates the characterisation of the certain payments. While the taxpayer contends that the payment received is in lieu of services and not grant of rights, the Revenue Authorities contends otherwise. The most talked about controversy here relates to transmission of data through undersea cables, satellites etc. Other could be where the taxpayer contends that there is transfer of rights in perpetuity and hence the transaction qualifies a sale. The most talked about controversy here relates to usage of off the shelf software products.

The second leg of controversy relates to the treatment of the cost incurred in the hands of the Indian user entity. For the purposes of this article, we are limiting the discussion to the transfer pricing challenges, which arise when the transaction is between two related entities of the group.

Take a simple scenario, a manufacturing enterprise or an inventor may have incurred substantial sums on the development of the property generating the royalties. However, the work of research and testing involves considerable capital outlays and does not always yield successful results. The issue lies in determining an appropriate arm's length return for using such property, which is rather complex. The Revenue Authorities generally raise the challenge from a variety of perspectives, such as (a) why user entity per se has taken up the right; (b) what is the technology granted and how it has benefited the Indian entity; and (c) how to determine the arm's length price.

In this article, we have taken a deep dive into these controversies.

CONTROVERSIES DISSECTED

One of the typical situations giving rise to the transfer pricing controversy involves a Foreign Multinational Group licensing technology/know-how to its Indian affiliate and charging a bundled Royalty. The Indian affiliate would deploy the technology in the manufacturing process and; thereafter would undertake selling and distribution function selling goods under the brand name of the Foreign Multinational Group. In lieu of the rights granted, Indian affiliate would pay a Royalty charge, of say 5%, which will be computed on its net sales. The entities would document their understanding through a written agreement.

The Revenue Authorities generally makes the following assertions upon encountering the above situation:

(a)

The taxpayer has not been able to provide substantial evidence of any tangible benefit arising from the use of such rights and as to why it entered into such an arrangement;

(b)

The taxpayer have not been able to demonstrate that its profits have increased, by use of technology or brand name and no cost benefit analysis was furnished;

(c)

The taxpayer has used Regulatory guidelines to justify the royalty rate and such treatment lacks judicial approval;

(d)

The taxpayer has failed to produce contemporary data, justifying the rate of royalty payout.

With the aid of some or all the assertions, Revenue Authorities at times adjudicate that value of such royalty payment charge is NIL.

In subsequent paragraphs, we deal with some of the key propositions which could be used to defend and justify the royalty payout.

(i) Test of commercial expediency

However, this argument is bound to fail in view of the very specific provisions under service tax laws. The Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infotech Software Dealers Association has held that transaction in relation to canned/off-the-shelf software can be service in case the developer of software retains the copyright while right to use of software is given to the subscriber. The scenario has become grave for the dealers who prior to introduction of service tax were charging only sales tax on the value of software. Now in view of the specific category under service tax, they need to charge both sales tax and service tax. Since the sales tax and service tax are indirect taxes and to avoid litigation, the dealers tend to charge both the taxes and it is only the end - consumer who has to suffer in view of multiplicity of taxes.

As regards the customized/uncanned software, the contract for development of such software perhaps at the best may be viewed as a service contract. The customized software means software developed for a specific customer to meet his specific requirements. The software industry prior to the introduction of new category of taxable service in the name of 'Information Technology Software Service' was at an advantageous position, as no indirect taxes were applicable on the development of customized software treating it as a service contract. However, the advantageous position got diluted after the introduction of new category as above, as now development of customized software attracts service tax. The dilution has further been deepened after the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. in which it has been held that even customized software may qualify as goods.

The sales tax authorities after taking recourse to the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court are issuing notices demanding tax on the transaction involving development of software. The judgment has opened a Pandora's Box of litigations in relation to customized/uncanned software.

Another area of litigation concerning software is supply of software through electronic downloads. In such a scenario, service tax gets attracted in view of the specific language of the taxable service under the category of 'Information Technology Software Service'. However, whether sales tax is also payable is another point where litigation surrounds the software industry. The Hon'ble Karnataka High Court recently in the case of Sasken Communication Technologies Ltd. has observed that intellectual property once put on a medium becomes goods and when transferred is leviable to sales tax. After this judgment, the industry players can hope that the sales tax authorities do not litigate on this issue.

The menace of double taxation is detrimental to the interests of users of goods/services as it results into high procurement costs, especially in those cases where credit of input taxes paid cannot be taken by the users. The domestic users only take a hit as the exporters of software generally enjoy the tax free status and, accordingly, no taxes are charged on the value of goods/services exported from India. Presently, the sales tax (local VAT) rate for software is either at 4% or at 5% and service tax rate is at 10%, which can significantly enhance the costs of procurements in case software suffers double taxation, specifically in cases where the credit of input taxes is not available either in full or in part.

Though the laws on sales tax and service tax are on the statute books for good number of years now, yet the provisions of these laws need alignment, which seems to be an uphill task in view of the fact that the Governments desire to garner more and more revenue and sometimes it happens by introducing provisions which put the taxpayer in a situation where he has no alternative but to resort to litigation.

2.2 Issues regarding Classification - Another controversy that surrounds the software revolves around its classification, especially in those cases where the software is not embedded in the hardware and is procured separately from the vendor of the hardware. The problem is generally faced by the importers of telecom equipments.

At present, the rate of customs duty on telecom equipments is generally at around 15% and on software it is at around 10% in case it is imported say on CD. Due to the difference in the rate of customs duty, the customs authorities always litigate on the genuineness of the imports and try to include the value of software in the value of hardware and, accordingly, make the value of software suffer higher rate of customs duty. This particular issue of telecom industry is yet to test the scrutiny of judiciary but apparently, both hardware and software are classifiable into different customs tariff classifications and different customs duty structure is also justifiable.

2.3 Issues regarding Withholding Tax - Another issue that hovers around software is whether the payments remitted by a resident to a non-resident for software can be said to be one for use of copyright or can be categorised as one for copyrighted article. The issue has over a period of time been interpreted differently by the Appellate Tribunals across India. In case, the amount is categorised as royalty, the Indian entity making the payment is required to do withholding of tax under section 195 of the Income-tax Act.

The Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Novel Inc. v. Dy. DIT [2011] 16 taxmann.com 186 has held that payments made by the Indian distributors to a non-resident for procuring rights to further sell the software to customers in India would not amount to royalty.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import. The payments made by HCL to SAP India were in relation post-importation activities. Pursuant to the import of the CD containing the software, HCL paid license fee to SAP India for obtaining license key codes to unlock the full version of the software upon expiry of trial period. Hence, the license fee was not a condition of sale for the import of CDs containing software.

This apart, right to use the software is different from the sale of goods and HCL is only provided a non-exclusive right to use the SAP Software. Thus, there is no "sale".

As a result, the Tribunal held that the license fee paid by HCL to SAP India could not be included in the valuation of imported CDs containing software. Consequently, duty demand, interest and penalties were set aside.

Why does this case matter?

This judgment sheds clarity and sets a sound precedent that not every overenthusiastic attempt to automatically include license fee/royalty is appropriate – especially when these payments don't meet the strict statutory criteria under Rule 9(1)(c) of the CVR.

The judgment decisively burst several prevalent myths regarding the inclusion of license fee/royalty payments in customs valuation: Myth#1: License fee/royalty must always be included in value of the imported goods if the same is part of the agreements; Myth#2: License fee/royalty for obtaining additional licenses post-import of the goods, must be included for the purposes of Customs Valuation; Myth#3: Electronic delivery of software is treated the same as physical import for Customs purposes; and Myth#4: "Right to use" the imported goods is same as that of "sale of goods."

The Tribunal arrived at such conclusions on the basis of the specific terms mentioned in the EULA. In essence, the judgment highlights that assessing the inclusion of license fee/royalty in valuation of the imported goods is akin to reading fine print under a magnifying glass—every detail in the agreement can shift the outcome. Thus, each licensing agreement needs a careful, case-by-case look to decide if the license fee/royalty emanating therefrom becomes a part of customs valuation.

Beyond the Judgement: Practical Insights for Importers

This struggle isn't just about numbers or tax compliance. It's about language of the agreement. Misinterpretation could mean hefty penalties, but overzealous inclusion of license fee/royalty in the valuation of the imported goods could suffocate the cost structure of businesses. Every contract clause is dissected with the precision once reserved for engineering specs: Is this a 'condition of sale'? Does the license fee payment flow directly to the seller? Could it be included in the transaction value of the imported goods and consequently trigger customs duty?

Given the wide variety of contractual arrangements, it is essential to closely examine each agreement to determine whether any license fee/royalty is includible in the transaction value of the imported goods. If the contract or agreement is still in the drafting stage, it becomes even more critical to analyse these clauses thoroughly to ensure that the correct legal course is taken. Ultimately, it is best to review each of your agreements to ensure a sound risk management for imports.

Navigating the landscape of valuation for the imports

In the complex world of imports, businesses often consider the value of the physical goods to be paramount. However, they sometimes overlook that beyond the physical cargo lies something less visible yet crucial — the royalty/license fee payments. Royalties arise from licensing agreements which grant the importer rights inter alia to use manufacturing know-how, brand names, or software embedded within imported goods.

As the nature of contracts pertaining to imports/exports and associated license fee/royalty has evolved, the Customs valuation has also come a long way. Once upon a time, a physical shipment was all that customs authorities cared about for determining its value and imposition duties. Today's imports bundle licensed software, technology, trademarks, and other rights, making valuation of such shipments more complicated. While the goods themselves represent the tangible aspect for customs valuation, the accompanied intangible rights and their payments may significantly contribute to the overall value of the import transaction. This evolution sets the stage for courts to demystify when license fee/royalty should be included in the transaction value of the imported goods.

The recent judgement by CESTAT, New Delhi in the judgment of HCL Technologies Ltd. and SAP India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication) [Final Order No. 51379-51462 of 2025 dated 29-9-2025] bring these complexities to the forefront. It deals with critical questions regarding includability of license fee in the value of the imported goods, specifically in the context of delivery of software through physical and electronic media.

Under the Lens: CESTAT's approach in the case of HCL Technologies Ltd.

Facts at a Glance

HCL Technologies Ltd. ('HCL') entered into an End-User License Agreement ('EULA') with SAP India Private Limited ('SAP India') to obtain non-exclusive and perpetual license to use propriety software, documentation and other information of SAP India. As per terms of the EULA, the software was to be delivered electronically. In the year 2006, SAP India raised substantial invoices on HCL for payment of license fee relating to rights provided under the EULA.

During the same time, HCL received some imported CDs containing SAP Software via courier, wherein a nominal value was declared under the courier bill of entry, for customs purposes. Perhaps, this is what caught the eye of the Customs Department – A CD with a software... only for pocket change?

An investigation was initiated against inter alia HCL for such imports. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Customs Department rejected the declared value of the CDs under Rule 10A of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 ('CVR') [now Rule 14 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] and sought to include the license fee in the valuation of imported CDs in terms of Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR.

The allegation of the Customs Department was that unless the license fee is paid, the software on the CD cannot be accessed or used; thereby, making the license fee integral to the transaction value of the imported CDs.

Tribunal's Verdict: Four Conditions for Royalty Inclusion in Customs Valuation

The Tribunal determined that for inclusion of royalties to the value of the imported goods, the following four key conditions under Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR needed to be satisfied:

1.

The license fee must relate to the imported goods;

2.

The fee must be payable directly or indirectly by the importer at the time of import;

3.

The license fee must be a condition of sale of the goods; and

4.

The fee must not already be included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods.

Guided by these conditions, the Tribunal took a closer look at the terms of the EULA entered between HCL&SAP India, and made the following findings:

The license fee was not related to the physical import of the CDs; rather, it was related to the intangible right to use the software in India. The EULA had itself provided electronic delivery as the mode of delivery of the software. Thus, the license fee was for usage of software rights and not for the import of physical CDs themselves.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import.

Revenue contended that the protocol appended to the subject DTAA showed that the benefit of the lower rate of withholding tax would be available only if the country with which India entered into a DTAA were a member of the OECD at the time of the execution of the subject DTAA. On writ, Delhi High Court held that a bare perusal of Clause IV(2) of the protocol appended to the subject DTAA shows that it incorporates the principle of parity between the subject DTAA and the DTAAs executed thereafter. However, the principle of parity kicks-in, only if the third State with whom India enters into a DTAA is a member of the OECD. Once the aforementioned conditions are fulfilled, then, from the date on which the DTAA between India and a third State comes into force, the same rate of withholding tax or scope as provided in the DTAA executed between India and the third State would necessarily have to apply to the subject DTAA.

Therefore, the beneficial withholding tax rate of 5% in India-Slovenia DTAA will apply from the date when Slovenia became an OECD member, i.e., from August 2010. However, India - Slovenia DTAA came into force in February 2005.

The assessee was a tax resident of the USA. Assessee earned income from cloud services, including cloud hosting and other supporting and ancillary services provided to Indian Customers. The assessee filed the return of income and the notes stating that the cloud hosting services were not taxable as 'royalties' under Article 12 of the India-US tax treaty.

The Mumbai ITAT held that the agreement between the assessee and its customer was for providing hosting and other ancillary services to the customer and not for the use of or leasing of any equipment.

The Data Centre and the Infrastructure therein were used to provide these services belonging to the assessee. The agreement was to provide simpliciter hosting services and not give the underlying equipment on hire or lease. The customer did not know any server location in the data centre, webmail, websites, etc.

Thus, the income from cloud hosting services had erroneously been held as royalty within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) as well as article 12(3)(b) of the India-USA DTAA by AO and DRP.

The Mumbai Tribunal held that its difficult to visualize an SPV in isolation with the owner of that structure. The Assessing Officer (AO) held that the excess profit worked out in the context of TP was not entitled for deduction under Section 10A of the Act. The Tribunal ruled that the anti-avoidance provisions contained in Chapter X of the Act are a separate code enacted for the specific purpose of computing income from international transactions having regard to the ALP. Any adjustment that the AO would like to make with reference to the income would have to be made independent of the order of TPO. THE DOCUMENTATION PROCESS

NEED FOR DOCUMENTATION

4. Transfer pricing calculation produces at least two consequences. First, it puts national tax jurisdictions under stress because it is an income-shifting system that allows MNEs to maximize their after-tax profits by channelling their taxable income to low tax jurisdictions. Second, it provides a substantial advantage to MNEs in comparison with non-multinational firms because only the former can use that strategy.1 0

Tax jurisdictions are constantly challenged to ensure that MNEs do not take undue advantage of their exposure vis-a-vis a localized operator. The only way to guarantee that a MNE is playing by the rules is through proper assessment of its cross-border transactions. That is possible through a detailed study of the company’s functions, assets, and risks that are distributed across tax jurisdictions because those three factors will ulti- mately determine where the profit should be taxed. Thus, there is a need for detailed documentation providing not only the details of the related-party cross-border transaction, but also a logical justification of the prices charged for the transaction.

4.1 ARM’S LENGTH PRINCIPLE - That brings one to the concept of arm’s length principle, which simply means replicating an open market where transactions occur between unrelated entities. It is the principle or international standard that OECD member countries have agreed should be used for determining transfer prices for tax purposes. As mentioned in the OECD guidelines:

Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention : where ‘conditions are made or imposed between the two enterprises in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enterprises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly.’

The arm’s length principle implies that the profits of an MNE should follow where the company has the bulk of its functions, assets, and risks. That is the basic principle, a common underlying concept that most tax authorities across jurisdictions tend to comply with and incorporate as the basis of their transfer pricing principles. A tax authority in any jurisdiction would correctly expect to see a corresponding share of the profit.

The arm’s length principle is equally applicable whether one is dealing with the transfer of tangible goods, intangibles, or services between related parties. The facts and circumstances of each case and the nature of the related-party transactions that are being considered, however, dictate the nuances of application of the principle. While there may be significant variations in the expectations of tax authorities on the documentation requirements, which are usually determined based on each jurisdiction’s tax legislation, some fundamentals do remain the same. For instance, one of the best ways to prove that royalties paid for the transfer of an intangible are at arm’s length is to find comparable arm’s length agreements in the wider marketplace. Also, for a transfer of value added services, it is always preferable to find comparable service transactions between unrelated third parties to prove that the charges paid for the services rendered are at arm’s length. From our experience in the field of transfer pricing documentation for various industries (software, automobile, lumber, rubber, and so on) and for the various types of transactions, it is advisable to use the assistance from experts in the field while preparing documentation to be presented to the tax authorities.

The tax treatment of the Permanent Establishment in such a case is under consideration in this circular. During the last decade or so, India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated enterprises of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision of services itself like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. The non-resident entity or the foreign company will be liable to tax in India only if the IT-enabled BPO unit in India constitutes its Permanent Establishment. The extent to which the profit of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board.

A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc. or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment become taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as are attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deduction expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if, instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm’s length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profits that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm’s length principle".

"Arm’s length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(iii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm’s length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.

Status of BPO entity

8. The BPO entity in India carrying on the outsourcing activities for a non-resident company, may be its branch or subsidiary company or an independent company.

A branch connotes a physical presence of the foreign enterprise in India. It is an office with an independent administration. Where a non-resident has an office in India and employs staff to carry on its business, it is its branch. A branch office is not regarded as a separate legal entity. Its profits are the profits of a company owning the branch office. It is different from a subsidiary which has a legal entity of its own - CIT v. Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. [1987] 165 ITR 416 (Cal.)—and which is regarded as a domestic company in the country where it is established. The subsidiary company may be a branch office of a foreign establishment under certain circumstances. If it is engaged in transactions with or on behalf of the foreign enterprise as an agent of the parent company in circumstances pointing out to a trading in a host country, it can be said to be performing functions on behalf of that enterprise in the same way as any could do - Fire Stone Tyre and Rubber Co. Ltd. v. Lewellin 37 TC 111. To that extent the subsidiary is the branch office of the foreign enterprise, in spite of it having independent and own legal status.

Section 9 which extends the scope of taxation laid down under section 5 of the ITA, states that "all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India6, or through or from any property in India, or through or from any asset or source of income in India, or through the transfer of a capital asset situate in India" would be deemed to accrue or arise in India. The most significant condition for extended scope of taxation is that there should be "business connection" in India. This term has not been defined in the ITA. Aggarwal & Co.7 which was before Circular 23 was issued, the Apex Court held that there should be a real and intimate relation between trading activity carried on outside the taxable territories and trading activity carried on within the territories.

The ITA explains that if all the operations are not carried out in India then entire income will not be liable to taxation in India. Explanation 1( a) to section 9(1)(i) reads as follows :

"in the case of a business of which all the operations are not carried out in India, the income of the business deemed under this clause to accrue or arise in India shall be only such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India."

A combined reading of section 9(1)(i), the views expressed by the Supreme Court of India in the case of R. D. Aggarwal and the above Explanation, leads to the conclusion that the income of a non-resident will be liable to taxation in India only when the trading activity in India and the trading activity outside India, have real and intimate relationship. Further, only that income would be taxable in India which can be reasonably attributed to the operations carried out in India. In fact, the OECD subscribes to similar views.

OECD Model Tax Convention on PE and Transfer Pricing

It has been internationally accepted that the source country should not tax income of a foreign entity unless there is some longer economic relationship between the source country and the entity. This has been incorporated in the OECD Model tax treaty. Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of the Model states: "The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to that permanent establishment." When it comes to defining the term "permanent establishment" ("PE") Article 5 identifies the following categories – fixed PE, service PE and agency PE. So far as the first PE is concerned, broadly speaking, there is requirement of permanent relationship. Agency PE requires the agent to be dependent and some more conditions to be satisfied. Similarly, for service PE to exist, the services provided by a foreign entity should be over a sufficiently longer period and should satisfy certain conditions.

The authorized OECD approach on attribution of income to permanent establishments (July 2008) has led to an interplay between PE and the transfer pricing approaches. The authorized OECD approach rests on the foundation of Article 7(1) and Article 7(2) of the OECD Model Tax convention. As mentioned above, Article 7 (1) permits the host country to tax the "profits of the enterprise" but only so much as is "attributable to" a PE in the host country. Article 7(2) states that the profits to be attributed to the PE are the profits "it might be expected" to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a part.

Based on the above, the authorized OECD approach prescribes a two step approach for attributing profits to a PE. Step 1 is to hypothesize the PE as a "functionally separate entity" and Step 2 is to compute arm’s length remuneration as per the OECD transfer pricing guidelines.

Payment of Royalties and Technology Fees to Foreign Affiliates

Typically, the Indian manufacturer would tend to rely primarily on the technical know-how, technical assistance and training provided by their foreign affiliates for its manufacturing operations, for a significant period of operations.

Further, one or more foreign affiliates could invest continuously and substantially in research and development activities which benefit, the Indian manufacturer, who is completely dependent on the affiliates for the technology required for the manufacturing operations.

The royalty and fee arrangements need to be carefully constructed. The arrangements must reflect the commercial reality of the underlying transaction, and must correspond to what independent parties are likely to agree in arm's length dealings.

From a documentation perspective, it is necessary to elaborately document the precise nature of the intangible and/or the technology support received from the foreign affiliate. The valuation of the intangible (if and to the extent possible), use of the intangible in the value chain, significance of the intangible etc., should also be thoroughly evaluated and documented. The benefits derived by the Indian manufacturer from use of the intangible, including process improvement, quality improvement, cost savings, etc. should also be documented, and if possible, even quantified.

The arm's length nature of these payments has been disputed by the Indian revenue authorities in several cases by questioning the commercial expediency and the quantum of benefit derived by the Indian entity. In cases where Indian taxpayers have been unable to substantiate the benefits received by them, the revenue authorities have been determining the arm's length price for such payments as NIL. This approach of the authorities has also been upheld in few cases where the taxpayer was not able to substantiate the rationale or benefits from the royalty payments6.

Further, the royalty/fee arrangements need to be evaluated regularly to confirm that they continue being relevant from an arm's length perspective, for the period for which royalties/fees are being paid. For instance, assume that a certain technology was provided to the Indian manufacturer in year 1 and a royalty was charged for use of the technology. Further, assume that this technology became obsolete in Year 10, or that it started becoming freely available (say, due to expiration of the underlying patent or otherwise) starting Year 10. The MNE group must re-examine if in these circumstances, whether any royalty indeed ought to be paid by the Indian manufacturer, starting Year 10 under arm's length circumstances.

Another aspect to be considered here is that in a case where the Indian manufacturer is able to generate some intangibles (for instance, improved designs or processes) as a part of its manufacturing process, and the said intangible is then provided to other manufacturing units of the MNE group, in arm's length circumstances, the Indian manufacturer could also be entitled to a remuneration for allowing the use of intangibles developed by it.

Imports from Foreign Affiliates

Machinery and equipments needed for a new manufacturing facility could be imported from abroad. Especially in cases where an existing manufacturing plant is being relocated to India, a vast majority of the machinery and equipments could be imported from overseas affiliates. These can either be used or new machinery/equipments. The Indian transfer pricing regulations provide for determination of arm's length price of such capital purchases also.

The machinery and equipments imported from foreign affiliates need to be valued by a valuation expert. Especially in cases of used machinery, the written down value of the machinery in the books of the foreign affiliate may not necessarily be the correct indication of the arms length price of the machinery. The arm's length price of such machinery needs to be determined based on the current commercial valuation of the machinery, considering options, if available, in the market for similar machinery. Quotations from independent third parties could also serve as useful guides for approximating the arm's length price of the machinery. In any case, a balance needs to be maintained between the valuation requirements under the transfer pricing regulations and Customs regulations. Any imbalance in valuation/pricing could lead to additional tax cost under either set of applicable regulations.

Similarly, in the initial period, the Indian manufacturer might not be able to localize its raw material requirements, and consequently, it may be dependent on its foreign affiliates for its raw material requirements. Again, the pricing policy for such raw materials needs to balance the requirements under Transfer Pricing and Customs Regulations.

CONCEPT OF PERMANENT ESTABLISHMENT

5. The concept of PE was introduced into the Income-tax Act, 1961 as part of the statutory provisions of transfer pricing by the Finance Act, 2001. In section 92F(iii), the word ‘enterprise’ is defined to mean ‘a person including a PE of such person who is proposed to be engaged in any activity relating to the production’. The CBDT Circular No. 14 of 2001 has clarified that the term P.E. has not been defined in the Act, but its meaning may be understood with reference to the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) entered into by India. The article 5 of the DTAA1 4, which India enters into with other countries, lays down that ‘a permanent establishment means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on’. Thus, the intention was to rely upon the concept and definition of PE in the DTAA.

However, vide the Finance Act, 2002 the definition of PE was inserted in the Income-tax Act, 1961 vide section 92F (iiia) which states that the PE shall include a fixed place of business through which the business of the Multi National Enterprise (MNE) is wholly or partly carried on. The difference lies therein between the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the inclusive sense under the Income-tax Act as against the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the exhaustive sense under the DTAA. This analysis is important because it indicates the intention of the Parliament in adopting an inclusive definition of PE so as to cover all forms of PE inclusive of service PE, agency PE, software PE, Construction PE, etc.

In a ruling given by the Authority for Advance Rulings, India (‘AAR’), the AAR has held that a subsidiary may be regarded as a PE, if it does not have significant independent activities of its own.15 In another ruling, the AAR has held that if the agent does not have the authority to conclude contract, then he cannot constitute a PE16 . However, on the other hand, if the parent executes mass contracts made on standard forms without being scrutinized by it, then the agent may constitute a PE. The Supreme Court of India in DIT (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc.1 7 [2007] 162 Taxman 165 has gone a long way in demystifying the concept of permanent establishment in India.

THE DOCUMENTATION PROCESS

NEED FOR DETAILED DOCUMENTATION

4. Transfer pricing calculation produces at least two conse quences: Firstly, it puts national tax jurisdictions under stress because it is an income-shifting system that allows multination als to maximize their after-tax profits by channelling their taxable income to low tax jurisdictions. Secondly, it provides a substantial advantage to multinationals in comparison with non-multinational firms because only the former can use this strate gy.10

Tax jurisdictions are thus constantly challenged to ensure that MNEs do not take undue advantage of their exposure vis-a-vis a localized operator. The only way to guarantee that an MNE is playing by the rule is through proper assessment of their cross-border transactions. This is possible through a detailed study of the company’s functions, assets and risks that are distributed across tax jurisdictions, as these three factors will ultimately determine where the profit should be taxed. Thus the need for a detailed documentation providing not only the details of the related party cross-border transaction, but also a logical justi fication of the prices charged for the transaction.

ARM’S LEGNTH PRINCIPLE

5. This brings us to the concept of arm’s length principle, which simply means replicating the working of an open market where transactions occur between unrelated entities. It is the princi ple or international standard that the OECD member countries have agreed should be used for determining transfer prices for tax purposes. As mentioned in the OECD Guidelines:

It is set forth in Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention as follows: where "conditions are made or imposed between the two enterprises in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enter prises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly".

The arm’s length principle implies that the profits of an MNE should follow where the company has the bulk of its functions, assets and risks. This is the basic principle, a common underly ing concept that most tax authorities across jurisdictions tend to comply with and incorporate as the basis of their transfer pricing principles. A tax authority in any jurisdiction would correctly expect to see a corresponding share of the profit.
