to 'royalty' is as follows:-

- payment of any kind received as a consideration for the use of or the right to use, any copyright of literary, artistic or scientific work.

It has been universally accepted that a literary work is entitled to copyright and, wherefore, a literary work is entitled to be registered as copyright. Under section 2(o ) of the Copyright Act, 1957, computer software has been recognized as copyright work in India also. [Para 19] In the instant case, in the software licence agreement, it is averred that customer accepts an individual, non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use the licensed software program(s) program(s) on the terms and conditions enumerated in the agreement. It is further averred that the customer-assessee shall protect confidential information and shall not remove any copyright, confidentiality or other proprietary rights provided by the non-resident. However, what is granted under the said licence is only a licence to use the software for internal business without having any right for making any alteration or reverse engineering or creating sub-licences. What is transferred under the said licence is the licence to use the software and copyright continue to be with the non-resident as per the agreement, Even as per the agreement entered into with the other distributors as also the end-user licence agreement, it is clear that the distributor would get exclusive non-transferable licence within the territory for which he is appointed and he has got right to distribute via resellers the software, upon payment of the licenses set forth in the agreement only to end-users pursuant to a valid actuate shrink wrap or other actuate license agreement and except as expressly set forth in the said agreement, distributor may not rent, lease, loan, sell or otherwise distribute the software the documentation or any derivative works based upon the software or documentation in whole or in part. Distributor shall not reverse engineer, decompile, or otherwise attempt to derive or modify the source code for the software. Distributor shall have no rights to the software other than the rights expressly set forth in the agreement. Distributor shall not modify or copy any part of the software or documentation. Distributor may not use sub-distributors for further distribution of the software and documentation without the prior consent of actuate. What is charged is the licence fee to be paid by the distributor of the software as enumerated in the agreement. Further, clause 6.01 of the agreement dealing with title states that the distributor acknowledges that actuate and its suppliers retain all rights, title and interest in and to the original, and any copies (by whomever produced), of the software or documentation and ownership of all patent copyright, trademark, trade secret and other intellectual property rights pertaining thereto, shall be and remain the sole property of actuate. Distributor shall not be an owner of any copies of, or any interest in, the software, but rather is licenced pursuant to the agreement to use and distribute such copies. Actuate represents that it has the right to enter into the agreement and grant the licences provided therein and confidentiality is protected. Therefore, on reading the contents of the respective agreement entered into by the assessee with the non-resident, it is clear that under the agreement, what is transferred is only a licence to use the copyright belonging to the non-resident subject to the terms and conditions of the agreement as referred to above and the non-resident supplier continues to be the owner of the copyright and all other intellectual property rights. If is well-settled that copyright is a negative right. It is an umbrella of many rights and licence is granted for making use of the copyright in respect of shrink wrapped software/off-the-shelf software under the respective agreement, which authorizes the end user, i.e., the customer to make use of the copyright software contained in the said software, which is purchased off the shelf or imported as shrink wrapped software and the same would amount to transfer of part of the copyright and transfer of right to use the copyright for internal business as per the terms and conditions of the agreement. Therefore, the contention of the assessee that there is no transfer of copyright or any part thereof under the agreements entered into by it with the non-resident supplier of software cannot be accepted. [Para 20]

It is well-settled that the intent of the Legislature in imposing sales tax and income-tax are entirely different as income tax is a direct tax and sales tax is an indirect tax and, wherefore, mere finding that the computer software would be included within the term 'sales tax" would not preclude the Court from holding that the said payments made by the assessee to the non-resident company in the instant case would amount to 'royalty' unless the assessee is able to prove that the said payment is for the sale of computer software, wherein the income would be from the business and in the absence of any permanent establishment of the non-resident supplier, there is no obligation on the part of the payee to make deduction under section 195(1). [Para 22]

, it would not be legally correct to state that the copyright itself or right to use copyright has been transferred to any extent. Thus as the assessee had only been granted a non-exclusive and non-transferable license to use the copyrighted article i.e 'Blaze advisor' software by its AE which had retained with itself the copyrights of the same, the amount received by the licensor its AE from the assessee did not give rise to any royalty income within the meaning of article 12(3). The remittance of USD 100,000 made by the assessee to Fair for grant of license to the assessee to use its copyrighted product viz. As no liability was cast upon the assessee to deduct tax at source at the time of making of the aforesaid remittance, hence the latter cannot be held as being an assessee in default within the meaning of section 201.

headnotes.text: Section 9 ,  read with sections 195 and 40(a)(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee company claimed Rs. 93.63 lakhs towards Software expenses paid to its parent company, Atmel Corporation, USA, however it had not deducted TDS on ground that mere reimbursement of expenses on cost to cost basis without any mark-up did not attract TDS under section 195 - However, Assessing Officer was of opinion that it was payment in nature of royalty as per provisions of section 9(1)(vi) and since software was used in India for purpose of business or profession carried on by assessee in India, he invoked provisions of section 195 and disallowed expenditure since there was no deduction of TDS - Assessee contended that it was only purchase of software to use in assessee's business and it had not acquired copyright of programme- Further, revenue was also not able to show that assessee had got any right to use copyright as software programme - Whether thus where assessee made payment for acquisition of software from its parent company to be used for its business purpose only, without any right of utilizing copyright of said programme, payment made in respect of same did not give rise to any royalty income - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee made payment for acquisition of software from its parent company to be used for its business purpose only, without any right of utilizing copyright of said programme, payment made in respect of same did not give rise to any royalty income

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the India-USA DTAA- Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Others) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in healthcare business for General Electric (GE) group - In year under dispute, assessee received certain amount towards software licence fee cross charged to its affiliates in India which was not offered to tax in India by assessee being reimbursement from affiliates -- Whether since what had been sold to affiliates was copyrighted article and not any right to use copyright, receipts in dispute could not be taxable as royalty income falling under article 12 and alternatively, it could have been taxed as business income under article 7, however, in absence of a Permanent Establishment (PE), it could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 19 and 20] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a tax resident of USA, received certain amount towards software licence fee cross charged to its affiliates in India, since what had been sold to affiliates was copyrighted article and not any right to use copyright, receipts in dispute could not be taxable as royalty income falling under article 12 of India-US DTAA  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a non-resident corporate entity, sublicensed certain standard commercial software licenses to its Indian affiliates, receipts from such sublicensing of software licenses could not be brought to tax under residuary clause of other income as provided under section 56(1) as well as article 23 of India US DTAA

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee, a company incorporated in USA, engaged in development and manufacture of hydraulic and electro-hydraulic and electro-hydraulic controls for off-highway and automotive applications, purchased different software products and transferred some of them to Indian entity at cost, without any markup - Whether since licensors permitted assessee only to install, operate and use their software products to extent of copies purchased by it, without any right to copy same, it could not have transferred anything more than that to its entities globally including India and therefore, there could be no question of treating amount received from Indian entity on transfer of copyrighted articles as royalty in hands of assessee within meaning of article 12(3) - Held, yes [Para 10][In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, purchased different software products and transferred some of them to Indian entity at cost, since assessee itself obtained only a limited access to software products without any right to copy same, it could not have transferred anything more than that to its entities globally including India, therefore, there could be no question of treating amount received from Indian entity on transfer of copyrighted articles as royalty in hands of assessee within meaning of article 12(3) of DTAA between India and USA  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, purchased certain number of licenses of different software and charged, inter alia, Indian entity for licenses issued, in absence of PE in India, software license fee would not be taxable as business profits

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 12 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA (Royalty) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee US company developed shrink wrap software and sold same to its customers in India through distributors - Assessing Officer held that payment received on account of supply of software by assessee was in nature of royalty and he, accordingly, brought same to tax - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee relating to earlier assessment year observed that end user of software in case of shrink wrap software did not have any access to source code and he had only right to use software for his personal or business use - Tribunal further held that sale of software by assessee to distributor or end user, did not involve any transfer of copyright either in part or in whole; therefore consideration paid by distributor cannot be said to be a payment for right of use copyright or transfer of use of copyright - Further, Delhi High Court in case of DIT v. Ericsson A.B. [2012] 204 Taxman 192/[2011] 16 taxmann.com 371 has held in favour of assessee - Whether following said decision it was to be held that consideration received by assessee merely for right to use software was not royalty and receipts would constitute business receipts in hands of assessee - Held, yes - Whether since assessee who was a non-resident did not have a permanent establishment, business income of assessee could not be taxed in India in absence of a permanent establishment - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/Fees for technical services- Software) - Assessment years 2003-04, 2004-05, 2006-07 and 2010-11 - Assessee, a non-resident company, received consideration for supply of software to Reliance and claimed same to be business income not taxable in India in absence of any permanent establishment in India - Assessing Officer took a view that consideration received by assessee was towards a license to use software and, thus, taxable as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) - Said issue was covered by authoritative pronouncement of Supreme Court in case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC) wherein it was held that amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, was not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software and that same did not give rise to any income taxable India - Whether therefore, following aforesaid decision, consideration received by assessee for supply of software could not be brought to tax as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATION TAXATION : Amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties and fee for technical services - Intellectual property rights, use of) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was a non-resident company incorporated in USA - During relevant year, assessee provided off-the-shelf software and related support services to its associates in India - Assessing Officer as well as DRP held that payments received by assessee were in nature of 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) and hence, taxable in India - It was undisputed that software supplied by assessee to Indian companies was not customized software but were purchased off-the-shelf - Further, agreement for supply of software with Indian companies merely provided right to use off-the-shelf program and no copyright in those software was granted - Whether, on facts, since assessee merely provided to Indian affiliates rights in copyrighted software and not rights of use of copyright itself, amount received by assessee was not in nature of royalty and, hence, same was not taxable in India - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/Fees for technical services- Software) - Assessment years 2003-04, 2004-05, 2006-07 and 2010-11 - Assessee, a non-resident company, received consideration for supply of software to Reliance and claimed same to be business income not taxable in India in absence of any permanent establishment in India - Assessing Officer took a view that consideration received by assessee was towards a license to use software and, thus, taxable as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) - Said issue was covered by authoritative pronouncement of Supreme Court in case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC) wherein it was held that amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, was not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software and that same did not give rise to any income taxable India - Whether therefore, following aforesaid decision, consideration received by assessee for supply of software could not be brought to tax as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Engineering services) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee US based company purchased software from third-party vendor outside India for and on behalf of its AE in India and made payment of software charges for same - Assessee claimed software charges recovered from its AE as reimbursement on an 'at-cost' basis and without any profit element and, accordingly, did not offer it for tax - Assessing Officer treated reimbursement of software charges received by assessee as royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and article 12 of DTAA - It was noted that assessee did not render any service in connection with such reimbursement of software charges by AE - Whether once character of payment received by assessee was found to be in nature of reimbursement of expenses, it could not be considered as income chargeable to tax as royalty - Held, yes [Para 32] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and article 7 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Business profit) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Lionbridge US had entered into an agreement with another company (Microsoft) for purchase of standard off shelves software to be used by its group entities including assessee, an Indian company - Lionbridge US allocated cost of software amongst various group entities and no mark-up was charged and, accordingly, assessee had reimbursed its share of cost to Lionbridge US - Whether said reimbursement being not chargeable to tax in India, assessee was not required to withhold tax under section 195 - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where US company had purchased standard off shelves software to be used by assessee, Indian company, and allocated cost of software and, accordingly, assessee had reimbursed its share of cost to U.S. company, said reimbursement was not chargeable to tax in India

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India [Royalties] - Assessment year 2006-07 -Assessee, an American company, purchased PeopleSoft Software which helped in improving visibility, tracking, and control with a single source of information that provided complete, real-time reporting and reconciliation of operational and financial data - Out of total amount incurred by assessee, a proportion of license cost and maintenance cost for PeopleSoft was allocated by assessee to its Indian subsidiary, CIS, which was reimbursed by CIS to assessee - Whether purchase of software would fall within category of copyrighted article and not towards acquisition of any copyright in software and, hence, consideration would not qualify as royalty under article 12 - Held, yes [Para 12.7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 5 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA (Permanent establishment) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee, a company incorporated in United States and resident of USA for taxation purposes, was a leading provider of information solutions - In India, it entered into joint venture company with 'NIPL'- In terms of agreement, assessee received certain amount from NIPL towards direct sale of software, which were, subsequently, resold by NIPL to its end customers - Assessee claimed such amount from sale of software as business income and in absence of it having permanent establishment in India as per Article 5 of India-USA treaty, not chargeable to tax - Assessing Officer held that amount declared by assessee as business income from sale proceeds of software represented royalty income covered under article 12(3) - It was noted that as per terms of agreement, product as such had been acquired by NIPL from assessee which was further sold without any modification or alteration - Thus, it was apparent that no license was granted to NIPL for duplicating computer software products of assessee but products as such were sold to NIPL who then resold them to end users on profit - Whether on facts, it was a case of consideration received by assessee for transfer of its copyrighted products and not for transfer of copyrights in computer software programme - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income arising from sale of copyrighted product was to be considered as business profit and in absence of assessee's PE in India, same could not be brought to tax - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Where assessee, a US Company, sold its copyright software programme to joint venture company in India but, there was no transfer of copyright in said software programme, income arising to assessee was to be regarded as business profit and in absence of assessee's PE in India, same could not be brought to tax

Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee, a US based company, was engaged in manufacturing and selling a software programme - For purposes of marketing its software, assessee entered into agreements with various distributors/resellers in India - Assessee’s case was that software was being sold to customers for their personal use without transfer of any copyright, trademark or patent, etc. - Accordingly, assessee claimed that payment received for supply of software was not royalty but only business income and since it did not have a PE in India, business income so earned was not taxable as per article 7 of Indo-US DTAA - Assessing Officer rejected assessee’s claim taking a view that payment received by assessee for use of software was in nature of royalty as defined under Indo-US DTAA - Accordingly, he brought to tax amount received by assessee - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order passed by Assessing Officer - Whether in view of order passed by Tribunal in assessee’s own case in respect of earlier assessment year, it was to be held that payment received by assessee was not in nature of royalty within meaning of article 12(3) of Indo-US DTAA and, therefore, impugned order passed by Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes

Section 9 ,  read with section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and article 12 of OECD Model Tax Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Whether to constitute 'royalty' under India-USA DTAA, it is consideration for transfer of 'use of copyright in work' and not 'use of work' itself; however, 'Explanation 4' inserted under section 9(1)(vi) by the Finance Act, 2012, provides that transfer of rights includes and has always included right to use a computer software including granting of a license - Held, yes - Whether thus, it cannot be said that definition of royalty under Income-tax Act is in pari materia with that under DTAA; Even otherwise, TDS liability does not arise on basis of retrospective amendment in definition of royalty - Held yes - Whether fair use of work for purpose of which it is being purchased and doing of such other acts including making of copy for protection from damage or loss cannot, in any case, be said to be any infringement of copyright, whether or not any license in this respect has been granted by author/owner of work - Held, yes - Assessee-company purchased different types of software from non residents which were used in its business of oil and gas exploration - Software purchased by assessee was a standardized software for use in own business of assessee only - Assessee had not been given any commercial right to reproduce and sell copies of software and party from whom assessee acquired software was not having any permanent establishment (PE) in India and there was no time limit of expiry of said software - Whether consideration paid by assessee as per clauses of DTAA could not be said to be royalty and same would be outside scope of definition of 'royalty' as provided in DTAA and would be taxable as business income of recipient but in absence of P.E. could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 30  49] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 , of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties and fees for included services) - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee made payment towards purchase of software to US based company - Assessee claimed that 'Off Shelf software' purchased by it did not have tax implication in India inasmuch as assessee had not purchased any copyright in software but only a copyright product - Assessing Officer held that amount paid to US based company for purchase of software was taxable in hands of said company under section 9(1)(vi) as also under applicable tax treaty - Held that while payment for use of copyright is indeed covered by definition of 'royalty', payment for use of copyright article would not be covered by definition of 'royalty' - Accordingly, amount received by US based company was held to be not taxable in India as 'royalty' [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 12 and  7    of Indo-Swiss DTAA -  Income  -  Deemed to accrue or arise in India  (Royalties or Fees for technical services - Software) - Assessment year  2016-17  - Assessee, a Swiss company, earned certain sum from sale/licensing of computer software to Indian customers and claimed that, in absence of a PE in India, these receipts constituted business profits not taxable in India - Assessing Officer treated these receipts as royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and taxed them under section 115A - Commissioner (Appeals) examined four contracts undertaken during year and noted that no copyright was transferred; licenses were only for use; and any software maintenance, if required, was to be contracted separately with an Indian affiliate (no AMC was included) - It was concluded that receipts were neither for transfer of copyright nor fees for technical services; they were business profits not taxable in India as assessee had no PE - Whether in view of judgment rendered by Supreme Court in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC)/[2021] 281 Taxman 19 (SC)/[2021] 432 ITR 471 (SC), order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 3.1] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA -  Income deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or Fees For Technical Services  - Computer Software) - Assessment years  2001-02 to 2004-05  -Assessee-company, incorporated in USA, had a wholly owned subsidiary in India, namely, OIPL, which carried on software distribution and software development support activities - In respect of global software licensing deals entered into outside India, revenue attributable to India was transferred to OIPL under Software Support Services Agreement - Assessing Officer held that such revenue transfers on global deals represented royalty under section 9(1)(vi) read with article 12(7)(b) and brought same to tax in hands of assessee - It was noted that under said agreement, OIPL was only granted licence to use software and render support services and did not undertake any duplication of software in India, and there was no contractual obligation on OIPL to pay royalty to assessee on revenue transfers - Whether revenue transfers on global deals were not chargeable to tax in India as royalty under section 9(1)(vi) or article 12 of DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 44 to 48] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the India-USA DTAA- Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Others) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in healthcare business for General Electric (GE) group - In year under dispute, assessee received certain amount towards software licence fee cross charged to its affiliates in India which was not offered to tax in India by assessee being reimbursement from affiliates -- Whether since what had been sold to affiliates was copyrighted article and not any right to use copyright, receipts in dispute could not be taxable as royalty income falling under article 12 and alternatively, it could have been taxed as business income under article 7, however, in absence of a Permanent Establishment (PE), it could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 19 and 20] [In favour of assessee] II. Section 9, read with section 56, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 23 of the India-USA DTAA- Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Others) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Whether an item of income, which does not fall under any specific heads of income, such as, salary, house property, business and profession and capital gain, will fall under residuary head 'income from other sources' as per section 56(1) - Held, yes - Whether similarly, article 23(3) of DTAA provides for taxation of residuary items of income which are not dealt with in other articles of DTAA - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in healthcare business for General Electric (GE) group and software licences were sold as tools of business in furtherance of assessee's business activity, receipts therefrom had to be treated as business income and could not be treated as other income under section 56(1) and article 23(3) of DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 20] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 ,  read with section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and article 12 of OECD Model Tax Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Whether to constitute 'royalty' under India-USA DTAA, it is consideration for transfer of 'use of copyright in work' and not 'use of work' itself; however, 'Explanation 4' inserted under section 9(1)(vi) by the Finance Act, 2012, provides that transfer of rights includes and has always included right to use a computer software including granting of a license - Held, yes - Whether thus, it cannot be said that definition of royalty under Income-tax Act is in pari materia with that under DTAA; Even otherwise, TDS liability does not arise on basis of retrospective amendment in definition of royalty - Held yes - Whether fair use of work for purpose of which it is being purchased and doing of such other acts including making of copy for protection from damage or loss cannot, in any case, be said to be any infringement of copyright, whether or not any license in this respect has been granted by author/owner of work - Held, yes - Assessee-company purchased different types of software from non residents which were used in its business of oil and gas exploration - Software purchased by assessee was a standardized software for use in own business of assessee only - Assessee had not been given any commercial right to reproduce and sell copies of software and party from whom assessee acquired software was not having any permanent establishment (PE) in India and there was no time limit of expiry of said software - Whether consideration paid by assessee as per clauses of DTAA could not be said to be royalty and same would be outside scope of definition of 'royalty' as provided in DTAA and would be taxable as business income of recipient but in absence of P.E. could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 30  49] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: To constitute 'royalty', it is consideration for transfer of 'use of copyright in the work' and not 'use of work' itself; however, 'Explanation 4' inserted under section 9(1)(vi) by the Finance Act, 2012, provides that the transfer of rights includes and has always included right for use or right to use a computer software including granting of a license and, thus, it cannot be said that definition of royalty under Income-tax Act is in pari materia with that under DTAA

Section 9, read with section 40(a)(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of OECD Model Tax (Convention) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Software) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2011-12 - Assessee imported software for its business - Assessing Officer held payment made for import of software as royalty and disallowed same under section 40(a)(i) for non-deduction of tax at source - Assessee contended that payment for purchase of software was for acquiring of copyrighted article and not for transfer of any right in copyright and payment could not be construed as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) - Whether payment for transfer of 'copyrighted article' as against payment for transfer of 'copyright' does not qualify as 'royalty' and, thus, same is not taxable in India in absence of PE of seller - Held, yes - Whether however, since in instant case Assessing Officer had not at all deliberated on factual aspect of issue and had not considered agreements entered into by assessee with vendors for import of software and merely by relying upon certain judicial precedents and statutory provisions had come to conclusion that payment made by assessee for import of software was in nature of 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi), issue was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer for de novo adjudication after examination of agreements entered into by assessee for import of software in light of law laid down by Supreme Court in Engineering Analysis Centre for Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 - Held, yes [Paras 19  20] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with sections 90 and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA and OECD Model Commentary - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 2000-01 to 2003-04 - Whether as per India-USA DTAA, royalty in respect of subject-matter of a copyright includes only payments for use, i.e., exploitation of copyright of such literary/artistic or scientific work - Held, yes - Whether therefore, in order to be classified as royalty, right of person in possession of subject-matter of a copyright should be to utilize such copyright in manner which is otherwise protected by respective copyright law in favour of owner of copyright - Held, yes - Whether as per clause 13.1 of OECD model commentary, payment can constitute royalty only if transferor grants to transferee right to use copyright of product - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of providing networking solutions to its customers - Said activity of assessee included sale of software packages to customers - For purpose of its business, assessee had imported readymade software packages from one ‘H’ of USA and sold same to its customers in packed condition - Whether payment made by assessee to ‘H’ for import of software packages was in nature of royalty - Held, no - Whether said payment was commercial income which is subject-matter of article 7 of India-USA DTAA but, since ‘H’ did not have permanent establishment in India, assessee had no obligation to deduct tax at source on payment made to ‘H’ - Held, yes

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Business profits - Business profit vs. Royalty) - Assessment years 2007-08, 2009-10 to 2012-13 - Assessee was a US based company - It was engaged in sale of licenses of its copyrighted software product called as Project Management Software (PMS) - PMS is considered as a Business Intelligence Tool - It assisted users in regulating and effectively utilizing programmer's time on a collective basis with efficiency - Assessing officer took a view that consideration received by assessee fell in category of 'royalty' - Whether payment received by assessee from its customers from sale of software products/licenses was not in nature of royalty under section 9(1)(vi) of IT Act, 1961 and also as per article 12(3)(a) and article 12(3) (b) of Indo US DTAA - Held, yes - Whether amount received by assessee was normal business income of assessee on account of sale of copy righted products (licenses) and not taxable in India in absence of permanent establishment - Held, yes [Para 34] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amount received by assessee, a US based company, from sale of copyrighted software products/licences was in nature of business income which in absence of assessee's PE of India, could not be brought to tax said amount was not as 'royalty' under article 12 of India-USA DTAA

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and China - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/Fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee, a US based company, received certain amount of consideration towards rendering usage of Microsoft license services to its Indian subsidiary for execution of sub-contract with Tower India - Assessing Officer treated aforesaid services offered as royalty in terms of article 12 of India-USA DTAA and held that same were liable to be taxed in India - It was observed that license for usage of copyrighted products were with Microsoft only and assessee had acquired global right and transferred said licenses to its group entities based on requirements - Whether since no vestige of copyright was at all transferred either to assessee or to end user, said services would not fall in category of royalty or copyrights - Held, yes [Paras 14 and 16] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, received certain amount of consideration towards rendering usage of Microsoft license services to its Indian subsidiary for execution of sub-contract with Tower India, since no vestige of copyright was transferred either to assessee or to end user, said services would not fall in category of royalty  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Payment received by assessee, a US based company, from its Indian subsidiary, for providing service desk facility to employees of TW group entities to monitor IT enabled glitch for execution of sub-contract with TW India was business profits as per article 7 of India-US DTAA

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2006-07 - Whether amount paid by resident Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amount paid by resident Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India

Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Software) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee, a non-resident located in USA, was engaged in business of software development/distribution and rendition of related services - It received consideration from outright sale of software to end user customers in India and claimed same as business income - Assessing Officer treated impugned consideration as royalty payment - Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that consideration received by assessee from outright sale of software was for a copyrighted article and could not be considered as royalty payment - Whether impugned payments were not royalty but were payments made towards purchase of copyrighted article which was to be treated as business income of assessee, not taxable in India in absence of PE of assessee in India - Held, yes - Whether further payments made to assessee were not for any process or for any information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience so as to make such payments fall within purview of definition of 'royalty' under India-USA DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amounts paid by resident Indian end users to non-resident computer suppliers as consideration for use of computer software is not payment of royalty

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty and fees for technical services) - Assessment years 2003-04, 2004-05, 2007-08 to 2010-11 - Assessee a US company, earned revenue from licensing of software and supply of "contact solutions" to customers in India which was a combination of software and compatible hardware that enables customers to better manage customer interactions via voice, email, web and fax - Whether consideration received by assessee for supply of 'contact solutions' is not royalty under article 12 of Tax Treaty - Held, yes - Whether since there was no transfer of any right in respect of copyright by assessee and it was a case of mere transfer of a copyrighted article, receipts would constitute business receipts in hands of assessee to be assessed as business income subject to assessee having business connection/ PE in India - Held, yes [Para 42] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Consideration received by assessee for supply of 'contact solutions' used for better management customer interaction, comprising of sale of hardware alongwith license of embedded software to end user is not royalty under article 12 of DTAA between India and USA  IT/ILT : Provision of implementation and maintenance services are inextricably and essentially linked to supply of software; where supply of software is itself not taxable as 'royalty', these services are also not royalty  IT/ILT : Where assessee did not carry on business in India through a building site or construction, there could be no 'installation PE' of assessee in India   IT/ILT : To tax income earned by a US company from customers located outside India under section 9(l)(vi)(c)/9(1)(vii)(c), revenue must prove that customers carry on business in India and that they have used rights in IPs/services for purpose of making or earning income from a source in India

III. Section  9, read with section 40(a)(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Reimbursement of Expenses) - Assessment year 2013-14 - During assessment year 2013-14, assessee made reimbursement on account of various expenses inter alia including software charges incurred by group companies on behalf of assessee on cost to cost basis without any mark-up - Assessing Officer classified such reimbursement as royalty and FIS - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471, amounts paid by resident Indian end users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturer/supplier as consideration for resale/use of computer software through end users license agreements (EULAs)/distribution agreements is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software and same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes - Whether on facts issue whether software supplied by AE to assessee was standard/off-shelf software or customized software was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer for verification and if, on verification it was found that software supplied by AE was standard software without any customization being done by AE, Assessing Officer would reconsider this issue in light of decision of Supreme Court in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra) and modify assessment accordingly - Held, yes [Paras 23.2 and 24] [Matter remanded]

Section 9 read with Section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and articles 7 and 12 of DTAA between India and US - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Whether computer software after being put on to a media and then sold, becomes goods like any other audio cassette or painting on canvas or a book and, thus, payment made in respect of it could not be termed as 'royalty' - Held, yes - Assessee entered into a license agreement with TIBCO USA in terms of which it had granted to assessee and affiliates perpetual, non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free, unlimited, non-transferable license in connection with software maintained by TIBCO which allowed internal operations including use of software as its backward infrastructure for ASP services and web hosting services - Assessing Officer having examined software agreement, opined that assessee was getting only license to use software and no other title or interest in software was being transferred to assessee - Accordingly, Assessing Officer held that payment made for license to use software amounted to royalty within meaning of section 9(1)(vi) - He, thus, passed an order under section 195(2) directing assessee to deduct tax at source before making payment to party for purchase of software - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) took a view that assessee under software contract acquired only a copy of software program and did not acquire any copyright over such software; thus, payment was made only for purchase of copyrighted article which did not amount to royalty - It was accordingly, held that Assessing Officer was not justified in directing to deduct tax at source under section 195 - Whether since payment in question was for a copyrighted article and not for copyright itself, it could not be considered as 'royalty' either under Act or under Indo-US DTAA - Held, yes - Whether once payment was not royalty, it could only be taxed as 'business profits' in hands of non-resident company - Held, yes - Whether since non-resident company did not have permanent establishment in India, payment made to it was not taxable in India and, therefore, there was no question of deducting tax at source from said payment - Held, yes

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 12 of the DTAA between India and Germany (Royalties and fees for technical services) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee, a German Company, was engaged in business of providing insurance and other financial services worldwide - In India, assessee owned 26 per cent of shareholding in two insurance companies, namely, 'BA Life' and 'BA General' - Assessee acquired user right in a software programme developed by another non-resident company, namely , 'CGI' - Subsequently, assessee entered into license agreement with its Indian affiliates, namely, BA Life and BA General, whereby Indian affiliates had been granted simple, non-exclusive and non-transferable right to use aforesaid software programme - Assessee filed its return wherein licence charges received from Indian affiliates were claimed to be exempt from tax - Assessing Officer took a view that license charges received by assessee constituted 'royalty' within meaning of section 9(1)(vi) and was, therefore, subject to taxation in India - Whether since copyright of software vested only with CGI and what was transacted in licence agreement between assessee and its Indian affiliates was only grant of user right in copyrighted software and not use of copyright itself, licence charges received by assessee were its business income which could not be brought to tax as royalty - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 12, 7 and 5 of DTAA between India and Singapore - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee an Indian company and NPL a Singapore based company entered into an agreement whereby NPL licensed a software to assessee and assessee made payment for same - Assessing Officer held that payment for use of software was for use of secret process and, therefore, payment in question would be in nature of royalty and that assessee ought to have deducted tax at source at time of making payment to NPL - However, perusal of clauses of agreement between assessee and NPL, clearly showed that assessee only had a right to use computer software and did not have right to use copyright in computer software - Whether therefore payment in question made by assessee to NPL could not be regarded as 'royalty' within meaning of DTAA between India and Singapore and amount received by NPL would be in nature of business income which would be chargeable to tax in India under article 7(1) of DTAA - Held, yes - Whether however, since NPL did not have a PE in India payment in question would not chargeable to tax in India - Held, yes [Paras 20  26 ][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Payments made by assessee an Indian company to a Singapore based company for right to use software could not be ragarded as royalty, as assessee only had a right to use computer software and did not have right to use copyright in computer software

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Software) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Whether where payment was made by assessee (end-users/distributors) to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through distribution agreement, since distribution agreement did not create any interest or right in assessee, which would amount to use of or right to use any copyright, said payment did not amount to royalty and same did not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Paras 8-11] [Matter remanded]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where amount was paid by assessee-Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through distribution agreement, since distribution agreement did not create any interest or right in assessee, which would amount to use of or right to use any copyright, said payment did not amount to royalty and it did not give rise to any income taxable in India

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2007-08 - Whether where payments were made by Indian-company to non-resident company which was computer software manufacturer/supplier for resale/use of computer software through distribution agreements, said payment did not amount to royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and same did not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where payments were made by Indian company to non-resident-company which was computer software manufacturer/supplier for resale/use of computer software through/distribution agreements, said payment did not amount to royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and same did not give rise to any income taxable in India

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 5 of DTAA between India and US - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Permanent establishment - Liaison office) - Assessment years 2017-18 to 2020-21 - Assessee, a US based company, was engaged in business of supplying goods from outside India - During relevant period, assessee made offshore sale of goods and offshore sale of software and related support services to its various customers in India - Assessing Officer held that Liaison Office (LO) of assessee in India constituted a PE of assessee in India - Accordingly, he attributed profits to assessee’s PE in India - It was found that assessee had closed its LO operations and no expat employee were engaged by assessee at LO - Revenue had not placed on record any material to show that even after closure of LO operations, assessee still had business connection that could be termed as PE in India - Whether since no business activity was carried out by assessee during relevant period through LO, assessee had no PE in India during impugned assessment year and, hence, question of attribution of profits to PE in India did not arise - Held, yes [Paras 16  20] [In favour of assessee] II. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2017-18 to 2020-21 - Whether amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributions to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

Section  9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and articles  5 and 13 of DTAA between India and UK - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2007-08 to 2011-12 - Assessee entered into a software license agreement with a British company, ASL - As per agreement, assessee was granted a 'non-exclusive' and 'non-transferable' license to purchase license for software products developed by ASL and distribute same to end customers in India who would pay sub-licensing fee to assessee - Assessing Officer held that assessee was in receipt of royalty as payments made by it to ASL for distribution of software products would qualify as royalty in hands of ASL - However, assessee claimed that same could not be treated as royalty - It was noticed that as per agreement, assessee did not have any right to generate license key or make copies of license key - ASL was sole owner of IPR of patents, copyrights, trademarks, modifications and updates and assessee was not given any of these proprietary rights - Further, assessee had no role in developing a software, it was just distributing software to end users - Whether, therefore, payment by assessee to ASL for procuring and distributing copyrighted software could not be treated as payment towards royalty - Held, yes - Whether further, since ASL was not having a PE in India, assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where assessee, an Indian company entered into a software license agreement with a British company, since said agreement did not permit assessee to modify and develop software products and UK company was sole owner of IPR of patents, copyrights and trademarks and assessee was not given any of these proprietary rights, payments by assessee to ASL for procuring and distributing copyrighted software could not be treated as payment towards royalty

Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 5, 7 and 12 of DTAA between India and Israel - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee was a company incorporated in, and tax resident of, Israel - It entered into an agreement with an Indian company 'RIL' for supply and licence of software for RIL's wireless network in India - In terms of agreement, assessee granted to RIL, and its affiliates, a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty free, worldwide licence to install, use, operate or copy software and documentation licensed under agreement solely for implementation, operation, management and maintenance of RIL's Network within India - Assessee filed its return disclosing nil income - Assessee's contention was that payment received for supply of software was in nature of business profits which could only be taxed under article 7 of India-Israel DTAA as business income, but since assessee did not have a permanent establishment, in terms of article 5 of India-Israel DTAA, its business profits could not be taxed in India at all - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's contention holding that amount received by assessee for supply of software was in nature of 'royalty' which was liable for taxation in India - Whether payment made by RIL to assessee could not be said to be a 'payment for use of, or right to use of, copyright' rather, it was a mere payment for 'purchase of copyright material' which did not amount to royalty within meaning of article 12(3) of India-Israel DTAA - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2006-07 - Whether amount paid by resident Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12, of the DTAA between India and China - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Software) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee, a Chinese company, was engaged in business of supply/licensing of automobile related software - It entered into a License Agreement with MG India, one of its group companies, for granting of license to incorporate software into head unit which was supplied from outside India and got fitted into MG India's cars - Assessee granted a non-transferable, non-exclusive, non-assignable license to incorporate software into vehicles manufactured/sold by MG India to end customers - MG India was required to get terms of legally binding End User License Agreement (EULA) agreed by its customer before allowing use of licensed products - Further, all intellectual property rights in licensed products shall belong to assessee and its licensors only - Whether since impugned receipts were for supply of software which was a standardized/off shelf software and not for use of copyright or imparting information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience, it would not fall within scope of article 12(3) of India-China DTAA to be taxed as royalty income - Held, yes [Paras 11.5 and 12] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a Chinese company, supplied software to an Indian company for granting of licence to incorporate software into head unit which was supplied from outside India and got fitted into cars and claimed it as non-taxable under India-China DTAA, since assessee had only supplied a standard/off the shelf software to Indian company and had not transferred copyright/right to use copyright of software, impugned receipts would not fall within scope of article 12(3) of India-China DTAA to be taxed as royalty income

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the Model OECD Convention - Income - Deeemd to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee-non resident company was engaged in business of research, creation of software products and selling same through its subsidiaries across world - Assessee sold software against end users order to BEA Systems India, who in turn, finally sold it to end users - Assessing Officer held that payment received from Indian-company on account of distribution of software product was royalty - Whether payment made for purchase of 'shrink-wrapped software' by Indian-company to assessee amounted to royalty - Held, yes [Para 3.4] [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT: Payment made for purchase of 'shrink-wrapped software' by Indian-company to assessee amounted to royalty

Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and New Zealand -  Income -  Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or Fees For Technical Services-Computer Software) - Assessee, a New Zealand company, was involved in designing and providing fully tailored, off shelf wireless broadband solutions - During year under consideration, assessee-company sold 'off the shelf' software through a non-exclusive license rights to an Indian company to utilize technology in certain areas in India - Assessing Officer opined that income from licensed IMS software was taxable under section 9(1)(vi) read with article 12 of Indo-NZ-Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement as royalty - However appellate authority held that right that was transferred was not a right to use copyright but was only limited to right to use copyrighted material and same did not give rise to any royalty income - It was noted that Supreme Court in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax & Anr.[2021] 432 ITR 471/195 Taxman 137/67 taxmann.com 137 had held that consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreement was not royalty for use of copyright of software and same did not give rise to any taxable income in India - Whether since revenue did not contest applicability of said judgment, no substantial question of law arose for consideration - Held, yes [Paras 9 to 11] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of India Ireland DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2007-08 and 2010-11 to 2015-16 - Whether where assessee, a Ireland based company, distributed shrink-wrapped/off shelf/electronic download computer software for supplies in India to its Indian distributors, consideration paid by distributors to assessee for resale/use of computer software was not payment of royalty for purpose of copyright in computer software and same did not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]  Section 9, read with  section 92C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 7 of OECD Model Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Business profit - Profit attributable to PE, Apportionment of income) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2007-08 and 2010-11 to 2015-16 - Whether once a transfer pricing analysis has been undertaken in respect of Indian AE, i.e., PE of foreign company, nothing further would be left to be attributed to it and, accordingly, that would automatically extinguish need for attribution of any additional profits to PE - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 9, read with sections 195 and 40(a)(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Article 12 of the Indo-Australia DTAA and Article 12 of Indo-Singapore DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2003-04 to 2010-11 - Assessee, an Indian company, made payment to two non-resident entities towards procurement of standard software - Assessee was supplying those procured software products to various customers in India - Assessing Officer treated those payments as royalty and disallowed same under section 40(a)(i) on account of non-deduction of TDS - However, software under consideration was standard software and also copyrighted - Assessee company had no right of ownership in copyright and also no right to make copies or use said software - Relationship between assessee company and non-resident companies was on a principal-to-principal basis - Software products were delivered to assessee on a CD/any other media specified in invoice - Technical role of assessee was limited in installing and running software product in systems of customers in India - Whether since purchase and sale of software was only a trading transaction, payment made to non-resident companies was only purchase consideration for procuring copyrighted software products and was not in nature of royalty - Held, yes - Whether there was no requirement to deduct tax at source under section 195 and therefore, assessing authority was not justified in invoking section 40(a)(i) and make disallowance in respect of amounts paid by assessee company - Held, yes [Paras 48, 51 and 60] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Payment made to non-resident companies for procuring standard and copyrighted software products, for distribution or re-sale purpose on principal to principal basis could not be treated as payment towards royalty  IT/ILT : Where assessee company was working on a principal-to-principal basis, bears risk of failure of contracts and also functions on independent basis, it could not be said to be a PE of non-resident in India

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and Germany - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or Fees For Technical Services - Computer Software) - Assessment year 2022-23 - Assessee, a company incorporated in Germany, was engaged in providing flight and navigational informational solutions and in developing software used for flight planning and operational execution - During year, it earned Rs. 47.61 crores from Indian customers for navigational/aeronautical data and information supplied electronically or in paper form, for restricted licences of Electronic Flight Bag and ground tools software with linked implementation, training and support, and for sale of printed charts and related items - Assessing Officer held receipts to be 'royalty' under article 12 of DTAA and section 9(1)(vi), noting that assessee compiled data from government/public and customer sources based on its accumulated experience and that there was no material change from earlier years when similar income was offered as royalty - Whether consideration received from Indian customers for provision of flight/navigation data, restricted software licences (EFB/Ground Tools) with ancillary services, and sale of printed charts was not taxable in India as 'royalty' under article 12 of India-Germany DTAA read with section 9 but constituted 'business income' not taxable in India in absence of PE - Held, yes [Paras 12 to 17] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a German company, earned receipts from Indian customers for providing flight/navigation data, restricted software licences with ancillary services and sale of printed charts, such receipts were not taxable as royalty but constituted business income, not taxable in India in absence of permanent establishment

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and Sweden - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties\FTS Computer Software) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee, a Sweden based company, was engaged in development, production and marketing of personal care products, tissues, packing solutions, paper and solid wood products - During assessment year, assessee had receipts on account of SAP Licence charges from Indian subsidiary company (SCA-India) - Assessing Officer issued notice under section 142(1) seeking reasons as to why aforesaid receipts were not offered to tax - Assessee contended that aforesaid amounts were merely reimbursements of expenditure by SCA India to assessee and it had supplied SAP Licence on cost to cost basis without any mark up - However, Assessing Officer made addition on account of receipts from SAP licence charges treating it as royalty - Tribunal in earlier year on similar facts in assessee's own case held that said receipt was reimbursement of software licence fees paid by assessee to a third party, and, therefore, it could not constitute income taxable in hands of assessee - Whether, on facts, receipts of SAP Licence by assessee was reimbursement and was not taxable as royalty - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where receipts on account of SAP licence by assessee, a foreign company, from Indian subsidiary was reimbursement of software licence fees paid by assessee to a third party, same was not taxable as royalty either under domestic tax laws or under provisions of Indo-Swedish Tax Treaty

I. Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and articles 12 and 7 of DTAA between India and Netherland - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Associated Enterprise of assessee-company had purchased software on licence from a company for use by all its group entities and licence fees paid by its group companies for software was apportioned at actuals to all group entities and share of assessee was reimbursed to its AE on basis of actuals - Assessee claimed that said sum represented purely reimbursement of expenses to its AE and assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source on said payment - Assessing Officer observed that said amount was paid by assessee for use of software and since it was taxable as royalty as per provisions of Act as well as DTAA between India and USA, assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195 - Whether since payment made by assessee was not in nature of royalty but it was towards purchase of software, it would have to be assessed as business profits in hands of Associated Enterprise and since said Associated Enterprise did not have a permanent establishment in India, business profits could not be taxed in India under article 7 - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had paid a certain sum to its Associated Enterprise as its share of licence fee and claimed said payment as reimbursement of expenses, since amount in question paid by assessee was not in nature of royalty but said amount was paid towards purchase of software, it would have to be assessed as business profits in hands of Associated Enterprise  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/TRANSFER PRICING : Where nature of products manufactured in two segments of assessee-company were different and business model or business process adopted by assessee in these two segments was also different, said transactions could not be compared for purpose of transfer pricing analysis in order to determine arm's length price   INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/TRANSFER PRICING : Where a sum was claimed to be paid by assessee for internal audit services received from its Associated Enterprise and assessee-company submitted that it did not have any internal audit department and, hence, internal audit services were required to be availed in order to have an internal audit system commensurate with its size and nature of business and even benefits received from such internal audit services were explained by assessee, authorities below were not justified in making addition on ground that no tangible benefit was derived by assessee

Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2006-07 - High Court by impugned order held that amount paid by resident Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - On SLP, it was noted that issues raised in this special leave petition had been answered by a judgment by Three Judges Bench of this Court in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC) - Whether since judgment in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. (supra) was holding field, said judgment would have to be followed in instant case and, thus, special leave petition filed by revenue was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [In favour of revenue]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that amount paid by resident Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2013-14 - High Court by impugned order held that where assessee, a US based company, earned revenue from sale of software to its Indian clients, since grant of right to install and use software did not include providing copyright of said software to clients, revenue earned from said sale would not be taxable in hands of assessee as royalty in India - Whether in view of judgment of this Court in case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC)/[2022] 3 SCC 321 and CIT (International Taxation) v. MOL Corporation [SLP( C) Diary No. 5669 of 2024, dated 11-3-2024], SLP filed by revenue against impugned order was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Para 3] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that where assessee, a US based company, earned revenue from sale of software to its Indian clients, since grant of right to install and use software did not include providing copyright of said software to clients, revenue earned from said sale would not be taxable in hands of assessee as royalty in India  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that where assessee, a US based company, provided cloud computing infrastructure to its Indian clients through subscription agreement and even though cloud based services were based on patents/copyright but subscribers did not get any right of reproduction, thus, subscription fee was merely a consideration for online access of cloud computing services and would not be taxable as royalty in India

I. Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 13 of the DTAA between India and UK - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Software) - Assessment years 2012-13 to 2015-16 - Assessee had entered into an agreement with IBM for procurement of licence of GSAP Software and same was customized as per requirements of assessee and cost incurred towards licence and for Go-Live were allocated to group companies on a cost to cost basis based on  number of users - During year under consideration, assessee received certain sum towards access to GSAP application and towards GSAP Go-Live charges - Assessing Officer held that receipt was royalty both under DTAA and under section 9(1) - It was noted that amount received towards cost allocation of expenses incurred towards acquiring licence to access GSAP Software and cost incurred towards modification for Go-live did not result in any right to use copyright, but only right to use copyrighted software of GSAP - Further, amount received by assessee was on a cost to cost basis without any income element in it and on that count also, amount received could not be treated as taxable in India - Whether amount received by assessee could not be treated as royalty both under DTAA and under section 9 - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of OECD Model Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Whether amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Paras 10 to 12] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and same does not give rise to any income taxable in India

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and Israel - Income -  Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Software) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Whether consideration received by assessee, a company incorporated and based in Israel, for sale of software to Indian company was not royalty since there was no transfer or use of copyright in sale of 'off shelf' software that could come within ambit of royalty and, hence, it was not taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 25] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Consideration received by assessee, a company incorporated in Israel, for sale of software to Indian company was not royalty since there was no transfer of copy right in sale of 'off shelf' software
