Why does this case matter?

This judgment sheds clarity and sets a sound precedent that not every overenthusiastic attempt to automatically include license fee/royalty is appropriate – especially when these payments don't meet the strict statutory criteria under Rule 9(1)(c) of the CVR.

The judgment decisively burst several prevalent myths regarding the inclusion of license fee/royalty payments in customs valuation: Myth#1: License fee/royalty must always be included in value of the imported goods if the same is part of the agreements; Myth#2: License fee/royalty for obtaining additional licenses post-import of the goods, must be included for the purposes of Customs Valuation; Myth#3: Electronic delivery of software is treated the same as physical import for Customs purposes; and Myth#4: "Right to use" the imported goods is same as that of "sale of goods."

The Tribunal arrived at such conclusions on the basis of the specific terms mentioned in the EULA. In essence, the judgment highlights that assessing the inclusion of license fee/royalty in valuation of the imported goods is akin to reading fine print under a magnifying glass—every detail in the agreement can shift the outcome. Thus, each licensing agreement needs a careful, case-by-case look to decide if the license fee/royalty emanating therefrom becomes a part of customs valuation.

Beyond the Judgement: Practical Insights for Importers

This struggle isn't just about numbers or tax compliance. It's about language of the agreement. Misinterpretation could mean hefty penalties, but overzealous inclusion of license fee/royalty in the valuation of the imported goods could suffocate the cost structure of businesses. Every contract clause is dissected with the precision once reserved for engineering specs: Is this a 'condition of sale'? Does the license fee payment flow directly to the seller? Could it be included in the transaction value of the imported goods and consequently trigger customs duty?

Given the wide variety of contractual arrangements, it is essential to closely examine each agreement to determine whether any license fee/royalty is includible in the transaction value of the imported goods. If the contract or agreement is still in the drafting stage, it becomes even more critical to analyse these clauses thoroughly to ensure that the correct legal course is taken. Ultimately, it is best to review each of your agreements to ensure a sound risk management for imports.

Navigating the landscape of valuation for the imports

In the complex world of imports, businesses often consider the value of the physical goods to be paramount. However, they sometimes overlook that beyond the physical cargo lies something less visible yet crucial — the royalty/license fee payments. Royalties arise from licensing agreements which grant the importer rights inter alia to use manufacturing know-how, brand names, or software embedded within imported goods.

As the nature of contracts pertaining to imports/exports and associated license fee/royalty has evolved, the Customs valuation has also come a long way. Once upon a time, a physical shipment was all that customs authorities cared about for determining its value and imposition duties. Today's imports bundle licensed software, technology, trademarks, and other rights, making valuation of such shipments more complicated. While the goods themselves represent the tangible aspect for customs valuation, the accompanied intangible rights and their payments may significantly contribute to the overall value of the import transaction. This evolution sets the stage for courts to demystify when license fee/royalty should be included in the transaction value of the imported goods.

The recent judgement by CESTAT, New Delhi in the judgment of HCL Technologies Ltd. and SAP India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication) [Final Order No. 51379-51462 of 2025 dated 29-9-2025] bring these complexities to the forefront. It deals with critical questions regarding includability of license fee in the value of the imported goods, specifically in the context of delivery of software through physical and electronic media.

Under the Lens: CESTAT's approach in the case of HCL Technologies Ltd.

Facts at a Glance

HCL Technologies Ltd. ('HCL') entered into an End-User License Agreement ('EULA') with SAP India Private Limited ('SAP India') to obtain non-exclusive and perpetual license to use propriety software, documentation and other information of SAP India. As per terms of the EULA, the software was to be delivered electronically. In the year 2006, SAP India raised substantial invoices on HCL for payment of license fee relating to rights provided under the EULA.

During the same time, HCL received some imported CDs containing SAP Software via courier, wherein a nominal value was declared under the courier bill of entry, for customs purposes. Perhaps, this is what caught the eye of the Customs Department – A CD with a software... only for pocket change?

An investigation was initiated against inter alia HCL for such imports. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Customs Department rejected the declared value of the CDs under Rule 10A of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 ('CVR') [now Rule 14 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] and sought to include the license fee in the valuation of imported CDs in terms of Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR.

The allegation of the Customs Department was that unless the license fee is paid, the software on the CD cannot be accessed or used; thereby, making the license fee integral to the transaction value of the imported CDs.

Tribunal's Verdict: Four Conditions for Royalty Inclusion in Customs Valuation

The Tribunal determined that for inclusion of royalties to the value of the imported goods, the following four key conditions under Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR needed to be satisfied:

1.

The license fee must relate to the imported goods;

2.

The fee must be payable directly or indirectly by the importer at the time of import;

3.

The license fee must be a condition of sale of the goods; and

4.

The fee must not already be included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods.

Guided by these conditions, the Tribunal took a closer look at the terms of the EULA entered between HCL&SAP India, and made the following findings:

The license fee was not related to the physical import of the CDs; rather, it was related to the intangible right to use the software in India. The EULA had itself provided electronic delivery as the mode of delivery of the software. Thus, the license fee was for usage of software rights and not for the import of physical CDs themselves.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import.

The assessee was a tax resident of the USA. Assessee earned income from cloud services, including cloud hosting and other supporting and ancillary services provided to Indian Customers. The assessee filed the return of income and the notes stating that the cloud hosting services were not taxable as 'royalties' under Article 12 of the India-US tax treaty.

THE DOCUMENTATION PROCESS

NEED FOR DOCUMENTATION

4. Transfer pricing calculation produces at least two consequences. First, it puts national tax jurisdictions under stress because it is an income-shifting system that allows MNEs to maximize their after-tax profits by channelling their taxable income to low tax jurisdictions. Second, it provides a substantial advantage to MNEs in comparison with non-multinational firms because only the former can use that strategy.1 0

Tax jurisdictions are constantly challenged to ensure that MNEs do not take undue advantage of their exposure vis-a-vis a localized operator. The only way to guarantee that a MNE is playing by the rules is through proper assessment of its cross-border transactions. That is possible through a detailed study of the company’s functions, assets, and risks that are distributed across tax jurisdictions because those three factors will ulti- mately determine where the profit should be taxed. Thus, there is a need for detailed documentation providing not only the details of the related-party cross-border transaction, but also a logical justification of the prices charged for the transaction.

4.1 ARM’S LENGTH PRINCIPLE - That brings one to the concept of arm’s length principle, which simply means replicating an open market where transactions occur between unrelated entities. It is the principle or international standard that OECD member countries have agreed should be used for determining transfer prices for tax purposes. As mentioned in the OECD guidelines:

Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention : where ‘conditions are made or imposed between the two enterprises in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enterprises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly.’

The arm’s length principle implies that the profits of an MNE should follow where the company has the bulk of its functions, assets, and risks. That is the basic principle, a common underlying concept that most tax authorities across jurisdictions tend to comply with and incorporate as the basis of their transfer pricing principles. A tax authority in any jurisdiction would correctly expect to see a corresponding share of the profit.

The arm’s length principle is equally applicable whether one is dealing with the transfer of tangible goods, intangibles, or services between related parties. The facts and circumstances of each case and the nature of the related-party transactions that are being considered, however, dictate the nuances of application of the principle. While there may be significant variations in the expectations of tax authorities on the documentation requirements, which are usually determined based on each jurisdiction’s tax legislation, some fundamentals do remain the same. For instance, one of the best ways to prove that royalties paid for the transfer of an intangible are at arm’s length is to find comparable arm’s length agreements in the wider marketplace. Also, for a transfer of value added services, it is always preferable to find comparable service transactions between unrelated third parties to prove that the charges paid for the services rendered are at arm’s length. From our experience in the field of transfer pricing documentation for various industries (software, automobile, lumber, rubber, and so on) and for the various types of transactions, it is advisable to use the assistance from experts in the field while preparing documentation to be presented to the tax authorities.

In such a case, the resident Indian entity could be treated as the Permanent Establishment of the non-resident entity. The tax treatment of the Permanent Establishment in such a case is under consideration in this circular. During the last decade or so, India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated enterprises of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision of services itself like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. The non-resident entity or the foreign company will be liable to tax in India only if the IT-enabled BPO unit in India constitutes its Permanent Establishment. The extent to which the profit of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board.

A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc. or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment become taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as are attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deduction expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if, instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm’s length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profits that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm’s length principle".

"Arm’s length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(iii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm’s length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.

A non-resident company may outsource revenue generating business activities to an IT-enabled entity in India, such as the services of a travel agent, software developer, software maintenance, investment consultant, debt collection service, etc., and the IT-enabled entity in India may render the services either directly to the customers abroad or through the non-resident principal.

There may be certain other incidental activities outsourced which are incidental to the business of carrying on manufacture and sale of goods or merchandise or provision of services outside India, such as conclusion of contracts and procurement of orders to an IT-enabled entity in India.

Status of BPO entity

8. The BPO entity in India carrying on the outsourcing activities for a non-resident company, may be its branch or subsidiary company or an independent company.

A branch connotes a physical presence of the foreign enterprise in India. It is an office with an independent administration. Where a non-resident has an office in India and employs staff to carry on its business, it is its branch. A branch office is not regarded as a separate legal entity. Its profits are the profits of a company owning the branch office. It is different from a subsidiary which has a legal entity of its own - CIT v. Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. [1987] 165 ITR 416 (Cal.)—and which is regarded as a domestic company in the country where it is established. The subsidiary company may be a branch office of a foreign establishment under certain circumstances. If it is engaged in transactions with or on behalf of the foreign enterprise as an agent of the parent company in circumstances pointing out to a trading in a host country, it can be said to be performing functions on behalf of that enterprise in the same way as any could do - Fire Stone Tyre and Rubber Co. Ltd. v. Lewellin 37 TC 111. To that extent the subsidiary is the branch office of the foreign enterprise, in spite of it having independent and own legal status.

They agree with the concept of Permanent Establishment ("PE") and taxation of business income under accepted international taxation principles as laid down in the Model tax conventions issued by the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development ("OECD") as well as the United Nations ("UN"). An interesting question that arises is whether the clarification provided here goes beyond the scope of the provisions in the ITA. Section 9 which extends the scope of taxation laid down under section 5 of the ITA, states that "all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India6, or through or from any property in India, or through or from any asset or source of income in India, or through the transfer of a capital asset situate in India" would be deemed to accrue or arise in India. The most significant condition for extended scope of taxation is that there should be "business connection" in India. This term has not been defined in the ITA. However, it has been explained in various decisions by the Supreme Court of India. In the case of R. D. Aggarwal & Co.7 which was before Circular 23 was issued, the Apex Court held that there should be a real and intimate relation between trading activity carried on outside the taxable territories and trading activity carried on within the territories.

The ITA explains that if all the operations are not carried out in India then entire income will not be liable to taxation in India. Explanation 1( a) to section 9(1)(i) reads as follows :

"in the case of a business of which all the operations are not carried out in India, the income of the business deemed under this clause to accrue or arise in India shall be only such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India."

A combined reading of section 9(1)(i), the views expressed by the Supreme Court of India in the case of R. D. Aggarwal and the above Explanation, leads to the conclusion that the income of a non-resident will be liable to taxation in India only when the trading activity in India and the trading activity outside India, have real and intimate relationship. Further, only that income would be taxable in India which can be reasonably attributed to the operations carried out in India. In fact, the OECD subscribes to similar views.

OECD Model Tax Convention on PE and Transfer Pricing

It has been internationally accepted that the source country should not tax income of a foreign entity unless there is some longer economic relationship between the source country and the entity. This has been incorporated in the OECD Model tax treaty. Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of the Model states: "The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to that permanent establishment." When it comes to defining the term "permanent establishment" ("PE") Article 5 identifies the following categories – fixed PE, service PE and agency PE. So far as the first PE is concerned, broadly speaking, there is requirement of permanent relationship. Agency PE requires the agent to be dependent and some more conditions to be satisfied. Similarly, for service PE to exist, the services provided by a foreign entity should be over a sufficiently longer period and should satisfy certain conditions.

The authorized OECD approach on attribution of income to permanent establishments (July 2008) has led to an interplay between PE and the transfer pricing approaches. The authorized OECD approach rests on the foundation of Article 7(1) and Article 7(2) of the OECD Model Tax convention. As mentioned above, Article 7 (1) permits the host country to tax the "profits of the enterprise" but only so much as is "attributable to" a PE in the host country. Article 7(2) states that the profits to be attributed to the PE are the profits "it might be expected" to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a part.

Based on the above, the authorized OECD approach prescribes a two step approach for attributing profits to a PE. Step 1 is to hypothesize the PE as a "functionally separate entity" and Step 2 is to compute arm’s length remuneration as per the OECD transfer pricing guidelines.

Considering the difference in the ostensible compensation structures across different categories of manufacturers, it becomes pertinent for MNEs to clearly identify the functional characterization as well as the compensation structure at the outset, i.e., even before the Indian Taxpayer begins the actual manufacturing activity. Adopting a particular characterization initially without thinking through the entire life cycle of the proposed manufacturing operation could be fraught with significant transfer pricing and tax costs. For instance, an Indian manufacturer set up as a full-fledged entrepreneurial manufacturer could be rightfully expected to incur losses during the initial period of set up. However, as a part of its manufacturing operations, it may develop valuable intangibles, and may achieve significant economies of scale. Therefore, the start up losses would need to be balanced with an expectation of, or at least, a probability of extraordinary profits going forward. Now, if the MNE group wishes to re-characterize the manufacturer as a contract manufacturer going forward, the group may be faced with significant business restructuring related implications, and associated tax costs.

Payment of Royalties and Technology Fees to Foreign Affiliates

Typically, the Indian manufacturer would tend to rely primarily on the technical know-how, technical assistance and training provided by their foreign affiliates for its manufacturing operations, for a significant period of operations.

Further, one or more foreign affiliates could invest continuously and substantially in research and development activities which benefit, the Indian manufacturer, who is completely dependent on the affiliates for the technology required for the manufacturing operations.

The royalty and fee arrangements need to be carefully constructed. The arrangements must reflect the commercial reality of the underlying transaction, and must correspond to what independent parties are likely to agree in arm's length dealings.

From a documentation perspective, it is necessary to elaborately document the precise nature of the intangible and/or the technology support received from the foreign affiliate. The valuation of the intangible (if and to the extent possible), use of the intangible in the value chain, significance of the intangible etc., should also be thoroughly evaluated and documented. The benefits derived by the Indian manufacturer from use of the intangible, including process improvement, quality improvement, cost savings, etc. should also be documented, and if possible, even quantified.

The arm's length nature of these payments has been disputed by the Indian revenue authorities in several cases by questioning the commercial expediency and the quantum of benefit derived by the Indian entity. In cases where Indian taxpayers have been unable to substantiate the benefits received by them, the revenue authorities have been determining the arm's length price for such payments as NIL. This approach of the authorities has also been upheld in few cases where the taxpayer was not able to substantiate the rationale or benefits from the royalty payments6.

Further, the royalty/fee arrangements need to be evaluated regularly to confirm that they continue being relevant from an arm's length perspective, for the period for which royalties/fees are being paid. For instance, assume that a certain technology was provided to the Indian manufacturer in year 1 and a royalty was charged for use of the technology. Further, assume that this technology became obsolete in Year 10, or that it started becoming freely available (say, due to expiration of the underlying patent or otherwise) starting Year 10. The MNE group must re-examine if in these circumstances, whether any royalty indeed ought to be paid by the Indian manufacturer, starting Year 10 under arm's length circumstances.

Another aspect to be considered here is that in a case where the Indian manufacturer is able to generate some intangibles (for instance, improved designs or processes) as a part of its manufacturing process, and the said intangible is then provided to other manufacturing units of the MNE group, in arm's length circumstances, the Indian manufacturer could also be entitled to a remuneration for allowing the use of intangibles developed by it.

Imports from Foreign Affiliates

Machinery and equipments needed for a new manufacturing facility could be imported from abroad. Especially in cases where an existing manufacturing plant is being relocated to India, a vast majority of the machinery and equipments could be imported from overseas affiliates. These can either be used or new machinery/equipments. The Indian transfer pricing regulations provide for determination of arm's length price of such capital purchases also.

The machinery and equipments imported from foreign affiliates need to be valued by a valuation expert. Especially in cases of used machinery, the written down value of the machinery in the books of the foreign affiliate may not necessarily be the correct indication of the arms length price of the machinery. The arm's length price of such machinery needs to be determined based on the current commercial valuation of the machinery, considering options, if available, in the market for similar machinery. Quotations from independent third parties could also serve as useful guides for approximating the arm's length price of the machinery. In any case, a balance needs to be maintained between the valuation requirements under the transfer pricing regulations and Customs regulations. Any imbalance in valuation/pricing could lead to additional tax cost under either set of applicable regulations.

Similarly, in the initial period, the Indian manufacturer might not be able to localize its raw material requirements, and consequently, it may be dependent on its foreign affiliates for its raw material requirements. Again, the pricing policy for such raw materials needs to balance the requirements under Transfer Pricing and Customs Regulations.

CONCEPT OF PERMANENT ESTABLISHMENT

5. The concept of PE was introduced into the Income-tax Act, 1961 as part of the statutory provisions of transfer pricing by the Finance Act, 2001. In section 92F(iii), the word ‘enterprise’ is defined to mean ‘a person including a PE of such person who is proposed to be engaged in any activity relating to the production’. The CBDT Circular No. 14 of 2001 has clarified that the term P.E. has not been defined in the Act, but its meaning may be understood with reference to the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) entered into by India. The article 5 of the DTAA1 4, which India enters into with other countries, lays down that ‘a permanent establishment means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on’. Thus, the intention was to rely upon the concept and definition of PE in the DTAA.

However, vide the Finance Act, 2002 the definition of PE was inserted in the Income-tax Act, 1961 vide section 92F (iiia) which states that the PE shall include a fixed place of business through which the business of the Multi National Enterprise (MNE) is wholly or partly carried on. The difference lies therein between the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the inclusive sense under the Income-tax Act as against the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the exhaustive sense under the DTAA. This analysis is important because it indicates the intention of the Parliament in adopting an inclusive definition of PE so as to cover all forms of PE inclusive of service PE, agency PE, software PE, Construction PE, etc.

In a ruling given by the Authority for Advance Rulings, India (‘AAR’), the AAR has held that a subsidiary may be regarded as a PE, if it does not have significant independent activities of its own.15 In another ruling, the AAR has held that if the agent does not have the authority to conclude contract, then he cannot constitute a PE16 . However, on the other hand, if the parent executes mass contracts made on standard forms without being scrutinized by it, then the agent may constitute a PE. The Supreme Court of India in DIT (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc.1 7 [2007] 162 Taxman 165 has gone a long way in demystifying the concept of permanent establishment in India.

THE DOCUMENTATION PROCESS

NEED FOR DETAILED DOCUMENTATION

4. Transfer pricing calculation produces at least two conse quences: Firstly, it puts national tax jurisdictions under stress because it is an income-shifting system that allows multination als to maximize their after-tax profits by channelling their taxable income to low tax jurisdictions. Secondly, it provides a substantial advantage to multinationals in comparison with non-multinational firms because only the former can use this strate gy.10

Tax jurisdictions are thus constantly challenged to ensure that MNEs do not take undue advantage of their exposure vis-a-vis a localized operator. The only way to guarantee that an MNE is playing by the rule is through proper assessment of their cross-border transactions. This is possible through a detailed study of the company’s functions, assets and risks that are distributed across tax jurisdictions, as these three factors will ultimately determine where the profit should be taxed. Thus the need for a detailed documentation providing not only the details of the related party cross-border transaction, but also a logical justi fication of the prices charged for the transaction.

ARM’S LEGNTH PRINCIPLE

5. This brings us to the concept of arm’s length principle, which simply means replicating the working of an open market where transactions occur between unrelated entities. It is the princi ple or international standard that the OECD member countries have agreed should be used for determining transfer prices for tax purposes. As mentioned in the OECD Guidelines:

It is set forth in Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention as follows: where "conditions are made or imposed between the two enterprises in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enter prises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly".

The arm’s length principle implies that the profits of an MNE should follow where the company has the bulk of its functions, assets and risks. This is the basic principle, a common underly ing concept that most tax authorities across jurisdictions tend to comply with and incorporate as the basis of their transfer pricing principles. A tax authority in any jurisdiction would correctly expect to see a corresponding share of the profit.

[2002]122 TAXMAN 93 (ART) ROYALTY AND TRANSFER PRICING NORMS

S. Murlidharan*

The transfer pricing norms introduced by the Finance Act, 2001 by insertion of sections 92 to 92F in the Income-tax Act, 1961 have serious implications for the concerned assessees as well as the revenue and many of these implications are not easy to foresee. In this article, the author examines the consequences of these provisions in case of dealings between a foreign company and its 51 per cent Indian subsidiary with which the former has a collaboration agreement. The author gives a brief account of the tax treatment likely to be given on a strict interpretation of the provisions to the income of the foreign company by way of royalty on the use of technology supplied by it to its Indian subsidiary - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The transfer pricing norms ushered in by the Finance Act, 2001 and enshrined in sections 92 to 92F of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’) may have unexpected, if not bizarre, consequences in dealings between a foreign company and its fifty-one per cent Indian subsidiary with which the former has a collaboration agreement. Let us take the case of an Indian car manufacturer in collaboration with a foreign automobile company. Let us say, it pays a royalty of five per cent on the ex-factory price of the cars manufactured by it meant for indigenous sale and a royalty of eight per cent on the ex-factory price of cars manufactured for the export market to the foreign collaborator in keeping with the industrial policy of the Government of India on foreign collaborations.

Hitherto, both the sides would not have encountered any difficulties with the Indian tax authorities. The Indian company would have got deduction from its revenues for the royalty thus paid provided it had taken care to deduct tax at source which is a flat rate of 20 per cent of the royalty assuming India has no Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) with the Government of which the foreign collaborator is the resident of and that the collaboration agreement was signed after May 31, 1997 because if the agreement was signed earlier, the rate of tax would be 30 per cent. But the financial year 2001-2002 may mark the beginning of stand off with the Indian tax administration and a protracted legal battle.

Associated enterprise relationship and its consequences

2. A fifty-one per cent subsidiary brings about the relationship of ‘associated enterprise’ between the two companies. In fact, that relationship is attracted even at the twenty-six per cent threshold. In the example on hand, a mere technical collaboration without any financial relationship will attract this relationship, should the Indian company be wholly dependent on the use of the technology supplied by its foreign partner for carrying on its manufacturing operations in India. Now the payment of royalty by the Indian company to its foreign collaborator would be considered as an ‘international transaction’ within the meaning of section 92B as at least one party to the transaction is a non-resident. Section 92(1) says that any income arising from an international transaction shall be computed having regard to the ‘arm’s length’ price. For good measure, section 92(2) follows this up and makes it categorical that in computing income under section 92(1), the allowance for any expense or interest shall also be determined having regard to the ‘arm’s length’ price. Section 92C has prescribed six methods to zero in on the arm’s length price including such method which the CBDT may prescribe. But for royalty, only the first method - comparable uncontrolled price method - would be the best fit because all other methods fail to simply lend themselves to quantification of the ‘arm’s length’ price. The ‘resale price’ method is not appropriate for royalty because the Indian company does not pay for royalty with a view to further transferring the technology to others but for its own manufacturing operations. The ‘cost plus method’ too would be inappropriate for the simple reason that a technology like an invention is priceless and defies costing. Often a technology would belong to the category of costless assets inasmuch as over the years expenses on scientists, etc., would have been charged to the respective year’s profits.

PARA 1 OF ARTICLE 7 OF TREATY

4. In parts (b) and ( c) of para 1, containing ‘restricted force of attraction rule’, there is no ‘requirement of the profits being through permanent establishment’. Conclusion of AAR does not seem to be correct, as explained below:

Technical explanation by US treasury on para 1:

The computation of the business profits attributable to a permanent establishment under this paragraph is subject to the rules of paragraph 3 for the allowance of expenses incurred for the purposes of earning the income. The profits attributable to a permanent establishment may be from sources within or without a Contracting State. Thus, certain items of foreign income source described in section 864(c)(4)(B) of the Code may be attributed to a U.S. permanent establishment of an Indian enterprise and subject to tax in the United States.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)] Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

Most DTAAs between India and other countries define 'royalties' to include payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment. If the specific DTAA between India and the country of which the foreign country is a resident includes 'payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' in its definition of royalty, then the income would be classified as royalty under the DTAA. In such a case, the income would be taxable in India at the rate specified in the DTAA, provided the foreign company is the beneficial owner and the income is not effectively connected to a PE in India. If the DTAA does not include such payments in its royalty definition (under the OECD Model), the income would be treated as business profits and taxable in India only if the foreign company has a PE in India and the profits are attributable to that PE.

8.5-11d Classification as FTS - Section 9(7)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(7)(b) defines 'fees for technical services' as any consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). Where the foreign company also provides the installation and training services for the capital goods, equipment, or tooling to the Indian manufacturer to use them, any fees paid by the Indian manufacturer for these services would squarely fall within the definition of FTS under section 9(7)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India.

Most DTAAs have a specific article on FTS (Fees for Included Services). These articles may include a 'make available' clause, meaning the services must not only be technical but also 'make available' technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to the recipient. If the foreign company is merely providing equipment and not imparting any technical knowledge or skills to the Indian manufacturer that enable the latter to apply the technology independently, the 'make available' test (if present in the DTAA) would not be met. In such a situation, the FTS will not be taxable in India. If the DTAA does not explicitly contain a 'make available' clause, then any service of a managerial, technical, or consultancy nature will be taxable as FTS.

(a)

Whether the foreign company has a PE in India

(b)

Whether the income is such that the presumptive scheme as specified in Section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 applies (corresponding to Section 44BBD of the ITA 1961) (Business of providing services or technology in India, for the purposes of setting up an electronics manufacturing facility).

The taxable income, taking these factors into account, will be as follows.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India, and the business income earned in India is connected to such PE, the tax liability in such a case shall be computed as per the ITA. If the conditions of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 is fulfilled; the taxable business income shall be computed on a presumptive basis at the rate of 25% of the specified amount. Business income not connected to PE in India

If the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the business income earned by him in India shall not be taxable in India. In such a situation, the presumptive scheme of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 will have no relevance.

3.4-3 Purchase of goods in India for export [Section 9(8)(c)(ii)(A) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961 provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export. In the corresponding section 9(9)(c)(ii) of the ITA 2025, the words used are "purchase of goods in India for the purposes of export out of India".

On a strict literal interpretation, the addition of "out of India" might seem redundant, since "export" universally means sending goods out of the country. However, the expression "export out of India" would primarily serve to explicitly remove any remote ambiguity. It could prevent an interpretation where "export" might be construed to include movement to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) within India (which is treated as foreign territory for certain purposes but is geographically within India) or other domestic transfers that are deemed exports for other regulatory purposes but do not involve physical exit from India's customs territory. It would clarify that the exemption applies only when goods physically leave the Indian customs territory.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively. This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

2.8 Amendments to section 9(1)(vi)

2.8.1 Amendments Explanations 4, 5 and 6 have been inserted in section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-4-1976 so as to clarify that—

(i) the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred (Explanation 4).

(ii) royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India (Explanation 5).

(iii) the expression 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret (Explanation 6).

2.8.2 Object

The objective of the amendments as explained in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2012 is as follows:

"II. Section 9(1)(vi) provides that any income payable by way of royalty in respect of any right, property or information is deemed to be accruing or arising in India. The term "royalty" has been defined in Explanation 2 which means consideration received or receivable for transfer of all or any right in respect of certain rights, property or information. Some judicial decisions have interpreted this definition in a manner which has raised doubts as to whether consideration for use of computer software is royalty or not; whether the right, property or information has to be used directly by the payer or is to be located in India or control or possession of it has to be with the payer. Similarly, doubts have been raised regarding the meaning of the term processed.

Considering the conflicting decisions of various courts in respect of income in nature of royalty and to restate the legislative intent, it is further proposed to amend the Income-tax Act in following manner:-

(i) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the consideration for use or right to use of computer software is royalty by clarifying that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information as mentioned in Explanation 2, includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

(ii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not

(a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.

(iii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the term "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.

These amendments will take effect retrospectively from 1st June, 1976 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 1977-78 and subsequent assessment years."

Royalty to include consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment

11.1 Under section 9(1)(vi), income by way of royalty payable is deemed to accrue or arise in India subject to certain conditions. The term ‘royalty’ has been defined in Explanation 2 to this clause.

Section 9 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 so as to provide that the term ‘royalty’ shall include :

(a) consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, but not including the amounts referred to section 44B.

(b) consideration for rendering of any services in connection with the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

The amendment provides that ‘royalty’ shall not include amounts referred to in section 44BB. Section 44BB, inter alia, provides that in the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of supply of plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the exploration for and exploitation of mineral oils, 10% of the aggregate of the amounts which have been specified in the section shall be deemed to be profits and gains of the business. Thus, hire charges for the plant and machinery used for exploration, etc., of mineral oils shall not be treated as ‘royalty’ and shall continue to be taxed under section 44BB.

Following points need to be noted :

● The amendment to section 9 brings it in line with the Double Tax Conventions (DTCs) entered into by India which provide that ‘royalty’ includes consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. These DTCs are based on the OECD Model Conventions 1963 and 1977. It may be noted, however, that the definition of ‘royalties’ in Article 12(2) of OECD Model was amended in 1992 by excluding payments for the use, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

● A distinction must be made between royalties paid for the use of equipment and payments constituting consideration for the outright sale of equipment. In CIT v. Davy Ashmore India Ltd.[1991] 190 ITR 626, the Calcutta High Court has held that where there is an outright sale or purchase, the consideration is for the transfer of designs, secret formula, etc., and cannot be treated as royalty. Applying the same ratio, consideration for outright sale of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment cannot be treated as royalty.

● Section 44D provides that no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C in computing the income by way of royalty or fees for technical services received from the Government or an Indian concern in pursuance of an agreement made by the foreign company with Government or with the Indian concern. For the purpose of section 44D, royalty has the same meaning as in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi). Hence if any income by way of royalty is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C, and tax will have to be paid on gross amount. If any income by way of consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment or consideration for rendering of any services in such connection is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), then the same will attract the same rate of tax as applicable to ‘royalty’.

● ‘Equipment’ includes anything used in equipping; furniture, outfit, warlike apparatus; necessaries for travelling, etc. (Oxford Dictionary). Vide the Finance Act, 1976, it was provided, inter alia, that in case of payments of interest, royalty or fees for technical services (FTS) received from a resident payer, income would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where the interest or royalty or FTS is relatable to a business or profession carried on by the resident payer outside India or for making or earning any income from any source outside India. The Finance Act, 2007 inserted an Explanation in section 9 with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 and clarified that where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(v), (vi) or (vii), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India1.

The amendment was made to neutralize the judgment of Supreme Court in Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. DIT[2007] 288 ITR 408/ 158 Taxman 259.

The Karnataka High Court in Jindal Thermal Power Co. Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 252 has held that the Explanation does not fully neutralise Supreme Court decision and has observed as follows:

“The Explanation incorporated in section 9(2) declares that ‘where the income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under clauses (v), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident; whether or not the resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India’. The plain reading of the said provision suggests that criterion of residence, place of business or business connection of a non-resident in India has been done away with for fastening the tax liability. However, the criteria of rendering service in India and the utilisation of the service in India laid down by the Supreme Court in Ishikawajima Heavy Industries Ltd.’s case (supra) to attract tax liability under section 9(1)(vii) remains untouched and unaffected by the Explanation to section 9(2).” (Emphasis supplied)

In view of the above, the Finance Act, 2010 substitutes the Explanation, with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 also to cover the situation left out earlier, that is, rendition of services in India and provides that the income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India whether the non-resident has rendered services in India or not.

After the amendment, based on source rule, interest, royalty and fees for technical services would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, to a non-resident, whether or not:

⮚ the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India; and

⮚ the non-resident has rendered services in India.

In other words, even if a non-resident does not have residence or place of business or business connection in India and has not rendered services in India, interest, royalty and fees for technical services, if paid by a resident (not utilised for the purposes of business outside India) would be deemed to accrue or arise in India and accordingly taxable in the hands of the non-resident.

It appears, even after the amendment, having regard to the facts and the circumstances, certain payments may not constitute income in the hands of a non-resident payee, like, fees for services not in the nature of ‘make available’ services and, accordingly, does not constitute fees for technical services (and, hence, in the nature of business or professional income) in terms of a Treaty.

22.1-3 Distinction between copyright and copyrighted software Copyright is different from the material object which is the subject of the copyright. So, a transfer of the material object does not necessarily involve a transfer of copyright - Copyright Act by Iyengar.

For example, sale of a book (which is a copyrighted article) does not mean sale of copyright in the book. The customer gets only limited rights in the book. He cannot copy the book or any part of it.

Similarly, sale of software recorded on CD is sale of a copyrighted article. The buyer does not get copyright in software. He has only limited right to use the software product.

Thus, source is where the transaction of sale has taken place. If the specified activity has taken place outside India, it may be argued that the source is not in India within the meaning of section 9(1)(i).

In CIT v. Havells India Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 476/208 Taxman 114 (Delhi), the Court had to interpret section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 which provides that fees for technical services do not accrue or arise in India to the extent they are paid by a resident for utilizing the services for making or earning any income from any "source" outside India. It observed as follows:

"Section 9(1)(vii)(b) contemplates a source located outside India. It is difficult to conceptualise the place/situs of the person who make payment for the export sales as the source located outside India from which assessee earned profits. The export contracts obviously are concluded in India and the assessee's products are sent outside India under such contracts. The manufacturing activity is located in India. The source of income is created at the moment when the export contracts are concluded in India. Thereafter the goods are exported in pursuance of the contract and the export proceeds are sent by the importer and are received in India. The importer of the assessee's products is no doubt situated outside India, but he cannot be regarded as a source of income. The receipt of the sale proceeds emanate from him from outside India. He is, therefore, only the source of the monies received. The income component of the monies or the export receipts is located or situated only in India. We are making a distinction between the source of the income and the source of the receipt of the monies. In order to fall within the second exception provided in Section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Act, the source of the income, and not the receipt, should be situated outside India. That condition is not satisfied in the present case."

Thus, the Court held that export sales proceeds received from goods manufactured and exported from India do not constitute a "source" outside India but is a source in India. Similarly, for the non-resident who sells the goods from outside India, it could be argued that it constitutes a source in the country from which the sale is made and not in India where the customer is situated.

Section 9

Finance Act, 2001

Royalty to include consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment

11.1 Under section 9(1)(vi), income by way of royalty payable is deemed to accrue or arise in India subject to certain conditions. The term 'royalty' has been defined in Explanation 2 to this clause.

Section 9 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 so as to provide that the term 'royalty' shall include :

(a)

consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, but not including the amounts referred to section 44B.

(b)

consideration for rendering of any services in connection with the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

The amendment provides that 'royalty' shall not include amounts referred to in section 44BB. Section 44BB, inter alia, provides that in the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of supply of plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the exploration for and exploitation of mineral oils, 10% of the aggregate of the amounts which have been specified in the section shall be deemed to be profits and gains of the business. Thus, hire charges for the plant and machinery used for exploration, etc., of mineral oils shall not be treated as 'royalty' and shall continue to be taxed under section 44BB.

Following points need to be noted :

The amendment to section 9 brings it in line with the Double Tax Conventions (DTCs) entered into by India which provide that 'royalty' includes consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. These DTCs are based on the OECD Model Conventions 1963 and 1977. It may be noted, however, that the definition of 'royalties' in Article 12(2) of OECD Model was amended in 1992 by excluding payments for the use, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

A distinction must be made between royalties paid for the use of equipment and payments constituting consideration for the outright sale of equipment. In CIT v. Davy Ashmore India Ltd. [1991] 190 ITR 626, the Calcutta High Court has held that where there is an outright sale or purchase, the consideration is for the transfer of designs, secret formula, etc., and cannot be treated as royalty. Applying the same ratio, consideration for outright sale of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment cannot be treated as royalty.

Section 44D provides that no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C in computing the income by way of royalty or fees for technical services received from the Government or an Indian concern in pursuance of an agreement made by the foreign company with Government or with the Indian concern. For the purpose of section 44D, royalty has the same meaning as in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi). Hence if any income by way of royalty is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C, and tax will have to be paid on gross amount. If any income by way of consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment or consideration for rendering of any services in such connection is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), then the same will attract the same rate of tax as applicable to 'royalty'.

'Equipment' includes anything used in equipping; furniture, outfit, warlike apparatus; necessaries for travelling, etc. (Oxford Dictionary). Issue arises whether 'equipment' includes airplanes/ships/satellites/vehicles? A ship was a part of the 'equipment' of the business of the shipowner whose ship carries ore/bulk/oil. [Coltman v. Bibby Tankers Ltd. [1987] 3 All ER 1068, 1071 (HL)].

MRP is not required to be printed on following categories of software - (i) software on optical media supplied free of charge, for which right to use or license is purchased separately (ii) full pack - packaged software with limited validity, not for resale and generally imported for demonstrations or for OEMs (iii) up-grade fully pack - packaged software supplied free of charge under annual maintenance/subscription/software assurance contract and (iv) updates for packaged software - supplied free of charge under annual maintenance/subscription/software assurance contract etc. - In these cases, excise duty/CVD will be charged only on the value, excluding the value representing consideration for transfer of right to use such packaged/canned software. However, service tax under the category of ITSS would be levied on such portion subsequently - MF(DR) circular No. 15/2011-Cus dated 18-3-2011.

Customised software - Customised software is subject to service tax - Para 6.4.5 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Really, if Vat is payable on entire value of goods, then value for purpose of service tax becomes Nil. However, most of software manufacturers are paying both Vat and service tax.

Income deemed to accrue or arise in India*

Income deemed to accrue or arise in India [Section 9]

5.1 Section 9 of the Act provides for situations where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Vide the Finance Act, 1976, it was provided, inter alia, that in case of payments of interest, royalty or fees for technical services (FTS) received from a resident payer, income would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where the interest or royalty or FTS is relatable to a business or profession carried on by the resident payer outside India or for making or earning any income from any source outside India.

The Finance Act, 2007 inserted an Explanation in section 9 with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 and clarified that where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(v), (vi) or (vii), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India1.

The amendment was made to neutralize the judgment of Supreme Court in Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. DIT[2007] 288 ITR 408/ 158 Taxman 259.

The Karnataka High Court in Jindal Thermal Power Co. Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 252 has held that the Explanation does not fully neutralise Supreme Court decision and has observed as follows:

“The Explanation incorporated in section 9(2) declares that ‘where the income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under clauses (v), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident; whether or not the resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India’. The plain reading of the said provision suggests that criterion of residence, place of business or business connection of a non-resident in India has been done away with for fastening the tax liability. However, the criteria of rendering service in India and the utilisation of the service in India laid down by the Supreme Court in Ishikawajima Heavy Industries Ltd.’s case (supra) to attract tax liability under section 9(1)(vii) remains untouched and unaffected by the Explanation to section 9(2).” (Emphasis supplied)

In view of the above, the Finance Act, 2010 substitutes the Explanation, with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 also to cover the situation left out earlier, that is, rendition of services in India and provides that the income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India whether the non-resident has rendered services in India or not.

After the amendment, based on source rule, interest, royalty and fees for technical services would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, to a non-resident, whether or not:

⮚ the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India; and

⮚ the non-resident has rendered services in India.

In other words, even if a non-resident does not have residence or place of business or business connection in India and has not rendered services in India, interest, royalty and fees for technical services, if paid by a resident (not utilised for the purposes of business outside India) would be deemed to accrue or arise in India and accordingly taxable in the hands of the non-resident.

It appears, even after the amendment, having regard to the facts and the circumstances, certain payments may not constitute income in the hands of a non-resident payee, like, fees for services not in the nature of ‘make available’ services and, accordingly, does not constitute fees for technical services (and, hence, in the nature of business or professional income) in terms of a Treaty.

2.1-1 Differences between the pre-amendment Explanation 2A and the post amendment Explanation 2A

Differences between the pre-amendment Explanation 2A and the post amendment Explanation 2A are as follows:— Explanation 2A(a) refers to "transaction in respect of any goods, services or property carried out by a non-resident with any person in India". Should the transaction be "in India" or the person with whom the non-resident is transacting should be "in India"? It appears that the person (counterparty) has to be in India. The transaction may or may not be in India. Likewise, the non-resident need not be in India.

The said counter party may be—

(a)

a resident of India or a non-resident;

(b)

an individual or any other corporate or non corporate entity;

(c)

carrying on business or not

The counterparty has to be in "India" which term has been defined in section 2(25A) as follows:

"India" means the territory of India as referred to in article 1 of the Constitution, its territorial waters, seabed and subsoil underlying such waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone or any other maritime zone as referred to in the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 (80 of 1976), and the air space above its territory and territorial waters.

The definition is very wide and read literally, Explanation 2A would cover even transactions between a non-resident airlines and a passenger in an aeroplane flying over India! It could be argued, however, that in the context, the wide meaning is not adopted.

It is pertinent to note that mere SEP does not constitute business connection; it is the SEP of a non-resident "in India" that constitutes business connection (the opening line of Explanation 2A). Now, the first proviso to Explanation 2A states that transaction or activities specified in the Explanation shall constitute SEP in India, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business "in India" or not or whether he renders services "in India" or not etc. Thus, the proviso by using the expression "in India", appears to constitute an SEP of a non-resident in India as used in the opening lines in Explanation 2A, and as contained in clauses (a) and (b) of Explanation 2A and hence, there is a business connection even if the non-resident is not in India.

Since the words "through digital means" are deleted in the amended definition, there could be an SEP if there is a specified business activity or interaction with prescribed number of users in India whether through digital or other means.

For a detailed discussion on SEP, see Taxmann's Master Guide to Income-tax Act, 2018, (see para 3.2).

Some aspects relating to SEP under the amended law which are common to the definition of SEP in pre-amended Explanation 2A are reiterated below:—

(a)

A transaction in respect of physical goods (including books) is also covered by the expression SEP.

(b)

A transaction in respect of shrink wrap software may result in SEP since it is now well settled that such software is "goods".

(c)

A transaction in respect of services which are not covered by definition of fees for technical services in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii) (e.g. consideration for construction project, etc.) may also constitute SEP.

(d)

The non-resident may carry out transaction directly or through a third party.

(e)

The provision in the DTAA with the country of which the non-resident is a resident will override the Explanation 2A and in the absence of a permanent establishment, a non-resident may not be liable to tax in India merely on account of SEP, if he complies with the requirements of section 90(4)/(5).

The accrual must be real taking into account the actuality of the situation. Whether an accrual has taken place or not must, in appropriate cases, be judged on the principles of real income theory. After accrual, non-charging of tax on the same because of certain conduct based on the ipse dixit of a particular assessee cannot be accepted. It is as if he has received only the original amount minus the amount to be surrendered. The amount surrendered is not part of the profits at all.2 Income surrendered because of contract is not likewise included.3
