The assessee is a tax resident of Singaore, hence, a non-resident entity. It is simly a distributor of softwares. It purchases softwares from non-resident manufacturers/sellers such as Microsoft, Adobe, etc. and distribute/sell them to distributors and customers in India. Thus the assessee itself is not the manufacturer or creator of softwares. Therefore, the assessee cannot own coyright over the softwares as the manufacturer or creator of the softwares can hold coyright over the softwares. Thus the products sold by the assessee are ready to use off the shelf or shrink wrapped softwares, which are nothing but coyrighted articles. From the nature of softwares sold by the assessee, it can be very well construed that the coyright over the softwares sold by the assessee was owned by the companies creating such softwares like Microsoft, Adobe, etc. The assessee is merely a trader of softwares, hence, has no domain or ownership over the softwares. Thus when the assessee does not have any ownership over the softwares sold, it could not have transferred the right to use of copyright of the softwares to distributors/customers in India.

The Supreme Court in the case of Engineering Analysis centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 had an occasion to examine when the consideration received from sale of software can be considered to be in the nature of royalty. The Supreme Court had segregated the transactions relating to the sale of software to following four categories:

(i)

The first category deals with cases in which computer software is purchased directly by an end-user, resident in India, from a foreign, non-resident supplier or manufacturer.

(ii)

The second category of cases deals with resident Indian companies that act as distributors or resellers, by purchasing computer software from foreign, non-resident suppliers or manufacturers and then reselling the same to resident Indian end-users.

(iii)

The third category concerns cases wherein the distributor happens to be a foreign, non-resident vendor, who, after purchasing software from a foreign, non-resident seller, resells the same to resident Indian distributors or end-users.

(iv)

The fourth category includes cases wherein computer software is affixed onto hardware and is sold as an integrated unit/equipment by foreign, non-resident suppliers to resident Indian distributors or end-users. [Para 10]

Undisputedly, the assessee's case falls within the third category. While deciding the issue whether the payment made is in the nature of royalty, the Supreme Court very clearly and categorically held that the amount paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufactures/suppliers as consideration for the resell/use of the computer software through end-user license agreement/distribution agreement is not in the nature of royalty for the use of copyright in the computer software, hence, cannot be treated as royalty. The aforesaid ratio laid down by the Supreme Court clearly applies to the facts of the instant appeal. Thus the Commissioner (Appeals) has adopted the right course of action while deleting the addition made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 11]

In view of the aforesaid, there was no infirmity in the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 12]

[2010] 322 ITR 125/188 Taxman 223 (AAR - New Delhi), CIT v. Dynamic Vertical Software India (P.) Ltd. [2011] 332 ITR 222/201 Taxman 78 (Mag.)/12 taxmann.com 431 (Delhi), DIT v. Ericsson A.B. In the present case, the assessee does not have ownership of the software and does not have right to reproduce the said software. From which it is clear that consideration paid for the use of/the right to use the copyright of any scientific work etc. would qualify as royalty. In other words if the payment is not for intellectual properties such as copyright, patents trademarks etc., the payment cannot be treated as royalty. The assessee had acquired right to sell the copyrighted article (software products) and not the right to use the copyright.

Here, hence is also made to Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) wherein royalty has been defined. As per the definition term royalty envisages payment for transfer of all or any rights in intellectual properties (such as copyrights, patents etc.) by the owner of such intellectual property by any other person. It is clear that the Act does not contain a definition of such intellectual properties that are included within the scope of term royalty. [Para 5.1.2]

A retrospective amendment has been made to Explanation to section 9(1)(vi) by Finance Act, 2012. The Finance Act, 2012 inserted Explanation 4 to the section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976. From the amendment it is clear that it covers the transfer of all or any right for use/right to use of computer software including grant of licence. The amendment has been made to the section i.e., to domestic law. But, there is no corresponding change in Tax Treaty. It is also to be remembered that the assessee had already made the payment before the amendment was introduced. At the point of making payment to ASL, the assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source. So, now it cannot be compelled to deduct tax. The basic principal of taxation stipulates that nobody is supposed to perform the impossible. In the case of B4U International Holdings Ltd. v. Dy. Similar is the position of Indo-UK DTAA, where term royalty has not been defined. Considering same, the definition of term royalty as appearing in the India UK DTAA apply and amendments made by Finance Act, 2012 would have no bearing on the present case. In the instant case, the DTAA is providing particular mode of computation for royalty. As per the agreement the assessee did not have any right to generate the license key or make copies of license key or was provided access to source code in the software. The ASL software products were developed and marketed by it were in the nature of Ashrink-wrap-software-products that are also known as off the shelf software products. On second appeal:

Section 9(1)(vi ) provides that royalty receivable by a non-resident from a person in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Further, section 90(2) provides that if the provisions of Tax Treaty between India and the country of the non-resident are more beneficial to such non-resident, then the provisions of Tax Treaty shall override the provisions of the Act. [Para 6]

Article 12(3) of the India-USA DTAA defines the term ‘royalty’. As per the India-USA DTAA royalty in respect of the subject-matter of a copyright includes only the payments for the use i.e., exploitation of the copyright of such literary/artistic or scientific work. Therefore, in order to be classified as royalty, the right of the person in possession of the subject-matter of a copyright should be to utilize such copyright in the manner which is otherwise protected by the respective copyright law in favour of the owner of the copyright. The use of the copyright of a copyrighted work is different from use of such work itself. The acquisition of a product, wherein the subject-matter of copyright is embedded, without right to exploit the copyright, does not amount to use or right to use the copyright of such literary/artistic/scientific i.e., copyrighted work. [Para 6.1]

Further, as per clause 13.1 of the OECD model commentary, payments made for acquisition of partial rights in copyright would represent a royalty where the consideration is for the right to use the programmes in a manner that would, without such license, constitute an infringement of the copyright. In other words, the payment can constitute royalty only if the transferor grants to the transferee the right to use the copyright of the product. If, on the other hand, the use of the programmes by the transferee (by acquiring a copy of such programme) is in a manner which does not constitute infringement of the copyright, the payment therefor would not amount to royalty.

Therefore, under the OECD model commentary also payments for acquiring a copy of a computer programme would not be treated as payments for right to use the copyright in the computer programmes. Accordingly such payments are to be considered as commercial income under article 7 and not as royalty under article 12 of the India-USA DTAA. [Paras 6.2 and 6.3]

Further, the computer programme may be copyrightable as intellectual property does not alter the fact that once in the form of a floppy disc or other medium, the programmes is tangible, movable and available in the market place. The fact that some programmes may be tailored for specific purposes need not alter their status as ‘goods’ because the code definition included ‘specially manufactured goods’. In the case of Tata Consultancy Services v. State of Andhra Pradesh [2004] 271 ITR 401/ 141 Taxman 132 the Apex Court after citing several decisions of the Courts of the USA has noted that acquisition of a copy of computer programmes, which is a copyrighted article, amounts to sale of such article. [Para 6.7]

Therefore, the payment made by the assessee to ‘H’ was not in the nature of royalty but was subject-matter of article 7 of the India-USA DTAA. The related payments made by the assessee to BT Canada were in the nature of reimbursements, and, as evident from the details taken to record earlier in this order, there were specific cost allocations which were borne by the assessee. These payments, could not be viewed as payments for right to use the equipment. The assessee was entitled to certain services, during rendition of which even if certain equipment were to be used, but that by itself did not result in any use of or right to use the equipment by the assessee. The service may involve use of equipment but that does not vest right in the assessee to use the equipment. Even if a part of consideration can be said to be on account of use of equipment by breaking down all the components of economic activity for which consideration is paid, it is neither practicable, nor permissible, to assign monetary value to each of the segment of this economic activity and consider that amount in isolation, for the purpose of deciding character of that amount. Similarly, even if the payment is to be considered as payment for use of software, as is the settled legal position as on now, unless there is no transfer of copyright, there cannot be any occasion to hold it as royalty. In any event, so far as the transaction between the assessee and the BT Canada is concerned, it is simply in the nature of reimbursement of expenses incurred by BT Canada, on behalf of the assessee, and it has no income element so far as BT Canada is concerned. II. IS THE RECEIPT A SOFTWARE ROYALTY?

The next contention put forth on behalf of the assessee is that the amount received from RIPL was in the nature of software royalty because it purchased certain software and transferred the same to it. In support of the contention that the receipt from RIPL is not royalty, the assessee relied on Engineering Analysis (supra). A proposition was bolstered that RIPL got copyrighted article from the assessee, which was different from the copyright in the software purchased. [Para 16]

Under such circumstances, in respect of works done in foreign countries or by foreign authors, the copyright does not automatically flow or extended to them. The rights of the foreign author are to be examined in the light of the Copyright Act and the relevant treaty or the convention, if any, signed by India with that country to which the foreign author belongs. The copyright in a foreign product thus does not flow automatically or impliedly, so far as the Indian copyright laws are concerned. [Para 43] Hence, while interpreting the definition of 'royalty' as provided in the DTAA, it is to be seen as to what has been purchased by the assessee, i.e., whether the 'copyright' itself has been purchased or what the assessee has purchased is only a 'copyrighted work'. It is also required to be analysed as to whether the use of such right would amount to infringement of copyright if a license or permission in this respect is not given by the owner; and when assessee has purchased a copyrighted product, whether the use of the same for the business purpose of the assessee is covered within the exceptions as provided under section 52 of the Copyright Act. Further, in case of imported work/product, whether the protection of copyright is available to the foreign author in terms of sections 40, 40A, 41 and 42 of the Copyright Act, 1957. [Para 44]

The provisions of the Copyright Act, are clear and unambiguous in this respect. If the assessee has purchased a copy of a computer software programme and he uses the said copy for his business purpose and if the said use falls within the scope and purview of the exceptions of section 52, such as the use of it for the purpose for which it is supplied and to make backup copies for temporary purpose as a protection against loss or damage and doing of any act necessary to obtain information essential for operating the software for the purpose for which it is purchased etc. as provided under section 52 of the copyright Act, then in that event it cannot be said to be an infringement of copyrights of the author or owner of the work. In view of above, when one see the definition as per the statutory provisions/domestic law of the country, i.e., Copyright Act, 1957 of India (the taxing State in this case), it is apparent that the fair use of the work for the purpose of which it is being purchased and doing of such other acts including making of copy for protection from damage or loss cannot, in any case, said to be any infringement of copyright whether or not any license in this respect has been granted by the author/owner of the work. Even in cases where the owner of the copyrighted work may restrict the use of or right to use the work by way of certain terms of the license/software agreement, the validity or the enforceability of the same may be subject matter in other laws such as Indian Contract Act 1872, Sale of goods Act 1930 or the Consumer Protection Act 1986 etc., but, the same in any way cannot be said to grant of or infringement of copyright in the light of specific statutory provisions of Copyright Act 1957. [Para 45]

In the instant cases, in the DTAA of India with respective countries the definition of royalty in none of the respective treaties specifically include any consideration for the use of or the right to use any 'computer software' and therefore, the same cannot be imported or read into it. [Para 47]

One may further clarify here that without expressing one's opinion or any view in relation to the definition of 'royalty' vis-à-vis'computer software' as provided under the Income-tax Act, findings are only in respect of the scope of 'royality' under the DTAA. [Para 48]

In view of detailed discussion made above, the assessee cannot be said to have paid the consideration for use of or the right to use copyright but has simply purchased the copyrighted work embedded in the CD-ROM which can be said to be sale of 'good' by the owner. The consideration paid by the assessee thus as per the clauses of DTAA cannot be said to be royalty and the same will be outside the scope of the definition of 'royalty' as provided in DTAA and would be taxable as business income of the recipient. The assessee is entitled to the fair use of the work/product including making copies for temporary purpose for protection against damage or loss even without a license provided by the owner in this respect and the same would not constitute infringement of any copyright of the owner of the work even as per the provisions of section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957. [Para 49]

YALTY?

The next contention put forth on behalf of the assessee is that the amount received from RIPL was in the nature of software royalty because it purchased certain software and transferred the same to it. In support of the contention that the receipt from RIPL is not royalty, the assessee relied on Engineering Analysis (supra). A proposition was bolstered that RIPL got copyrighted article from the assessee, which was different from the copyright in the software purchased. [Para 16] Insofar as the ratio in the case of Engineering Analysis (supra) is concerned, there is no dispute that it has been held by the Summit Court that ownership of copyright in a work is different from the ownership of the physical material in which the copyrighted work may happen to be embodied. Parting with copyright entails parting with the right to do any of the acts mentioned in section 14 of the Copyright Act. Where the core of a transaction is to authorize the end-user to have access to and make use of the 'licensed' computer software product, over which the licensee has no exclusive rights, no copyright is parted with. However, the facts of the instant case are entirely different. On a specific query, the assessee failed to point out as to the specific number of licenses purchased by the assessee from third party vendors and those transferred to RIPL. Rather it was fairly conceded during the course of proceedings and has been established that there was no direct transfer of software licenses to RIPL but it was a case of allowing user to RIPL from the centralized IT infrastructure maintained by the assessee in Switzerland. What is relevant is the amount of receipt by the assessee for rendering services and not the costs incurred in the purchase of software facilitating the provision of services. Here is situation in which the assessee purchased software from third party vendors and then licensed the same to RIPL for use. Rather all the software purchased by it were integrated by the assessee into its own centralized IT infrastructure for facilitating the provision of the IT services enlisted above to its group entities and RIPL is one of such beneficiary of the services. It is rather a case of the assessee only purchasing the software from third party vendors and the transactions qua such individual software coming to an end there itself. The ratio of Engineering Analysis (supra) can apply where the vendors demonstrate that what they transferred to the assessee was copyrighted article and not copyright. On the contrary, this is a second stage in which the software licenses, being in the nature of copyrighted article, were purchased by the assessee and then used in the providing various services, such as, Client Based Services (CBS), Business Applications for Sales, Marketing and Technology Users (BASMT), Business Applications for Parts and Service Users (BAPS), Business Applications for Operations Users (BAOP), Business Applications for Finance and Controlling Users (BAFC) etc. [Para 17]

The fact that the assessee utilized the software purchased from third party vendors for integrating them with its own software for making a common centralized integrated IT infrastructure so as to render the IT services is further fortified by the details of the alleged reimbursement submitted by the assessee. First table on the paper book has last two columns with captions `Weights for IT infrastructure cost allocation' and `Weighted average allocation'. On a specific query, the assessee submitted that the assessee company spent certain amount on IT infrastructure, independent of the software cost, which was allocated between all the 19 entities and the RIPL's share in it was determined at 17.09 per cent. This shows that apart from purchasing the software for the centralized IT infrastructure Centre, the assessee also incurred certain IT infrastructure costs for integrating them into its centralized system so as to render services to the worldwide entities, which was charged to RIPL at 17.09 per cent. This plentifully proves that the amount recovered by the assessee from RIPL is not towards transfer of any software so as to constitute software royalty. The contention of the assessee in this respect stands repelled. [Para 18]

The Tribunal observed that attribution of profits should be made in accordance with transfer pricing principles. As the charge for employees visiting India and those seconded to India was subsumed in the transfer pricing analysis of CIS, the Tribunal concluded that attribution was required to be made on account of free of cost assets and software provided by CMG to CIS.

The Tribunal held that Profit Split Method was not appropriate and computed the profit to be attributed to CMG's PE as under: While arriving at its conclusion, the Tribunal considered the decisions in Anglo French TextileCo. Ltd. v. CIT10 and Hukum Chand Mills Ltd. v. CIT11 and regarded 15% as being appropriate attribution in Convergys Customer Management's case (supra) (following the decision in Hukum Chand Mills Ltd. case (supra)).

The Tribunal did not comment on the issue of economic double taxation raised by CMG.

The decision correctly acknowledges that transfer pricing principles should be respected while attributing profits to the PE and that there can be no further attribution if the profile of the PE has been entirely considered. However, it falls slightly short as it does not discuss the relevance of the percentage of profits to be attributed (i.e. 15%) with respect to the specific facts in Convergys Customer Management's case (supra) as also the reason for applying the same on the profits retained in US.

In the past, courts have adopted different approaches for attributing profits, such as 35% of profits for marketing activities in India12, 20% of the net profits of Indian sales for preliminary negotiations of contracts and network planning13, 15% of revenues in respect of bookings made in India less expenses for equipment and agency PE14 and 50% of commission less expenses for substantial activities in India15. It thus becomes more complicated to decode the appropriateness and acceptability of the computation of profits attributable to the PE.

Receipts towards link charges and software cost – whether royalty

In the facts before the Tribunal, CMG had incurred charges for leased lines (under-sea cables) which allowed dedicated capacity for private, secure communication from India to US.CMG had also incurred licence cost in respect of packaged enterprise application software, PeopleSoft. A portion of these expenses were reimbursed by CIS to CMG.

The AO sought to tax these reimbursements as "royalty" in the hands of CMG.

Apart from arguing that the receipts from CIS were not royalties under Article 12 of the tax treaty, CMG contended that these were mere reimbursement of expenses incurred. In support of its claim, CMG relied on the decision in case of Expeditors International India Pvt. Ltd.16.

The Tribunal accepted CMG's contentions and held that the payments were mere reimbursement of expenses not taxable in India.The Tribunal also concluded that owing to the narrower interpretation of the term 'royalties' under the tax treaty, the payments were not in the nature of royalty.While doing so, the Tribunal confirmed that the interpretation under the tax treaty would not necessarily be altered due to amendment of the Act.

The decision of the Tribunal could come to the rescue of several multinational companies who cannot avoid incurring a certain level of common costs and recovering the same (cross-charged based on an appropriate allocation key) from their group entities. The entity cross-charging the cost to an Indian entity could examine whether the receipts can qualify as reimbursement of expenditure (as opposed to income) and be claimed as not taxable in India. Generally, receipts would be considered as reimbursement if the same are on a cost to cost basis without any mark-up17 (however, cross-charge of expenses is fraught with its own set of issues, such as applicability of withholding tax18 and allowance of the expenditure in the hands of the entity being cross-charged).

Summary

The decision of the Tribunal is certainly a welcome one with respect to the aspects of equipment royalties, software and reimbursements. However, it takes a very narrow view in regard to the creation of a PE by presence of the visiting employees. The Tribunal has now come with a new method of attributing profits which is different from the ones adopted in earlier precedents. The last thing that one would want is yet another method to add to the complexity of the computation of profits to an Indian PE.

It is hoped that the authorities will clarify the tax position, particularly with respect to Indian back office service providers, and allay the taxpayers' fears.

The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

8.7-11d Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on whether the foreign company has a PE in India.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India and the business income earned in India is connected to that PE, the tax liability shall be computed in accordance with the ITA.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the foreign company does not have a PE in India, its business income earned in India shall not be taxable in India.

8.7-12 Transaction with associated enterprises

Where an Indian entity provides data centre services to its associated enterprise (a foreign company), it may opt for the safe harbour framework under the transfer pricing provisions. If the Indian entity earns an operating profit margin of at least 15% of operating expenses from such international transactions, the transaction price will be deemed to be at arm's length, and no transfer pricing adjustment will be required. [see Para 12.2-2b]

There are five parties in the transaction relating to the data centre: SCloud Pte. Ltd. (a Singapore-based cloud management platform), DC Ltd. (an Indian data centre), RS India Ltd. (an Indian reseller), OTT Pvt. Ltd. (the Indian end user) and OS Inc. (the Singapore-based end user).

The details of the transaction between the parties are as follows:

DC enters into an agreement with SCloud to provide 50 servers, 10TB storage, power, cooling, and facility services for Rs. 7,00,000 per month. DC owns and operates all physical equipment, while SCloud has only API access to manage virtual resources and no ownership or physical control.

SCloud enters into a reseller agreement with RS, offering managed cloud services (including the DC infrastructure, SCloud proprietary management platform, orchestration software, 24/7 monitoring, technical support, and analytics) for Rs. 13,50,000 per month.

SCloud enters into a cloud service agreement with OS, under which OS offers managed cloud services for USD 50,000 per month.

CA.P.V.S.S. PRASAD*

1. Introduction

India as a tax jurisdiction is witnessing radical changes on the taxation front. More so, in the area of direct taxes and particularly on the International Taxation Front. Recent land mark judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India [2012]204 Taxman 408/17 taxmann.com 202, has laid down certain far reaching principles on "form" and "substance". The reaction of the Government to this judgment has been very notable in terms of bringing various retrospective amendments. Purport of the Vodafone judgment has been neutralized by bringing concept of taxation of indirect transfers happening outside India in respect of which underlying assets are located in India.

There are amendments in respect of withholding taxes under section 195, Tax Residence Certificate under section 90/under section 90A, introduction of Advance Pricing Agreements (APA) and all the more important introduction of General Anti Avoidance Rule (GAAR) in Finance Bill, 2012. In respect of "Royalty" there is a retrospective amendment which is of far reaching consequence. These are only some of the important amendments proposed in Finance Bill, 2012. More importantly, I would like to deal with the impact of GAAR on Indo Mauritius tax treaty.

2. Royalties

Software Payments: The issue of software payments to non-residents has been a vexed issue. A resident Indian purchasing a software product from a non-resident has been under scanner by the Revenue holding a view that such payment would amount to royalty liable for withholding taxes. Whereas, a software product which is a copyrighted article and is also generally known as "Shrink Wrapped Software" is nothing but software against which the buyer would only get the usage rights and nothing else. In other words, the buyer of such software is allowed to use and will not be legally entitled to amend or change the programme embodied in such software. Buyer has no right of copying and distribution of such software. Thereby, the buyer will have a limited right of usage of such software in his business or professional activity etc.

Appreciating this concept, Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Tata Consultancy Services v. State of Andhra Pradesh [2004] 271 ITR 401/141 Taxman 132 had held a view that software which is a copyrighted article is a product. Thereby, the seller of such product would earn business profits and not earn any royalty in such a transaction. However, the decision of the Apex Court was in the context of Sales Tax provisions. The whole issue relating to licence for usage of a copyrighted article (such as software) is whether there arises any transfer of rights to the licensee. In this context, judiciary has always referred to the provisions of the Copyright Act, 1957. It is now to be examined whether license in respect of copyrighted article such as a "Tally" software would result in transfer of rights as envisaged under Copyright Act, 1957, if the licensee is given limited right of usage for his own purposes without any right of altering, amending or changing the software or making copies and distributing the same. The rights enjoyed by such user are very limited and the same cannot be understood as transfer of rights under the Copyright Act, 1957. Courts have taken divergent views in deciding this issue. In the following case, it was held that there is no transfer of any right and thereby the payment for copyrighted article for granting licence to any user is not to be treated as "royalty".

Characterisation of income from software 12. The question as to whether consideration for transfer of computer software is royalty or business income or capital gains is a debatable question. Computer software means a computer programme recorded on any disc, tape, perforated media or other information storage device. It is a programme which contains instructions to the computer. Software is usually developed in three stages. First, a systematic analyst or designer prepares a specification, which normally includes data flow diagrams setting out the basic logic of the programme. Then a source code programme is written in computer language. The source code cannot be read directly by a computer. It is converted by an assembler or compiler into object code. Object code is essentially a form of source code which can be read or relied upon by microprocessor or Central Processor Unit (CPU) of the computer. Authorship of source code or the object code is protected by Copyright Act, as library work. Whether consideration involved in the transaction of software is business or service income or royalty depends upon transfer of the rights therein. Predominant amongst the considerations is whether the transferor has received not only the right to use the software in its business, but also the right to reproduce and redistribute the software to others. The rights transferred are: (1) less than all the rights; (2) outright alienation; or (3) mixture of both. Transaction in (1) above may yield business or royalty income depending on how the rights are transferred. It is the business income when the transfer is made for the personal or business use of the acquirer, on terms which make the acquisition anytheless than the full rights in the software. The owner still preserves copyright protection and restricts his acquirers use of the software. It is a transfer of the copyrighted article rather than the copyright itself. It is royalty income when the payment is received for a partial transfer of rights. Such transaction involves granting of licence to the other party to develop and market the software commercially, in the same manner as the author of a book grants rights to a publisher. However, if the transactions involve the disposition of the entire right such as an exclusive geographical licence for the useful life of the software, the income is not royalty. It is a sale of the copyright itself in a book. Such transactions involve outright alienation. Thus, transfer of a software is a sale of product (transfer of a standard form) like a copyrighted article; sale of copyright, or by way of grant of licence to develop and market commercially.

Transfer of a software is a sale of product (transfer of a standard form) like a copyrighted article; sale of copyright, or by way of grant of licence to develop and market commercially.

When the software payments are made under the mixed contracts (e.g. as part of a package or bundled scheme of payments for computer operated machine) then it would be necessary to break the payment units to be treated as royalty or business income or capital gains [for detailed discussion, see D.P. Mittal’s Indian Double Taxation Agreements, published by Taxmann, 4th Edn. (2004)]. Business income is taxable under article 7 on net basis, as already discussed, and royalty income under article 12 of the DTA on gross basis.gg*

Telecasting rights - Where payment made by assessee, a Singapore based company, to GCC (also tax resident of Singapore) for acquiring cricket telecast rights throughout licence territory including India had no connection with marketing activities carried out through its alleged PE in India, such payment held not to be 'royalty' and, hence, not chargeable to tax in India [DIT v. Set Satellite (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. [2014] 45 taxmann.com 100/225 Taxman 1 (Bom.)].

Telecom services outside India - Assessee, engaged in business of providing telecom services to its subscribers in India, entered into agreements with non-resident telecom operators for providing bandwidth and interconnect capacity outside India, in such a case payment made in consideration of said services held to be in the nature of 'royalty' [DDIT v. Vodafone South Ltd. [2014] 45 taxmann.com 227 (Kar.)].

Bandwidth payments made by Indian customers to a Singapore-based company for International Private Leased Circuit (IPLC) for providing end-to-end internet connectivity outside India (where connectivity for Indian leg was provided by VSNL due to Indian regulatory requirement) was taxable as 'royalty' [Verizon Communications Singapore Pte. Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 70/[2014] 224 Taxman 237 (Mag.) (Mad.)].

Where assessee-company, a tax resident of Singapore, was providing bandwidth services to various Indian telecom operators and services were provided from outside India, since there was neither a right to use process nor there was a transfer of technology consideration received by assessee for providing such services was not taxable as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) [Commissioner of Income-tax (International Taxation) v. Telstra Singapore Pte. Ltd. [2024] 165 taxmann.com 85 (Delhi)/[2024] 467 ITR 302 (Delhi)].

User manual - Where contract for supply of equipment and spare parts included stipulations for giving information so as to guide Indian party to install equipment at site and thereafter to use it, payment to Danish company held not to be 'royalty' since payment was made towards supply of equipments on principal-to-principal basis [DIT v. Haldor Topsoe [2014] 48 taxmann.com 67/225 Taxman 105 (Bom.)].

Other illustrations held not constitute 'royalty' - (1) Sum received for permitting the use of certain marks and intellectual property belonging to the assessee (a UK based company) for privilege of hosting and staging Formula F1 championship race which had been strictly confined and limited to use only for the promotion of the event and for no other purpose held not to be 'royalty' but 'business income' [Formula One World Championship Ltd. v. CIT [2017] 80 taxmann.com 347/248 Taxman 192 (SC)].

(2) Where assessee-company developed basic engine and sent the same to a non-resident company of Austria to design a new 3-valve cylinder head for improvement of fuel efficiency, performance and meeting Indian emission standard, payment made to Austrian company would not constitute 'royalty' [DIT v. TVS Motors Co. Ltd. [2018] 99 taxmann.com 40/259 Taxman 140 (Mad.)].

(3) Where subscription charges were received by TV channel operator from customers enabling them to view channels, since said receipt was not for transfer of any copyright in literary, artistic or scientific work, it could not be categorized as 'royalty income' [CIT v. MSM Satellite (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. [2019] 106 taxmann.com 353/265 Taxman 376 (Bom.)]. Also see, CIT v. Springer Nature Customer Services Centre GMBH [2023] 152 taxmann.com 277/294 Taxman 167 (Delhi).

Multinational companies doing business with India are increasingly confronted with questions relating to existence of a Permanent Establishment ("PE") in India, attribution of profits to the PE and taxability of other receipts from India.The issue is aggravated if the Indian entity plays a significant role in the value chain of the group or it receives considerable direction or support from foreign entities.

Recently, in the case of Convergys Customer Management Group Inc. v. Asstt. DIT [2013] 34 taxmann.com 24 (Delhi-Trib.), the Tribunal examined a few critical issues viz. whether certain receipts from India qualify as royalty,whether the foreign company had a PE in India and the extent of profits, if any,which could be attributed to the PE.

Convergys Customer Management Group Inc. ("CMG"), a provider of IT enabled customer management services,was a tax resident of US having no business operations in India. However, to service its customers outside India, it procured IT enabled/back office support services from its subsidiary viz. Convergys India Services Private Limited ("CIS"), on a principal to principal basis. Although CMG procured the services from CIS, substantial risk like market risk, price risk, and service liability was borne by CMG.Further, some of CMG's employees visited India for short durations and for providing training under a technical services agreement. CMG received from CIS service charges for training and reimbursement towards link charges and software payments.

The assessing officer ("AO") concluded that CMG had a Fixed Place PE, Agency PE and Service PE in India and attributed profits to it. The AO also treated the sums received from CIS towards link charges and software payments as royalty taxable in India.

CMG contended that it did not have a PE in India and claimed that the reimbursements from CIS (towards link charges and software payments) were not liable to tax in India. The service income earned from training was offered to tax as Fees for Included Services ("FIS").

The Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) ("CIT(A)") upheld most of the conclusions arrived at by the AO(although on different rationale in some instances), except the approach for attributing profits to the PE.

Both parties were before the Tribunal in cross appeals. A gist of the Tribunal's decision in this matter and related aspects with respect to the key issues are discussed below.

Existence of a PE in India

In Convergys Customer Management Group Inc's case (supra), the AO was of the view that CMG had a Fixed Place PE, Dependent Agent PE and Service PE in India. The CIT(A) agreed with the AO's conclusion that CMG had a Fixed Place PE in India but held that no Dependent Agent PE and Service PE was constituted.

Fixed place PE

The AO observed that employees seconded to CIS by CMG were holding key managerial positions such as Country Head and Managing Director, in CIS. Further, the seconded employees and other employees of CMG visiting India had a fixed place of business (in the form of CIS) at their disposal. CMG had borne pre-operative revenue expenditure for setting up CIS's call sites. It also provided CIS with free of cost assets, software and access to gateways, communication lines, etc. for its use. On account of these reasons, the AO concluded that CMG had a Fixed Place PE in India under Article 5(1) and 5(2)(c) and (d) of the India US tax treaty.

The CIT(A) held that CMG was carrying on business from the premises of CIS which were at its disposal and accordingly it had a Fixed Place PE in India as per Article 5(1) and a place of management in India under Article 5(2)(a) of the India US tax treaty. While determining that CMG had a Fixed Place PE in India, the fact that CIS was economically and functionally dependent on CMG and risk related to delivery of services was managed through employees of CMG (visiting India or on secondment to key positions) weighed against CMG.

CMG put forth detailed arguments to defend the position that it did not have a PE in India.

With respect to the scope of Article 5(1), CMG asserted that in the absence of domain or control over the place, wholly or partly, the place of business could not be regarded as satisfying the "place at disposal" test1. Further, the parent company would not have a PE in India merely because the subsidiary company was controlled by the parent company.

Access without transfer of control - Since, in terms of clauses of agreements entered into between assessee and TV channels, control of satellite or transponder would always remain with the assessee who had merely given access to a broadband available with transponder to particular customers, amount paid to assessee by its customers would not represent income by way of 'royalty' [Asia Satellite Telecommunications Co. Ltd. v. DIT [2011] 9 taxmann.com 168/197 Taxman 263 (Delhi)].

Where assessee-company, incorporated in Malaysia, entered into an agreement with its Indian AE for use of assessee's SAP system and related services to keep it functional, etc., since assessee had merely given access of SAP system to AE for a certain specific purpose and by allowing such access, assessee had not transferred any right or license in respect of any copyright of any literary or artistic or scientific work to AE, provisions of clause (v) of Explanation 2 to s. 9(1)(vi) could not be applied to such a transaction so as to tax consideration received by assessee [CIT v. Colgate Palmolive Marketing SDN BHD [2023] 152 taxmann.com 124 (Bom.)].

Advertisement/publicity charges - Payment received on services rendered by assessee to the Indian concern was for advertisement, publicity and sales promotion keeping in mind their mutual interest and in that context, use of trademark, trade name or other enumerated service referred to in agreement with assessee were incidental to said main service and, therefore, such payments were not in the nature of 'royalty' but 'business income' [DIT v. Sheraton International Inc. [2009] 178 Taxman 84 (Delhi)].

Customised product - Mere passing of information concerning design of machine which is tailor-made to meet requirement of a buyer, by itself, does not amount to transfer of any right of exclusive user so as to render payment made therefor being regarded as 'royalty' [CIT v. Nayveli Lignite Corporation Ltd. [2000] 113 Taxman 206 (Mad.)].

Export commission - Where assessee entered into export agreement with AE in terms of which it was granted approval to sell motor vehicles manufactured using technology licenced by AE abroad, since by way of export agreement HMCL had not rendered any managerial, technical or consultancy services, payment of export commission could not be regarded as 'royalty' taxable in India [CIT v. Hero Motorcorp Ltd. [2017] 81 taxmann.com 162/248 Taxman 14 (Delhi)].

Forex fluctuations - Where interest/royalty/FTS income was claimed as exempt as per DTAA on accrual basis in earlier years, then forex fluctuation gain or loss arising on receipt of such income in subsequent period could not be considered as exempt since such gain could not be considered as a part of royalty and it should be taxed [Ballarpur Industries Ltd. v. CIT [2017] 84 taxmann.com 61 (Bom.)].

Hire charges - Where assessee, engaged in business of moving coal from various ports in India to State Electricity Board, Chennai, hired ships from various non-resident companies for transportation of coal, payments of hire charges made to said companies under time charter agreement amounted to 'royalty' [Poompuhar Shipping Corporation Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 150/[2014] 220 Taxman 58 (Mad.)]. However, amount received by foreign company for hiring out dredgers to its Indian company would not be taxable in India as 'royalty' [CIT v. Van Oord ACZ Equipment BV [2014] 51 taxmann.com 356/[2015] 228 Taxman 199 (Mad.)].

Licence to use - Payment made to a non-resident in order to obtain licence to use database maintained by it is to be regarded as 'royalty' [CIT v. Wipro Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 275/203 Taxman 621 (Kar.)].

Where assessee engaged in rendering information technology solutions to companies within CGI group and other global customers, entered into an agreement with CGI Inc., a Canada based company, in terms of which assessee acquired a licence to use intranet facilities provided by non-resident company, payment made for utilising said facilities amounted to 'royalty' taxable in India [CIT v. Despite the COVID-19 pandemic, the Year 2021 has been busy for the Courts and Tribunals. Several significant rulings were delivered onInternational Taxation and Transfer Pricing matters, including the Supreme Court's landmark ruling on the treatment of sum received on the sale of software.In this article, we have shortlisted key 15 rulings related to International Taxation, and Transfer Pricing reported at taxmann.com during the year 2021.

1. Sum received by a non-resident for sale of computer software through EULAs not taxable as royalty : SC

Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd . v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC)

The Supreme Court of India held that as per the definition of royalties contained in Article 12 of the DTAAs, it is clear that there is no obligation under section 195 to deduct tax at source on payments towards software purchase. This is because the distribution agreements or EULAs of such software do not create any interest or right in such distributors/end-users, which would amount to the use of or right to use any copyright.

The provisions of section 9(1)(vi), along with Explanations 2 and 4 thereof, which deal with royalty, couldn't also be applied as the same is not more beneficial to the assessees in comparison to the provision contained in DTAAs.

Accordingly, amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for the resale/use of the computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, was not the payment of royalty for the use of copyright in the computer software.

2. Indian tax authorities cannot grant a refund of taxes paid in foreign jurisdictions: Mumbai ITAT

Bank of India v. Asstt.CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 155 (Mum. - Trib.)

The Mumbai Tribunal held that the tax credit schemes, as evident from the international tax literature and model convention commentaries, do not envisage any situation in which the excess foreign tax credit can result in a tax refund to the taxpayers from the exchequer of residence jurisdictions.

All the methods of eliminating double taxation, i.e., exemption method, credit method or hybrid method, restrict the liability to tax in the source jurisdiction. The relief sought in the instant case goes well beyond that and would result in a refund of taxes by India, and what is being termed as a refund is not even paid to the Indian exchequer.

Wherever tax credits exceed the tax liability, at best a carry forward or back of excess tax credit can be given when permitted by the domestic law, or at best when not restricted by the domestic law.

3. A non-resident is liable to tax in all years in which its project exceeding threshold limit for the creation of PE falls : AAR

Tiong Woon Project & Contracting (P.) Ltd., In re [2021] 124 taxmann.com 549 (AAR - Mumbai)

Applicant executed a project between 06-01-2011 to 30-01-2012 comprising nearly 13 months. The project was continued for a period of 85 days in the previous year 2010-11 and 306 days in the previous year 2011-12.

Before the Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR), the applicant took the view that no taxable income accrues or arises in India from its activities of execution of 'installation project' in the previous year 2010-11 since the duration of the project was only 85 days. The taxable income arises in the previous year 2011-12, where the duration of the project was 306 days resulting in the creation of permanent establishment (PE) in India in terms of Article 5 of DTAA between India and Singapore.

The revenue argued that article 5 clearly states that an installation project constitutes a PE if it continues for a period of 183 days in any fiscal year. That article refers to any fiscal year and not every or relevant fiscal year.

Attention is also invited to Article 15 of the DTAA, which deals with dependent personal services. The article mandates that the recipient should be present in the other State for a period or periods not exceeding in aggregate 183 days in the relevant fiscal year to escape taxation. Thus, it is emphasized that the phrase 'any fiscal year' in article 5 indicates that a PE is constituted if the whole duration of the project, which may be spread over more than one fiscal year, includes 183 days or above in any fiscal year.

Thus, it was held that the applicant's income is taxable in India as business profit in both the previous year's 2010-11 and 2011-12.

The explanations read as under:

"Explanation 4 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Explanation 6 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the expression "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-lining of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret."

On comparing Explanation 4 with Article 12(2) of OECD MC it is evident that the term "used or right to use" is succeeded by the word "a computer software" in the former and the word "copyright" in the later. It is also being discussed among the scholarly circles whether Explanation4 is amplifying the scope of Explanation2 or is it creating another dimension of the substantive provision. Is it legally acceptable in respect of a new Explanation providing an expanded meaning of term "royalty" which was already defined in Explanation 2 of section 9(1)(vi) ? If it amounts to altering the meaning of "royalty" can it be retrospective through an Explanation. It is well understood that the meaning of "royalty" under the Act is wider than the meaning provided under OECD MC. The gap is further widened by this new Explanation4.

2.2. Explanation 5 seeks to clarify that the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer or not would not make difference in deciding whether particular payment is "royalty". In the same manner, whether the payer used such right, property or information directly or not and whether the location of such right, property or information is in India or not would not make difference in deciding whether the payment is "royalty" or not. However, Hon'ble Delhi High Court while deciding the case of Ericsson A.B., (supra) has held that for the purpose of section 9(1) (v), (vi), (vii) it is not required to go into explanation to Sec.9 (2) of the Act, if the payment does not fall into any of the categories covered by (v), (vi) and (vii).

In view of the same, it is possible to argue that once sale of computer software is not covered by Explanation 2, so as to be treated as "royalty" than the new Explanation 5 would not have any bearing on such a transaction. It is also interesting to note that Explanations4 and 5 refer to the rights in respect of right, property or information leaving aside other terms such as "patent, process, invention etc," as mentioned in Explanation 2.

2.3 The newly inserted Explanations 4 and 5 would not bring finality for interpreting the term "royalty" either under the treaty law or under the post amended domestic law.

2.4 Explanation 6 has been inserted to neutralize the judgment of Asia Satellite Telecommunications Co. Ltd. v. DIT [2011] 332 ITR 340/197 Taxman 263/9 taxmann.com 168(Delhi), thereby providing the term "process" includes transmission by satellite, cable, optic fiber, any other similar technology whether or not such process is secret, whether or not the satellite etc are under the control of the customers. The amendment is widening the scope of the term "royalty".

2.5 The amendments brought in through these Explanations clarify the term "royalty" in such a way which is in conflict with the OECD MCC on Article 12 explained in paras 12 to 17 and at para 9.1 These amendments result in holding most of the software payments/telecom services to be within the ambit of term "royalty" unless specifically protected by the treaty or the exclusion provided under section 9(1)(vi)(b)/(c) of the Act.

3. Withholding Taxes – Section 195

1 SOURCE RULES - When a user gets a file using a torrent, he has obtained pieces of the file from dozens if not hundreds of people all over the world. In such a scenario, what is the source of the file? It can be argued to be the location of the master or "tracker" node but then new variations of "trackerless" systems are coming into vogue. The huge use of torrents, unfortunately both legally and illegally, clearly shows that existing source rules are stretched. 2.3-2 PERMANENT ESTABLISHMENT - The torrent file is distributed by random people all over the internet; if a company incorporated in the USA has a server in India which distributes intangible property (say, media files) to customers. If the Indian server uses torrents to distribute this media file will the server in India be considered the P.E. to which the profits of the intangible property transaction are to be attributed to? If so, how much of the profits should be attributed to it - if 1000 copies are distributed not all of them will be through the server, most of the data would be distributed through other "peers". If the system were "trackerless", then the server itself can’t be regarded as the master or central repository

CASE STUDY 3: Transfer of Bundled Intellectual Property – Web-based business model

3.1 Introduction - The traditional notion of software has been a company hiring engineers who sit in a building writing code to create a software program used for a specific purpose and such program once developed is sent to customers in the tangible form of CD’s or DVD’s. This model equated well with the assembly line manufacturing process and an age-old model of tangible products.

However, the above is not how a majority of software is developed nowadays; the Internet has brought forth new business model – both business to business (B2B) & business to consumer (B2C) models.

Today there exists "web" companies which are valued at billions of dollars whose "crown jewels" are usually the intangible intellectual property they own or their patented business models or their proprietary technology web-service platforms. Examples of such web companies are Google, Facebook, eBay5 2 etc.

3.2 A simple web-based business model - In this case study we take a web-based business model related to the online advertising market (also called SEM – Search Engine Marketing), one of the fastest growing markets in the world. This is similar to the case study presented in Elizabeth King’s case study on Replication of Internet-Based Business Model52.

Search engines like Google5 3 derive most of their income from such markets which allow advertisers to bid on keywords in an auction-model on their technology platforms; when users search for the keywords which have been bid upon they are shown text ads sorted in the descending order of their bid. Such a market gave rise to a host of web companies who provide service to advertisers to efficiently and optimally bid on millions of companies – they are essentially providing SEM solutions to online advertisers.

We consider a USA company, USCo, which provides SEM i.e. Search Engine Marketing solutions using its unique and patented algorithmic techniques for efficient and optimal bidding; in simple terms the company takes control of advertisers online campaigns of its clients and bids on keywords in the online advertisement marketplaces offered by search engines like Google Adwords54 . USCo’s clients are typically two-fold: companies who wants to advertise online to boost traffic to its website and sales of its products & services, advertising agencies who provide full-service to their clients and provide both offline (TV, newspapers etc.) & online advertising solutions for clients.

USCo has a successful and established business model and handles over $500 million in advertising spend on the various search engines. Parts of USCo’s business model are patented. Further, USCo has developed proprietary software for its internal usage – to process, analyze & model the huge amount of data it churns daily. USCo has also developed online marketing & solicitation tools which it uses to market to, obtain, test and sign-up clients.

Now an Indian company, lets call it IndCo, wants to replicate USCo’s business model in India. Towards this the top management gets training in USCo and on doing so provides the USCo’s business model of online advertising solutions to clients & ad agencies in India.

To summarize:

1.USCo transfers the intellectual property of its proprietary software modified to suit local conditions.

2.USCo also provides the right to use of its marketing and solicitation online tools to IndCo, again these pages have to be modified slightly for local conditions.

3.USCo will perform routine service, maintenance and upgrades on the proprietary software given to IndCo.

4.USCo will provide legal and financial planning and advisory services to IndCo.

5.IndCo has been issued the rights to use USCo’s trademark and name in the Indian market.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)] Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.

5-6 Value of subsequent re-sale if payable to foreign supplier

If any part of proceeds of subsequent re-sale of imported goods is payable to seller, directly or indirectly, its cost is includible. (This may happen if a distributor/agent imports goods and once he sells these goods in India, part of sales proceeds may be payable to foreign seller). [Rule 10(1)(d) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007]. 5.5-7 Charges for reproduction of goods in India not to be added

Interpretative Note to rule 10(1)(c) of Customs Valuation Rules makes it clear that charges for right to reproduce the imported goods in India shall not be added.

Sometimes, master copy of software like Page Maker, Norton, Windows, Autocad are imported and are licensed to be reproduced in India by the foreign owner of these softwares. Charges for reproducing these softwares will not be added.

In Sony Music Entertainment P Ltd. v. CC 2005 (189) ELT 227 (CESTAT), assessee was paying royalty to their foreign holding company on CDs manufactured or sold in India. This royalty was not a condition for imports of CDs from foreign principal. It was held that the royalty cannot be added to value of imported CD from foreign principal - followed in CC v. Sony BMG Music Entertainment (I) P Ltd. (2007) 218 ELT 699 (CESTAT) [Departmental appeal admitted for hearing by SC on 21-4-2008 - (2010) 256 ELT A18]

However, the term 'reproduction' is a term of art and used in commercial sense. Right to reproduce is not for convenience of user but for the purpose of distribution. Thus, if importer imports software and pays licence fee with permission to use its copies at various branches, making additional copies for its own use at various branches does not amount to 'reproduction'. Right to use countrywide is not right to 'reproduce'. Thus, the whole licence fee is includible in assessable value - State Bank of India v. CC 2000 AIR SCW 125 = 115 ELT 597 (SC 3 member bench).

5.5-8 Other payments made to seller to be added

If buyer has made, directly or indirectly, any payment to seller as a condition of sale, such payments should be included for obvious reason that 'ordinary' selling price has been reduced due to such payment. [Rule 10(1)(e) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

The royalty, license fee or other payment for process is to be added even if the goods may be subjected to such process after importation of the goods - Explanation to rule 10(1)].

This explanation was added in the context of SC judgment in case of CC v. J K Corporation Ltd. (2007) 208 ELT 485 (SC) - MF(DR) circular No. 38/2007-Cus dated 9-10-2007.

In CC v. J K Corporation Ltd. (2007) 208 ELT 485 (SC), it was held that any amount paid for post importation service or activity would not be includible in assessable value of imported goods. In this case, the importer imported plant and machinery. In addition to value of machinery, the importer paid USD 14 lakhs for license and know-how of the manufacturing process for production of goods, since the process know-how was also patented by foreign party. It was held that the amount paid for license and know-how of the process is not to be added to the assessable value, since it is post importation activity. (Now this decision may not be valid after 10-10-2007).

In CC v. Toyota Kirloskar Motor P Ltd. (2007) 213 ELT 4 (SC) it was held that pre-importation expenses are to be added. Post-importation charges are to be added only if they are a 'condition for import'. An amount payable in respect of manufacturing activities, which has nothing to do with the import of capital goods is not to be added to assessable value.

Royalty and license fee payable for cinematic rights, TV rights, video rights etc. are includible - In Star Entertainment P Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 297 ELT 529 (CESTAT), assessee imported recorded media such as tapes. Customs duty was paid only on transaction value. A prima facie view has been held that Royalty and license fee payable for cinematic rights, TV rights, video rights etc. are includible in assessable value of imported tapes.

Charges in respect of old machinery - In case of purchase of old machinery, all expenses connected with dismantling of old machinery, and making it ready for being transported including inspection charges of old machinery are includible - Bombay Dyeing & Mfg v. CC 1997 AIR SCW 1427= AIR 1997 SC 1329 = 90 ELT 276.

Introduction

Technology has always been at the cutting edge of the significant transformation that is taking place in the market place today. Mobile technology, analytics, cloud computing and wearables have emerged as new forms of technology, and even several traditional companies have started to add capabilities in these areas to cater to the growing customer preferences. In this digital revolution, leading the pack is the e-commerce segment, which is driving rapid growth of domestic IT-ITeS industry and is attracting unprecedented levels of global interest, funding and talent. Owing to such rapid revolution and growth, India ranks third in start-ups formed in the technology industry globally.

Keeping in pace with the growth in this industry, the controversies surrounding taxation of digital transactions are also ever on the rise. Governments and tax administrators of many countries are constantly evaluating the tax implications arising on operations of such entities, since transactions of the e-commerce players raises several contentious tax issues due to absence of national boundaries, physical presence of goods and non-requirement of physical delivery. In India, there are innumerable tax issues faced by the technology industry and in the ensuing paragraphs we have discussed the populist ones.

1. Withholding tax issues on cross border payments involving software

Transactions in the technology industry such as payments for purchase or usage of software, payments for online advertising, app stores, cloud computing are under the tax radar. Such transactions could involve:

-

Transfer of rights in a property (such as right to alter or reproduce work or issue copies of the work);

-

Few transactions could involve payment for services such as access / subscription to databases, standardised applications, e-library, online games, music, news etc.; and

-

Certain transactions could be a combination of both transfer of property rights and services. For e.g. customised software or configurable computing resources such as networks, servers, storage, applications along with services made available to the users through the internet.

The taxation and the related withholding tax implications on such payments to non-residents would be based on the characterisation of such income (business income or royalty or fees for technical services) under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("the Act") read with the beneficial provisions of the tax treaty. Non-resident tax payers in several instances were seeking to characterise their income from such transactions as business income and offer the same to tax in India only where such income was attributable to a permanent establishment ("PE") in India. Hence, in order to curb such mischief, in the garb of a clarification, the Government brought in a retrospective amendment in the Act to widen the scope of definition of "Royalty". The amended definition of "Royalty" seeks to include transfer of any right to use a software including the granting of a license, irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred. This amendment significantly targets transactions involving payments for shrink-wrap or embedded software.

The issue of taxation of cross border software licensing transactions including payments towards access to databases, online applications etc. have been a significant bone of contention between the Indian Revenue authorities and the tax payers over the last decade.

Some of the key illustrative factors considered relevant by the Courts for determining the characterisation of income are listed below:

Nature of rights granted to the payee - Whether rights in the property is transferred or mere right of usage of property is conferred;

Nature of software - Customised vis-à-vis standardised software;

Whether the payment is towards the use or right to use a copyrighted article or a copyright in the article.

Degree of possession and control of the server / database / application;

Recourse to the service provider for the further requirement of any services;

Whether any specific configuration is carried out for the payee?

Whether any information is made available to the payee and right of further commercial exploitation is conferred on the payee?

Whether the payment is made for right other that right in the intellectual property?

Determination of taxability of transactions should be based on a holistic evaluation of the intention of the parties involved and the primary purpose for which the payment is being made. Issues on taxability of software payments along with taxation aspects of e-commerce transactions were extensively researched and opined upon by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development ("OECD") - Technical Advisory Group almost two decades back. However, India differed on most of the views of the OECD on this issue and currently maintains an enhanced observer status to the OECD. The views expressed by India are in variance with most of the developed countries on characterisation of income on software payments. The current action plans initiated by the OECD under the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting ("BEPS") also do not deal with such issues adding to the woes of the technology industry players.
