If a PE is established under the DTAA, only the profits attributable to that PE are taxable in India. 8.5-11c Classification as royalty - Section 9(6)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of royalty to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. Since the foreign company provides capital goods, equipment, or tooling and retains ownership, while the Indian manufacturer uses them, any consideration paid by the Indian manufacturer for this arrangement would squarely fall within the definition of 'royalty' under section 9(6)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India, and the equipment is used in India.

Most DTAAs between India and other countries define 'royalties' to include payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment. If the specific DTAA between India and the country of which the foreign country is a resident includes 'payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' in its definition of royalty, then the income would be classified as royalty under the DTAA. In such a case, the income would be taxable in India at the rate specified in the DTAA, provided the foreign company is the beneficial owner and the income is not effectively connected to a PE in India. If the DTAA does not include such payments in its royalty definition (under the OECD Model), the income would be treated as business profits and taxable in India only if the foreign company has a PE in India and the profits are attributable to that PE.

8.5-11d Classification as FTS - Section 9(7)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(7)(b) defines 'fees for technical services' as any consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). Where the foreign company also provides the installation and training services for the capital goods, equipment, or tooling to the Indian manufacturer to use them, any fees paid by the Indian manufacturer for these services would squarely fall within the definition of FTS under section 9(7)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India.

Most DTAAs have a specific article on FTS (Fees for Included Services). These articles may include a 'make available' clause, meaning the services must not only be technical but also 'make available' technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to the recipient. If the foreign company is merely providing equipment and not imparting any technical knowledge or skills to the Indian manufacturer that enable the latter to apply the technology independently, the 'make available' test (if present in the DTAA) would not be met. In such a situation, the FTS will not be taxable in India. If the DTAA does not explicitly contain a 'make available' clause, then any service of a managerial, technical, or consultancy nature will be taxable as FTS.

8.5-11e Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on the two factors:

(a)

Whether the foreign company has a PE in India

(b)

Whether the income is such that the presumptive scheme as specified in Section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 applies (corresponding to Section 44BBD of the ITA 1961) (Business of providing services or technology in India, for the purposes of setting up an electronics manufacturing facility).

The taxable income, taking these factors into account, will be as follows.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India, and the business income earned in India is connected to such PE, the tax liability in such a case shall be computed as per the ITA. If the conditions of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 is fulfilled; the taxable business income shall be computed on a presumptive basis at the rate of 25% of the specified amount. If conditions are not fulfilled, the actual business income shall be computed as per the general provisions.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the business income earned by him in India shall not be taxable in India. In such a situation, the presumptive scheme of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 will have no relevance.

The deliberate inclusion of 'reasonably' in the ITA 2025 in the SEP context suggests a legislative intent for a potentially more nuanced or proportionate allocation based on overall business functions, assets, and risks. As a result, income attribution under SEP will no longer be distinct from attribution under ordinary business connection cases. Both will now be governed by the overarching principle of reasonable attribution, ensuring consistency and reducing the scope for disproportionate taxation.

3.4-3 Purchase of goods in India for export [Section 9(8)(c)(ii)(A) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961 provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export. In the corresponding section 9(9)(c)(ii) of the ITA 2025, the words used are "purchase of goods in India for the purposes of export out of India".

On a strict literal interpretation, the addition of "out of India" might seem redundant, since "export" universally means sending goods out of the country. However, the expression "export out of India" would primarily serve to explicitly remove any remote ambiguity. It could prevent an interpretation where "export" might be construed to include movement to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) within India (which is treated as foreign territory for certain purposes but is geographically within India) or other domestic transfers that are deemed exports for other regulatory purposes but do not involve physical exit from India's customs territory. It would clarify that the exemption applies only when goods physically leave the Indian customs territory.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

Till now, the Tribunals have been holding that packaged software being ‘goods’, there was no need for the importer to deduct tax at source and that the payment towards procurement of the packaged software cannot be considered as ‘royalty’. However, this latest decision from the Karnataka High Court would supersede such Tribunals’ decisions, at least, for importers in Karnataka. 2.2 The facts of the case, in brief: Certain importers of software licenses had taken a view that the payments made for software imports would not attract the provisions of section 195 of the Income-tax Act, necessitating the deduction of tax at source, since such payments would not constitute taxable income in the nature of royalty or scientific work, in the hands of the non-resident, in terms of section 9(1)(vi) read with the DTAA. The First and Second Appellate Authorities had upheld the importers’ contention that when the payments would be for acquiring a right to use a copyright and not the copyright itself it would not get treated as royalty payments in terms of the DTAAs and, hence, there was no need for deducting tax at source under section 195. The Tribunal had also upheld the importers’ contention that the import of software licenses would be in the nature of a transaction involving import of goods, in the light of the precedents set by the various Courts including the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the TCS case. The revenue contended that software is a ‘scientific work’ and payments for import of software would be covered under section 9(1)(vi) of the Act and that the importer cannot contend that the payment made by him would not constitute income in the hands of the non-resident recipient and that, the importer is duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195.

2.3 The gist of the judgment: In a sweeping judgment, which is perhaps the first judgment from a High Court on the contentious issue related to the applicability of section 195 on software imports, the Karnataka High Court has rejected, in toto, the decisions of the Bangalore Tribunal in various similar judgments and has held that the importer was duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195 for import of software licenses, based almost exclusively, on the Apex Court’s judgment in Transmission Corporation of AP Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 105 Taxman 742. The High Court’s judgment in leads to the premise that the obligation to deduct tax at source under section 195 has nothing to do, with the actual liability of the non-resident to tax under the provisions of the Act, including the quantum thereof. The importer could take recourse to the provisions of section 195(2) if he is of the view that only a part of the payment made by him would bear the character of income in the hands of the non-resident.

2.4 The implications arising out of this judgment: Due to this ruling of the Karnataka High Court, all overseas payments will now be subject to withholding tax, whether or not the income is taxable. Not only is this in dramatic contrast to previous High Court’s decisions, it is also a judgment that will lead to higher cost of business, increased uncertainty and may be even more litigation—at Least for a while.

The law itself as it reads, which is section 195, specifically says that it is a sum which is chargeable to tax under the Income-tax Act on which tax has to be deducted at source, if that payment, of course, is being made to a non-resident. Based on that, for example, the Rajasthan High Court in the SBI case has taken a view that if income is exempt under provisions of the Indian Income-tax Act, one does not need to withhold tax at source at all when the payment is being made to non-resident of such an exempt income.

But now, a judgment by the Karnataka High Court has turned this established principle.

•In terms of this judgment, the importer has only two options before him, vis-à-vis the payments to be effected to the non-resident, viz. either to deduct tax at source under section 195 or to make an application to the Department under section 195(2). In terms of the judgment, this principle would apply equally to import of goods or to import of services or for transactions involving import of goods and services as in the case of a works contract.

•It would look like that importer cannot get into issues related to the applicability of section 9(1) or to the provisions of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA) for purposes of discharging his liability under section 195. In other words, in terms of this judgment, the provisions of section 195 are quite draconian, requiring the resident payer to deduct tax at source without getting into issues related to the taxation of the receipts, in the hands of the non-resident.

the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively. This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

(TM) : It was a case pertaining to the assessment year 1997-98 for grant of non-exclusive license to use ‘Know-how’ and supply of process engineering documentation for use within the Indian Territory for 10 years. As per the terms of secrecy of license agreement, the assessee was to keep the know-how secret till 15 years and thereafter the secrecy terms were to expire. As per the license agreement clause, the assessee could not sub-license or assign the rights under the agreement, except with the prior permission of licensor, which could not be unreasonably withheld. The consideration for the ‘know-how’ was lump sum USD 250 lakhs and a royalty of USD 5.00 per metric tonne of product subject to maximum of Rs. USD 50 lakhs. The consideration for supply of technical engineering documentation was USD 35 lakhs. The counsel of the assessee stated that it was not a case of outright transfer of the formula or the process. On these facts, an issue before the Tribunal was whether payment of USD 250 lakhs and USD 35 lakhs was ‘royalty’. The Tribunal held that the payments were not in the nature of royalty under article 13(3) of the DTAA and they fell under article 7(1) of the DTAA between India and Italy, and thus, were business profits, not liable to tax.

2.8 Amendments to section 9(1)(vi)

2.8.1 Amendments Explanations 4, 5 and 6 have been inserted in section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-4-1976 so as to clarify that—

(i) the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred (Explanation 4).

(ii) royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India (Explanation 5).

(iii) the expression 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret (Explanation 6).

2.8.2 Object

The objective of the amendments as explained in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2012 is as follows:

"II. Section 9(1)(vi) provides that any income payable by way of royalty in respect of any right, property or information is deemed to be accruing or arising in India. The term "royalty" has been defined in Explanation 2 which means consideration received or receivable for transfer of all or any right in respect of certain rights, property or information. Some judicial decisions have interpreted this definition in a manner which has raised doubts as to whether consideration for use of computer software is royalty or not; whether the right, property or information has to be used directly by the payer or is to be located in India or control or possession of it has to be with the payer. Similarly, doubts have been raised regarding the meaning of the term processed.

Considering the conflicting decisions of various courts in respect of income in nature of royalty and to restate the legislative intent, it is further proposed to amend the Income-tax Act in following manner:-

(i) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the consideration for use or right to use of computer software is royalty by clarifying that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information as mentioned in Explanation 2, includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

(ii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not

(a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.

(iii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the term "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.

These amendments will take effect retrospectively from 1st June, 1976 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 1977-78 and subsequent assessment years."

11.1 Under section 9(1)(vi), income by way of royalty payable is deemed to accrue or arise in India subject to certain conditions. The term ‘royalty’ has been defined in Explanation 2 to this clause.

Section 9 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 so as to provide that the term ‘royalty’ shall include :

The amendment provides that ‘royalty’ shall not include amounts referred to in section 44BB. Section 44BB, inter alia, provides that in the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of supply of plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the exploration for and exploitation of mineral oils, 10% of the aggregate of the amounts which have been specified in the section shall be deemed to be profits and gains of the business. Thus, hire charges for the plant and machinery used for exploration, etc., of mineral oils shall not be treated as ‘royalty’ and shall continue to be taxed under section 44BB.

Following points need to be noted :

● The amendment to section 9 brings it in line with the Double Tax Conventions (DTCs) entered into by India which provide that ‘royalty’ includes consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. These DTCs are based on the OECD Model Conventions 1963 and 1977. It may be noted, however, that the definition of ‘royalties’ in Article 12(2) of OECD Model was amended in 1992 by excluding payments for the use, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

● A distinction must be made between royalties paid for the use of equipment and payments constituting consideration for the outright sale of equipment. In CIT v. Davy Ashmore India Ltd.[1991] 190 ITR 626, the Calcutta High Court has held that where there is an outright sale or purchase, the consideration is for the transfer of designs, secret formula, etc., and cannot be treated as royalty. Vide the Finance Act, 1976, it was provided, inter alia, that in case of payments of interest, royalty or fees for technical services (FTS) received from a resident payer, income would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where the interest or royalty or FTS is relatable to a business or profession carried on by the resident payer outside India or for making or earning any income from any source outside India. The Finance Act, 2007 inserted an Explanation in section 9 with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 and clarified that where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(v), (vi) or (vii), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India1.

The amendment was made to neutralize the judgment of Supreme Court in Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. DIT[2007] 288 ITR 408/ 158 Taxman 259.

The Karnataka High Court in Jindal Thermal Power Co. Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 252 has held that the Explanation does not fully neutralise Supreme Court decision and has observed as follows:

“The Explanation incorporated in section 9(2) declares that ‘where the income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under clauses (v), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident; whether or not the resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India’. The plain reading of the said provision suggests that criterion of residence, place of business or business connection of a non-resident in India has been done away with for fastening the tax liability. However, the criteria of rendering service in India and the utilisation of the service in India laid down by the Supreme Court in Ishikawajima Heavy Industries Ltd.’s case (supra) to attract tax liability under section 9(1)(vii) remains untouched and unaffected by the Explanation to section 9(2).” (Emphasis supplied)

In view of the above, the Finance Act, 2010 substitutes the Explanation, with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 also to cover the situation left out earlier, that is, rendition of services in India and provides that the income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India whether the non-resident has rendered services in India or not.

After the amendment, based on source rule, interest, royalty and fees for technical services would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, to a non-resident, whether or not:

⮚ the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India; and

⮚ the non-resident has rendered services in India.

In other words, even if a non-resident does not have residence or place of business or business connection in India and has not rendered services in India, interest, royalty and fees for technical services, if paid by a resident (not utilised for the purposes of business outside India) would be deemed to accrue or arise in India and accordingly taxable in the hands of the non-resident.

It appears, even after the amendment, having regard to the facts and the circumstances, certain payments may not constitute income in the hands of a non-resident payee, like, fees for services not in the nature of ‘make available’ services and, accordingly, does not constitute fees for technical services (and, hence, in the nature of business or professional income) in terms of a Treaty.

III. Royalty Contrary to the expectation that the retrospective amendment in respect of royalty will provide some finality, litigation on the issue has continued unabated. There is a sense of "déjà vu" inasmuch as different High Courts have once again taken differing views on taxability of income as 'royalty.'

In September 2012, in the case of DIT v. Nokia Networks OY [2013] 212 Taxman 68/[2012] 25 taxmann.com 225 the Delhi High Court held that payment for supply of software imbedded in hardware was not taxable as royalty under Article 13 of the India-Finland DTAA. Relying on its own ruling in DIT v. Ericsson A.B. [2012] 343 ITR 470/204 Taxman 192/16 taxmann.com 371, Delhi High Court rejected the arguments of the Revenue that the question of copyright and copyrighted article was not relevant for the taxability of software under the Act or the DTAA and that the 'right to use' simpliciter of software was a part of the copyright in the software, irrespective of whether a further right to make copies is granted. Delhi High Court observed that the language of the India-Finland DTAA differed from amended section 9(1)(vi) and retrospective amendment could not be read into the treaty.

In November 2013, the Madras High Court, in the case of Verizon Communications Singapore (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 70, ruled that the amount paid by Indian companies to a foreign company for dedicated broadband services constituted "royalty" and ought to be taxed in India under the Income-tax Act as well as the India Singapore treaty. Analyzing the technical aspects of providing bandwidth services in detail and interpreting the retrospective amendments to the definition of 'royalty' in section 9 made by Finance Act, 2012, the Madras High Court observed that the retrospective amendment had removed all doubts insofar as the expression 'use or right to use' was to be understood in the context of possession, control or location, thus approving that the term 'use or right to use' is of wide amplitude.

IBM and Sonata have now approached the Apex Court for determining whether packaged software can be taxed as royalty under DTAAs. It appears that only the verdict of the Supreme Court will put this debate to rest.

B. TRANSFER PRICING

Though transfer pricing is a relatively new area of law, we have all recently witnessed 2 high profile cases before the Bombay High Court that thrust the subject into limelight. Till a couple of years ago, only tax professionals dealing with international tax management/compliance of MNCs were concerned with the nuances of transfer pricing. However, there has been a noticeable change in this trend, with the print and electronic media reporting extensively on these cases. Suddenly, transfer pricing has become a topic of interest not only with most tax professionals but with the general public as well. The fact that transfer pricing has less to do with tax and more to do with market dynamics and economics definitely has a role to play in this development. But another, more important reason, for the increased interest in transfer pricing is the fact that most economies have started showing decreased tolerance to the practices adopted by MNCs for shifting profits to low tax jurisdictions, thereby depriving the "source countries" of their legitimate revenue. The vigour with which OECD is driving its Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) Action Plan and the frequency with which this problem is being discussed at international forums indicates the increasing concern of tax base erosion. Before I elaborate more on BEPS, I want to touch upon a few important issues that are currently in focus.

I. Vodafone II and Vodafone III before Bombay High Court

It seems that any litigation involving 'Vodafone' can never be a low-key affair. If foreign investors complained of flip flops on indirect share transfers in 2012, subjecting share issue transactions to transfer pricing provisions left them 'Shell Shocked' in 2013.

In a detailed judgment of 239 pages, the Bombay High Court cleared the air on some important procedural aspects in the realm of transfer pricing, including the powers of the AO, TPO and DRP. In this case popularly termed as "Vodafone II", the High Court clarified that the AO is not only bound by the TPO's decision in respect of ALP computation, but is also bound by the TPO's decision as regards the character of the transaction i.e. whether or not the transaction is an 'international transaction.' The High Court also held that the powers of the DRP are wide enough to consider all questions of fact/law raised before it. The DRP's power to 'confirm' a transfer pricing adjustment would also include the power 'not to confirm' the same, thereby empowering it to annul the variations as well.

Thus, source is where the transaction of sale has taken place. If the specified activity has taken place outside India, it may be argued that the source is not in India within the meaning of section 9(1)(i).

In CIT v. Havells India Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 476/208 Taxman 114 (Delhi), the Court had to interpret section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 which provides that fees for technical services do not accrue or arise in India to the extent they are paid by a resident for utilizing the services for making or earning any income from any "source" outside India. It observed as follows:

"Section 9(1)(vii)(b) contemplates a source located outside India. It is difficult to conceptualise the place/situs of the person who make payment for the export sales as the source located outside India from which assessee earned profits. The export contracts obviously are concluded in India and the assessee's products are sent outside India under such contracts. The manufacturing activity is located in India. The source of income is created at the moment when the export contracts are concluded in India. Thereafter the goods are exported in pursuance of the contract and the export proceeds are sent by the importer and are received in India. The importer of the assessee's products is no doubt situated outside India, but he cannot be regarded as a source of income. The receipt of the sale proceeds emanate from him from outside India. He is, therefore, only the source of the monies received. The income component of the monies or the export receipts is located or situated only in India. We are making a distinction between the source of the income and the source of the receipt of the monies. In order to fall within the second exception provided in Section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Act, the source of the income, and not the receipt, should be situated outside India. That condition is not satisfied in the present case."

Thus, the Court held that export sales proceeds received from goods manufactured and exported from India do not constitute a "source" outside India but is a source in India. Similarly, for the non-resident who sells the goods from outside India, it could be argued that it constitutes a source in the country from which the sale is made and not in India where the customer is situated.

Section 9

Finance Act, 2001

Royalty to include consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment

11.1 Under section 9(1)(vi), income by way of royalty payable is deemed to accrue or arise in India subject to certain conditions. The term 'royalty' has been defined in Explanation 2 to this clause.

Section 9 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 so as to provide that the term 'royalty' shall include :

(a)

consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, but not including the amounts referred to section 44B.

(b)

consideration for rendering of any services in connection with the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

The amendment provides that 'royalty' shall not include amounts referred to in section 44BB. Section 44BB, inter alia, provides that in the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of supply of plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the exploration for and exploitation of mineral oils, 10% of the aggregate of the amounts which have been specified in the section shall be deemed to be profits and gains of the business. Thus, hire charges for the plant and machinery used for exploration, etc., of mineral oils shall not be treated as 'royalty' and shall continue to be taxed under section 44BB.

Following points need to be noted :

The amendment to section 9 brings it in line with the Double Tax Conventions (DTCs) entered into by India which provide that 'royalty' includes consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. These DTCs are based on the OECD Model Conventions 1963 and 1977. It may be noted, however, that the definition of 'royalties' in Article 12(2) of OECD Model was amended in 1992 by excluding payments for the use, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

A distinction must be made between royalties paid for the use of equipment and payments constituting consideration for the outright sale of equipment. In CIT v. Davy Ashmore India Ltd. [1991] 190 ITR 626, the Calcutta High Court has held that where there is an outright sale or purchase, the consideration is for the transfer of designs, secret formula, etc., and cannot be treated as royalty. Applying the same ratio, consideration for outright sale of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment cannot be treated as royalty.

Section 44D provides that no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C in computing the income by way of royalty or fees for technical services received from the Government or an Indian concern in pursuance of an agreement made by the foreign company with Government or with the Indian concern. For the purpose of section 44D, royalty has the same meaning as in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi). Hence if any income by way of royalty is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C, and tax will have to be paid on gross amount. If any income by way of consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment or consideration for rendering of any services in such connection is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), then the same will attract the same rate of tax as applicable to 'royalty'.

'Equipment' includes anything used in equipping; furniture, outfit, warlike apparatus; necessaries for travelling, etc. (Oxford Dictionary). Issue arises whether 'equipment' includes airplanes/ships/satellites/vehicles? A ship was a part of the 'equipment' of the business of the shipowner whose ship carries ore/bulk/oil. [Coltman v. Bibby Tankers Ltd. [1987] 3 All ER 1068, 1071 (HL)].

It had entered into agreements with its Indian associate enterprises (AEs). In terms of said agreements, assessee provided management and governance supports functions in area of legal, tax, treasury, finance, information technology, human resources, enterprise risk management, etc. Assessee filed application under section 197 seeking 'NIL' withholding tax certificate in respect of cross charges received from its AEs for services rendered by it. AO rejected said application and held that charges paid to assessee by its AEs were taxable as fees for technical services (FTS) and fees for included services (FIS). The High Court noted that assessee rendered wide range of services to its AEs but none of services could be considered as 'included services' within meaning of article 12 of India-US DTAA as same was not ancillary and subsidiary to application or enjoyment of right, property or information for which assessee received royalty as covered under article 12(3) of India-US DTAA. Further, services rendered by assessee did not make available technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to AEs. On appeal, the High Court held that since service provided did not confer any right in favour of recipient in respect of knowledge, experience, skill or know-how, condition that services 'make available' such technical knowledge, know-how, skill, or process so as to fall with sweep of FIS would not be satisfied. Further, given fact that AEs did not acquire any copyright in software, cross charges paid by them could not be construed as royalties within scope of article 12(3) of India-US DTAA. Therefore, order u/s 197 was set aside, and AO was to be directed to issue necessary certificate or ‘NIL’ withholding Tax Certificate in respect of cross-cost charges as received by assessee from its AEs. The Supreme Court in case of Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. The difference between contract of service and contract of sale of goods is that, in the former, there is, in the person performing of work or rendering of ‘service’, and no property or the thing is produced as a whole notwithstanding that a part or even the whole of material used by him had been property. In the case of a contract for sale, the thing produced as a whole has individual existence as the sole property of party who produced it some time before the delivery and the property therein passed only under the contract relating thereto to the other party for price. A similar view was expressed by the Apex Court, in State of Tamil Nadu v. Anandam Viswanathan [1989] 1 SCC 613; (1989) 73 STC 1 (SC).

The Supreme Court in the case of Hindustan Shipyard Ltd. v. State of A.P. [2000] 119 STC 533, has held that manufacturing of ships as per plans and specification given by customer and supplying of the ship to the latter, after successful trial and being found to be to the satisfaction of the customer, for an ascertained price, was a case of sale of goods and not works contract. The Apex Court observed :

"If the thing to be delivered has any individual existence before the delivery as the sole property of the party who is to deliver it, then it is a sale. If ‘A’ may transfer property for a price in a thing in which B had no previous property, then the contract is for sale. On the other hand where the main object of work undertaken by the payee of the price is not the transfer of a chattel qua a chattel, the contract is one for work and labour." (p. 546)

9. If branch of liaison office is opened in India, issue of service tax arises.

Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 states that an establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

Maintenance of branch outside India

10. Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012 reads as follows - An establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

This Explanation has been given to definition of 'service'. In fact, this Explanation has nothing to do with definition of 'service' and is at a wrong place.

However, this Explanation is creating lot of difficulties (may be mainly because it has been placed at a wrong place). This Explanation is being interpreted to mean that HO in India and branch outside India are two different 'persons'. Hence, if the HO in India remits money to maintain branch outside India, it will be treated as 'import of service' i.e. branch outside India is providing service to Head Office in India.

Really, 'shall be treated as establishment of different persons' does not mean 'shall be treated as two different persons'.

Thus, Branch/office in India and branch/office of same business entity outside India will be treated as different 'establishments' and not 'different persons'.

A branch received service from its other branch outside India will not be subject to service tax under reverse charge mechanism as 'import of service', as they are not different persons.

Similarly, a branch in India cannot 'export' service to its branch outside India.

In KPIT Cummins v. CCE [2014] 43 GST 266/[2013] 38 taxmann.com 340 (Mum. - CESTAT), assessee was remitting money from India for maintaining various establishments outside India. A prima facie view has been held that when service is provided outside India and consumed outside India, no service tax is leviable in India. Further, the branches of assessee outside India were providing services from out of India and were getting payments outside India. Local taxes in that country were paid. It was held that it cannot be said that foreign branches have provided services on behalf of assessee and assessee cannot be held liable under Business Auxiliary Services under reverse charge. In any case, it would be export of service and not taxable.

Royalties in general means the payment made to the owners of certain types of rights by those who are permitted by the owners to exercise the rights. The term originated from the fact that in Great Britain for centuries gold and silver mines were the property of the Crown and such 'royal' metals could be mined only if a payment ("Royalty") were made to the Crown.

Royalties thus reflect usage-based payments made by one party (the "licensee") to another (the "licensor") for ongoing use of intangible or tangible assets. Intangible assets are defined as identifiable non-monetary assets that cannot be seen, touched or physically measured, which are created through time and/or effort and that are identifiable as a separate asset. There are two primary forms of intangibles - legal intangibles (such as trade secrets (e.g., customer lists), copyrights, patents, trademarks, and goodwill) and competitive intangibles (such as knowledge activities (know-how, knowledge, collaboration activities, leverage activities, and structural activities). Royalties can be determined as a percentage of gross or net sales derived from use of the asset or a fixed price per unit sold. Further, there also exist other modes and metrics of compensation.

The cross border transactions have given rise to tax controversies, which are pending adjudications before the Tribunals and Courts in India.

The first leg of the controversy relates to the taxability of the foreign entity, granting the rights. When the user of the right, property or information is resident in one country say India and pays royalties to the owner thereof who is resident in another country say the USA, the amount paid by the user is generally subject to withholding tax in India, the source country. The basic challenge, which is pending before courts relates the characterisation of the certain payments. While the taxpayer contends that the payment received is in lieu of services and not grant of rights, the Revenue Authorities contends otherwise. The most talked about controversy here relates to transmission of data through undersea cables, satellites etc. Other could be where the taxpayer contends that there is transfer of rights in perpetuity and hence the transaction qualifies a sale. The most talked about controversy here relates to usage of off the shelf software products.

The second leg of controversy relates to the treatment of the cost incurred in the hands of the Indian user entity. For the purposes of this article, we are limiting the discussion to the transfer pricing challenges, which arise when the transaction is between two related entities of the group.

Take a simple scenario, a manufacturing enterprise or an inventor may have incurred substantial sums on the development of the property generating the royalties. However, the work of research and testing involves considerable capital outlays and does not always yield successful results. The issue lies in determining an appropriate arm's length return for using such property, which is rather complex. The Revenue Authorities generally raise the challenge from a variety of perspectives, such as (a) why user entity per se has taken up the right; (b) what is the technology granted and how it has benefited the Indian entity; and (c) how to determine the arm's length price.

In this article, we have taken a deep dive into these controversies.

CONTROVERSIES DISSECTED

One of the typical situations giving rise to the transfer pricing controversy involves a Foreign Multinational Group licensing technology/know-how to its Indian affiliate and charging a bundled Royalty. The Indian affiliate would deploy the technology in the manufacturing process and; thereafter would undertake selling and distribution function selling goods under the brand name of the Foreign Multinational Group. In lieu of the rights granted, Indian affiliate would pay a Royalty charge, of say 5%, which will be computed on its net sales. The entities would document their understanding through a written agreement.

The Revenue Authorities generally makes the following assertions upon encountering the above situation:

(a)

The taxpayer has not been able to provide substantial evidence of any tangible benefit arising from the use of such rights and as to why it entered into such an arrangement;

(b)

The taxpayer have not been able to demonstrate that its profits have increased, by use of technology or brand name and no cost benefit analysis was furnished;

(c)

The taxpayer has used Regulatory guidelines to justify the royalty rate and such treatment lacks judicial approval;

(d)

The taxpayer has failed to produce contemporary data, justifying the rate of royalty payout.

With the aid of some or all the assertions, Revenue Authorities at times adjudicate that value of such royalty payment charge is NIL.

In subsequent paragraphs, we deal with some of the key propositions which could be used to defend and justify the royalty payout.

Income deemed to accrue or arise in India*

Income deemed to accrue or arise in India [Section 9]

5.1 Section 9 of the Act provides for situations where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Vide the Finance Act, 1976, it was provided, inter alia, that in case of payments of interest, royalty or fees for technical services (FTS) received from a resident payer, income would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where the interest or royalty or FTS is relatable to a business or profession carried on by the resident payer outside India or for making or earning any income from any source outside India.

The Finance Act, 2007 inserted an Explanation in section 9 with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 and clarified that where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(v), (vi) or (vii), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India1.

The amendment was made to neutralize the judgment of Supreme Court in Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. DIT[2007] 288 ITR 408/ 158 Taxman 259.

The Karnataka High Court in Jindal Thermal Power Co. Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 252 has held that the Explanation does not fully neutralise Supreme Court decision and has observed as follows:

“The Explanation incorporated in section 9(2) declares that ‘where the income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under clauses (v), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident; whether or not the resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India’. The plain reading of the said provision suggests that criterion of residence, place of business or business connection of a non-resident in India has been done away with for fastening the tax liability. However, the criteria of rendering service in India and the utilisation of the service in India laid down by the Supreme Court in Ishikawajima Heavy Industries Ltd.’s case (supra) to attract tax liability under section 9(1)(vii) remains untouched and unaffected by the Explanation to section 9(2).” (Emphasis supplied)

In view of the above, the Finance Act, 2010 substitutes the Explanation, with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 also to cover the situation left out earlier, that is, rendition of services in India and provides that the income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India whether the non-resident has rendered services in India or not.

After the amendment, based on source rule, interest, royalty and fees for technical services would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, to a non-resident, whether or not:

⮚ the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India; and

⮚ the non-resident has rendered services in India.

In other words, even if a non-resident does not have residence or place of business or business connection in India and has not rendered services in India, interest, royalty and fees for technical services, if paid by a resident (not utilised for the purposes of business outside India) would be deemed to accrue or arise in India and accordingly taxable in the hands of the non-resident.

It appears, even after the amendment, having regard to the facts and the circumstances, certain payments may not constitute income in the hands of a non-resident payee, like, fees for services not in the nature of ‘make available’ services and, accordingly, does not constitute fees for technical services (and, hence, in the nature of business or professional income) in terms of a Treaty.

However, this argument is bound to fail in view of the very specific provisions under service tax laws. The Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infotech Software Dealers Association has held that transaction in relation to canned/off-the-shelf software can be service in case the developer of software retains the copyright while right to use of software is given to the subscriber. The scenario has become grave for the dealers who prior to introduction of service tax were charging only sales tax on the value of software. Now in view of the specific category under service tax, they need to charge both sales tax and service tax. Since the sales tax and service tax are indirect taxes and to avoid litigation, the dealers tend to charge both the taxes and it is only the end - consumer who has to suffer in view of multiplicity of taxes.

As regards the customized/uncanned software, the contract for development of such software perhaps at the best may be viewed as a service contract. The customized software means software developed for a specific customer to meet his specific requirements. The software industry prior to the introduction of new category of taxable service in the name of 'Information Technology Software Service' was at an advantageous position, as no indirect taxes were applicable on the development of customized software treating it as a service contract. However, the advantageous position got diluted after the introduction of new category as above, as now development of customized software attracts service tax. The dilution has further been deepened after the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. in which it has been held that even customized software may qualify as goods.

The sales tax authorities after taking recourse to the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court are issuing notices demanding tax on the transaction involving development of software. The judgment has opened a Pandora's Box of litigations in relation to customized/uncanned software.

Another area of litigation concerning software is supply of software through electronic downloads. In such a scenario, service tax gets attracted in view of the specific language of the taxable service under the category of 'Information Technology Software Service'. However, whether sales tax is also payable is another point where litigation surrounds the software industry. The Hon'ble Karnataka High Court recently in the case of Sasken Communication Technologies Ltd. has observed that intellectual property once put on a medium becomes goods and when transferred is leviable to sales tax. After this judgment, the industry players can hope that the sales tax authorities do not litigate on this issue.

The menace of double taxation is detrimental to the interests of users of goods/services as it results into high procurement costs, especially in those cases where credit of input taxes paid cannot be taken by the users. The domestic users only take a hit as the exporters of software generally enjoy the tax free status and, accordingly, no taxes are charged on the value of goods/services exported from India. Presently, the sales tax (local VAT) rate for software is either at 4% or at 5% and service tax rate is at 10%, which can significantly enhance the costs of procurements in case software suffers double taxation, specifically in cases where the credit of input taxes is not available either in full or in part.

Though the laws on sales tax and service tax are on the statute books for good number of years now, yet the provisions of these laws need alignment, which seems to be an uphill task in view of the fact that the Governments desire to garner more and more revenue and sometimes it happens by introducing provisions which put the taxpayer in a situation where he has no alternative but to resort to litigation.

2.2 Issues regarding Classification - Another controversy that surrounds the software revolves around its classification, especially in those cases where the software is not embedded in the hardware and is procured separately from the vendor of the hardware. The problem is generally faced by the importers of telecom equipments.

At present, the rate of customs duty on telecom equipments is generally at around 15% and on software it is at around 10% in case it is imported say on CD. Due to the difference in the rate of customs duty, the customs authorities always litigate on the genuineness of the imports and try to include the value of software in the value of hardware and, accordingly, make the value of software suffer higher rate of customs duty. This particular issue of telecom industry is yet to test the scrutiny of judiciary but apparently, both hardware and software are classifiable into different customs tariff classifications and different customs duty structure is also justifiable.

2.3 Issues regarding Withholding Tax - Another issue that hovers around software is whether the payments remitted by a resident to a non-resident for software can be said to be one for use of copyright or can be categorised as one for copyrighted article. The issue has over a period of time been interpreted differently by the Appellate Tribunals across India. In case, the amount is categorised as royalty, the Indian entity making the payment is required to do withholding of tax under section 195 of the Income-tax Act.

The Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Novel Inc. v. Dy. DIT [2011] 16 taxmann.com 186 has held that payments made by the Indian distributors to a non-resident for procuring rights to further sell the software to customers in India would not amount to royalty.

Section 9

Finance Act, 2010

Income deemed to accrue or arise in India [Section 9]

5.1 Section 9 of the Act provides for situations where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Vide the Finance Act, 1976, it was provided, inter alia, that in case of payments of interest, royalty or fees for technical services (FTS) received from a resident payer, income would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where the interest or royalty or FTS is relatable to a business or profession carried on by the resident payer outside India or for making or earning any income from any source outside India.

The Finance Act, 2007 inserted an Explanation in section 9 with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 and clarified that where income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(v), (vi) or (vii), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India1.

The amendment was made to neutralize the judgment of Supreme Court in Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. DIT [2007] 288 ITR 408/158 Taxman 259.

The Karnataka High Court in Jindal Thermal Power Co. Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 182 Taxman 252 has held that the Explanation does not fully neutralise Supreme Court decision and has observed as follows:

"The Explanation incorporated in section 9(2) declares that 'where the income is deemed to accrue or arise in India under clauses (v), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1), such income shall be included in the total income of the non-resident; whether or not the resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India'. The plain reading of the said provision suggests that criterion of residence, place of business or business connection of a non-resident in India has been done away with for fastening the tax liability. However, the criteria of rendering service in India and the utilisation of the service in India laid down by the Supreme Court in Ishikawajima Heavy Industries Ltd.'s case (supra) to attract tax liability under section 9(1)(vii) remains untouched and unaffected by the Explanation to section 9(2)." (Emphasis supplied)

In view of the above, the Finance Act, 2010 substitutes the Explanation, with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976 also to cover the situation left out earlier, that is, rendition of services in India and provides that the income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India whether the non-resident has rendered services in India or not.

After the amendment, based on source rule, interest, royalty and fees for technical services would be deemed to accrue or arise in India, to a non-resident, whether or not:

the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India; and

the non-resident has rendered services in India.

In other words, even if a non-resident does not have residence or place of business or business connection in India and has not rendered services in India, interest, royalty and fees for technical services, if paid by a resident (not utilised for the purposes of business outside India) would be deemed to accrue or arise in India and accordingly taxable in the hands of the non-resident.

It appears, even after the amendment, having regard to the facts and the circumstances, certain payments may not constitute income in the hands of a non-resident payee, like, fees for services not in the nature of 'make available' services and, accordingly, does not constitute fees for technical services (and, hence, in the nature of business or professional income) in terms of a Treaty.

2.1-1 Differences between the pre-amendment Explanation 2A and the post amendment Explanation 2A

Differences between the pre-amendment Explanation 2A and the post amendment Explanation 2A are as follows:— Explanation 2A(a) refers to "transaction in respect of any goods, services or property carried out by a non-resident with any person in India". Should the transaction be "in India" or the person with whom the non-resident is transacting should be "in India"? It appears that the person (counterparty) has to be in India. The transaction may or may not be in India. Likewise, the non-resident need not be in India.

The said counter party may be—

(a)

a resident of India or a non-resident;

(b)

an individual or any other corporate or non corporate entity;

(c)

carrying on business or not

The counterparty has to be in "India" which term has been defined in section 2(25A) as follows:

"India" means the territory of India as referred to in article 1 of the Constitution, its territorial waters, seabed and subsoil underlying such waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone or any other maritime zone as referred to in the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 (80 of 1976), and the air space above its territory and territorial waters.

The definition is very wide and read literally, Explanation 2A would cover even transactions between a non-resident airlines and a passenger in an aeroplane flying over India! It could be argued, however, that in the context, the wide meaning is not adopted.

It is pertinent to note that mere SEP does not constitute business connection; it is the SEP of a non-resident "in India" that constitutes business connection (the opening line of Explanation 2A). Now, the first proviso to Explanation 2A states that transaction or activities specified in the Explanation shall constitute SEP in India, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business "in India" or not or whether he renders services "in India" or not etc. Thus, the proviso by using the expression "in India", appears to constitute an SEP of a non-resident in India as used in the opening lines in Explanation 2A, and as contained in clauses (a) and (b) of Explanation 2A and hence, there is a business connection even if the non-resident is not in India.

Since the words "through digital means" are deleted in the amended definition, there could be an SEP if there is a specified business activity or interaction with prescribed number of users in India whether through digital or other means.

For a detailed discussion on SEP, see Taxmann's Master Guide to Income-tax Act, 2018, (see para 3.2).

Some aspects relating to SEP under the amended law which are common to the definition of SEP in pre-amended Explanation 2A are reiterated below:—

(a)

A transaction in respect of physical goods (including books) is also covered by the expression SEP.

(b)

A transaction in respect of shrink wrap software may result in SEP since it is now well settled that such software is "goods".

(c)

A transaction in respect of services which are not covered by definition of fees for technical services in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii) (e.g. consideration for construction project, etc.) may also constitute SEP.

(d)

The non-resident may carry out transaction directly or through a third party.

(e)

The provision in the DTAA with the country of which the non-resident is a resident will override the Explanation 2A and in the absence of a permanent establishment, a non-resident may not be liable to tax in India merely on account of SEP, if he complies with the requirements of section 90(4)/(5).

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import. The payments made by HCL to SAP India were in relation post-importation activities. Pursuant to the import of the CD containing the software, HCL paid license fee to SAP India for obtaining license key codes to unlock the full version of the software upon expiry of trial period. Hence, the license fee was not a condition of sale for the import of CDs containing software.

This apart, right to use the software is different from the sale of goods and HCL is only provided a non-exclusive right to use the SAP Software. Thus, there is no "sale".

As a result, the Tribunal held that the license fee paid by HCL to SAP India could not be included in the valuation of imported CDs containing software. Consequently, duty demand, interest and penalties were set aside.

Why does this case matter?

This judgment sheds clarity and sets a sound precedent that not every overenthusiastic attempt to automatically include license fee/royalty is appropriate – especially when these payments don't meet the strict statutory criteria under Rule 9(1)(c) of the CVR.

The judgment decisively burst several prevalent myths regarding the inclusion of license fee/royalty payments in customs valuation: Myth#1: License fee/royalty must always be included in value of the imported goods if the same is part of the agreements; Myth#2: License fee/royalty for obtaining additional licenses post-import of the goods, must be included for the purposes of Customs Valuation; Myth#3: Electronic delivery of software is treated the same as physical import for Customs purposes; and Myth#4: "Right to use" the imported goods is same as that of "sale of goods."

The Tribunal arrived at such conclusions on the basis of the specific terms mentioned in the EULA. In essence, the judgment highlights that assessing the inclusion of license fee/royalty in valuation of the imported goods is akin to reading fine print under a magnifying glass—every detail in the agreement can shift the outcome. Thus, each licensing agreement needs a careful, case-by-case look to decide if the license fee/royalty emanating therefrom becomes a part of customs valuation.

Beyond the Judgement: Practical Insights for Importers

This struggle isn't just about numbers or tax compliance. It's about language of the agreement. Misinterpretation could mean hefty penalties, but overzealous inclusion of license fee/royalty in the valuation of the imported goods could suffocate the cost structure of businesses. Every contract clause is dissected with the precision once reserved for engineering specs: Is this a 'condition of sale'? Does the license fee payment flow directly to the seller? Could it be included in the transaction value of the imported goods and consequently trigger customs duty?

Given the wide variety of contractual arrangements, it is essential to closely examine each agreement to determine whether any license fee/royalty is includible in the transaction value of the imported goods. If the contract or agreement is still in the drafting stage, it becomes even more critical to analyse these clauses thoroughly to ensure that the correct legal course is taken. Ultimately, it is best to review each of your agreements to ensure a sound risk management for imports.

Navigating the landscape of valuation for the imports

In the complex world of imports, businesses often consider the value of the physical goods to be paramount. However, they sometimes overlook that beyond the physical cargo lies something less visible yet crucial — the royalty/license fee payments. Royalties arise from licensing agreements which grant the importer rights inter alia to use manufacturing know-how, brand names, or software embedded within imported goods.

As the nature of contracts pertaining to imports/exports and associated license fee/royalty has evolved, the Customs valuation has also come a long way. Once upon a time, a physical shipment was all that customs authorities cared about for determining its value and imposition duties. Today's imports bundle licensed software, technology, trademarks, and other rights, making valuation of such shipments more complicated. While the goods themselves represent the tangible aspect for customs valuation, the accompanied intangible rights and their payments may significantly contribute to the overall value of the import transaction. This evolution sets the stage for courts to demystify when license fee/royalty should be included in the transaction value of the imported goods.

The recent judgement by CESTAT, New Delhi in the judgment of HCL Technologies Ltd. and SAP India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication) [Final Order No. 51379-51462 of 2025 dated 29-9-2025] bring these complexities to the forefront. It deals with critical questions regarding includability of license fee in the value of the imported goods, specifically in the context of delivery of software through physical and electronic media.

Under the Lens: CESTAT's approach in the case of HCL Technologies Ltd.

Facts at a Glance

HCL Technologies Ltd. ('HCL') entered into an End-User License Agreement ('EULA') with SAP India Private Limited ('SAP India') to obtain non-exclusive and perpetual license to use propriety software, documentation and other information of SAP India. As per terms of the EULA, the software was to be delivered electronically. In the year 2006, SAP India raised substantial invoices on HCL for payment of license fee relating to rights provided under the EULA.

During the same time, HCL received some imported CDs containing SAP Software via courier, wherein a nominal value was declared under the courier bill of entry, for customs purposes. Perhaps, this is what caught the eye of the Customs Department – A CD with a software... only for pocket change?

An investigation was initiated against inter alia HCL for such imports. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Customs Department rejected the declared value of the CDs under Rule 10A of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 ('CVR') [now Rule 14 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] and sought to include the license fee in the valuation of imported CDs in terms of Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR.

The allegation of the Customs Department was that unless the license fee is paid, the software on the CD cannot be accessed or used; thereby, making the license fee integral to the transaction value of the imported CDs.

Tribunal's Verdict: Four Conditions for Royalty Inclusion in Customs Valuation

The Tribunal determined that for inclusion of royalties to the value of the imported goods, the following four key conditions under Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR needed to be satisfied:

1.

The license fee must relate to the imported goods;

2.

The fee must be payable directly or indirectly by the importer at the time of import;

3.

The license fee must be a condition of sale of the goods; and

4.

The fee must not already be included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods.

Guided by these conditions, the Tribunal took a closer look at the terms of the EULA entered between HCL&SAP India, and made the following findings:

The license fee was not related to the physical import of the CDs; rather, it was related to the intangible right to use the software in India. The EULA had itself provided electronic delivery as the mode of delivery of the software. Thus, the license fee was for usage of software rights and not for the import of physical CDs themselves.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import.

Unlike trade in goods, services do not cross the border or pass the frontier and, therefore, hard to regulate at that point. A ‘service’ is an intangible product and can be supplied easily by using information technology such as calls, fax and e-mail. The important characteristics of services are:—

(a) Services are process.

(b)Transaction in services may require personal contact between providers and consumers.

(c)Some services may have to be regulated.

Where ‘services’ itself moves without the provider or recipient having to travel to another country is referred to in terms as ‘Cross Border Provision of Services’5; whereas when the recipient of the service or ‘consumers’ moves to the country where service provider is established is known as ‘Consumption abroad’ or ‘Movement of consumer’6. Lastly, when the business itself moves to the country where services are to be provided it is considered to be commercial presence which is commonly referred as Permanent Establishment.

OUTSOURCING SERVICES IN INDIA

3. Of late, the outsourcing industry around the world has been confronted with the contentious question of whether outsourced services provided by companies — particularly by captive service providers/manufacturers — would lead to a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident service recipient to come into existence under the terms of the relevant tax treaty. India has been a major beneficiary in the outsourcing boom, and, hence, if Indian tax authorities were to hold that such activities are tantamount to a PE, the global profits attributable to the PE would be taxable in India at the rate of 42.23 per cent7. Further, the availability of a tax credit in the home jurisdiction for such tax paid in India would be uncertain, potentially leading to double taxation and wiping out the economic advantage of outsourcing to India. On the other hand, if no PE exists, no profits can be subjected to Indian corporate tax.

In India, tax liability is based on the structure of the outsourcing contract and the scope of activities being undertaken. The generally preferred models, like third-party service providers, captive centres set up as wholly owned subsidiaries or outsourcing to transition partners on a BOT basis are taxed differently under Indian tax laws. Companies establishing captive facilities and BOT arrangements have to consider issues relating to transfer pricing and permanent establishment.

The case of taxability of foreign companies engaged in maintaining and operating a Computerized Reservation System (‘CRS’) is an automated computerized system through which its subscribers are able to offer ticketing and reservation services to their clients.

The Delhi Bench of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal (‘ITAT’) has recently ruled in the case of two companies Amadeus Global Travels1 1 (‘Amadeus’) and Galileo International Inc.12 (‘Galileo’) that a foreign company operating a CRS has a taxable presence in India.13

In the above both cases, the facts remain almost same as:—Wherein a foreign company which had developed a fully automatic CRS had entered into an agreement with its subsidiary in India to provide data processing, software development services and services pertaining to the distribution of the foreign company’s products to several subscribers in India. These subscribers were travel agents in India who used these products to make airline or hotel bookings for their clients in India. Subsidiary company having presence in India had been authorized by parent company to enter into contracts with subscribers/travel agents within India. Hence, the parent company received payments from their participating carriers based on the net bookings made by such subscribers in India and across the world.

In both these rulings, the ITAT held that a foreign company having CRS through which subscribers/travel agents in India were able to offer ticketing and reservation services to the clients in India represented a business connection and the computer hardware/software provided to the travel agent by them constituted its Permanent Establishment (‘PE’) in India. As regards the attribution of profits, same principles were applied by the ITAT in both the rulings and 15 per cent of the revenue accruing to A Ltd. was attributed to the PE in India. The Tribunal held it as a permanent establishment because of:—

u The company had a fixed place of business as it exercised computer control over the computer installed at the premises of the subscribers; and since the supply of computers, its configuration and connectivity were all provided by foreign company.
