[Para 22] It is well-settled that in the absence of any definition of 'copyright' in the Income-tax Act or the DTAA with the respective Countries, in view of clause 3 of the DTAA, reference is to be made to the respective law regarding definition of 'Copyright', namely, Copyright Act, 1957, in India, wherein it is clearly stated that 'literary work' includes computer programmes, tables and compilations including computer [databases]. [Para 23]

It is clear from the provisions of the Copyright Act that the right to copyright work would also constitute exclusive right of the copyright holder and any violation of the said right would amount to infringement under section 51 of the said Act. However, if such copying of computer programme is done by a lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, the same would not constitute infringement of copyright and wherefore, but for the licence granted in these cases to the assessee to make copy of the software contained in shrink-wrapped/off-the-shelf software into the hard disk of the designated computer and to take a copy for back-up purposes, the end user has no other right and the said taking back-up would have constituted an infringement, but for the licence. Therefore, licence is granted for taking copy of the software and to store it in the hard disk and to take a back-up copy and right to make a copy itself is a part of the copyright. Therefore, when licence is granted to make use of the software by making copy of the same and to store it in the hard disk of the designated computer and to take back-up copy of the software, it is clear that what is transferred is right to use the software, an exclusive right, which the owner of the copyright, i.e., the supplier owns and what is transferred is only right to use copy of the software for the internal business as per the terms and conditions of the agreement. [Para 24]

Therefore, the contention of the assessee that there is no transfer of any part of copyright or copyright under the impugned agreements or licenses cannot be accepted. Accordingly, right to make a copy of the software and use it for internal business by making copy of the same and storing the same in the hard disk of the designated computer and taking back-up copy would itself amount to copyright work under section 14(1) of the said Act and licence is granted to use the software by making copies, which work, but for the licence granted would have constituted infringement of copyright and licencee is in possession of the legal copy of the software under the licence. Therefore, the contention of the assessee, that there is no transfer of any part of copyright or copyright and transaction only involves sale of copy of the copyright software, cannot be accepted. What is supplied is the copy of the software of which the supplier continues to be the owner of the copyright and what is granted under the licence is only right to copy the software as per the terms of the agreement, which, but for the licence would amount to infringement of copyright and in view of the licence granted, the same would not amount to infringement under section 52 of the Copyright Act. Therefore, the amount paid to the non-resident supplier towards supply of shrink-wrapped software, or off-the-shelf software is not the price of the C.D. alone nor software alone nor the price of licence granted. This is a combination of all and, in substance, unless licence is granted permitting the end user to copy and download the software, the dumb C.D. containing the software would not in any way be helpful to the end user as software would become operative only if it is downloaded to the hardware of the designated computer as per the terms and conditions of the agreement and that makes the difference between the computer software and copyright in respect of books or pre-recorded music software as book and pre-recorded music C.D. can be used once they are purchased, but so far as software stored in dumb C.D. is concerned, the transfer of dumb C.D., by itself, would not confer any right upon the end user and the purpose of the C.D. is only to enable the end user to take a copy of the software and to store it in the hard disk of the designated computer if licence is granted in that behalf and in the absence of licence, the same would amount to infringement of copyright, which is exclusively owned by non-resident suppliers, who would continue to be the proprietor of copyright. Therefore, there is no similarity between the transaction of purchase of the book or pre-recorded music C.D. or the C.D. containing software and in view of the same, the Legislature, in its wisdom, has treated the literary work like books and other articles separately from 'computer' software within the meaning of the 'Copyright' as referred to above under section 14 of the Copyright Act. It markets the licensed software products mostly through a distribution channel comprising of Value Added Resellers (VARs). According to the applicant, VARs are independent third party resellers who are in the business of selling software to end users. To authorize a VAR to act as the reseller of products, the applicant enters into a General VAR Agreement (‘GVA’). As per the business model, the product is sold to VAR for a consideration based on the standard listed price less discount. The VAR, in turn, sells such products to the end users at a price independently determined by it. The explanations read as under:

"Explanation 4 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Explanation 5 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not–

(a)

the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b)

such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c)

the ocation of such right, property or information is in India.

Explanation 6 – For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the expression "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-lining of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret."

On comparing Explanation 4 with Article 12(2) of OECD MC it is evident that the term "used or right to use" is succeeded by the word "a computer software" in the former and the word "copyright" in the later. It is also being discussed among the scholarly circles whether Explanation4 is amplifying the scope of Explanation2 or is it creating another dimension of the substantive provision. Is it legally acceptable in respect of a new Explanation providing an expanded meaning of term "royalty" which was already defined in Explanation 2 of section 9(1)(vi) ? If it amounts to altering the meaning of "royalty" can it be retrospective through an Explanation. It is well understood that the meaning of "royalty" under the Act is wider than the meaning provided under OECD MC. The gap is further widened by this new Explanation4.

2.2. Explanation 5 seeks to clarify that the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer or not would not make difference in deciding whether particular payment is "royalty". In the same manner, whether the payer used such right, property or information directly or not and whether the location of such right, property or information is in India or not would not make difference in deciding whether the payment is "royalty" or not. However, Hon'ble Delhi High Court while deciding the case of Ericsson A.B., (supra) has held that for the purpose of section 9(1) (v), (vi), (vii) it is not required to go into explanation to Sec.9 (2) of the Act, if the payment does not fall into any of the categories covered by (v), (vi) and (vii).

In view of the same, it is possible to argue that once sale of computer software is not covered by Explanation 2, so as to be treated as "royalty" than the new Explanation 5 would not have any bearing on such a transaction. It is also interesting to note that Explanations4 and 5 refer to the rights in respect of right, property or information leaving aside other terms such as "patent, process, invention etc," as mentioned in Explanation 2.

2.3 The newly inserted Explanations 4 and 5 would not bring finality for interpreting the term "royalty" either under the treaty law or under the post amended domestic law.

2.4 Explanation 6 has been inserted to neutralize the judgment of Asia Satellite Telecommunications Co. Ltd. v. DIT [2011] 332 ITR 340/197 Taxman 263/9 taxmann.com 168(Delhi), thereby providing the term "process" includes transmission by satellite, cable, optic fiber, any other similar technology whether or not such process is secret, whether or not the satellite etc are under the control of the customers. The amendment is widening the scope of the term "royalty".

2.5 The amendments brought in through these Explanations clarify the term "royalty" in such a way which is in conflict with the OECD MCC on Article 12 explained in paras 12 to 17 and at para 9.1 These amendments result in holding most of the software payments/telecom services to be within the ambit of term "royalty" unless specifically protected by the treaty or the exclusion provided under section 9(1)(vi)(b)/(c) of the Act.

Royalties in general means the payment made to the owners of certain types of rights by those who are permitted by the owners to exercise the rights. The term originated from the fact that in Great Britain for centuries gold and silver mines were the property of the Crown and such 'royal' metals could be mined only if a payment ("Royalty") were made to the Crown.

Royalties thus reflect usage-based payments made by one party (the "licensee") to another (the "licensor") for ongoing use of intangible or tangible assets. Intangible assets are defined as identifiable non-monetary assets that cannot be seen, touched or physically measured, which are created through time and/or effort and that are identifiable as a separate asset. There are two primary forms of intangibles - legal intangibles (such as trade secrets (e.g., customer lists), copyrights, patents, trademarks, and goodwill) and competitive intangibles (such as knowledge activities (know-how, knowledge, collaboration activities, leverage activities, and structural activities). Royalties can be determined as a percentage of gross or net sales derived from use of the asset or a fixed price per unit sold. Further, there also exist other modes and metrics of compensation.

The cross border transactions have given rise to tax controversies, which are pending adjudications before the Tribunals and Courts in India.

The first leg of the controversy relates to the taxability of the foreign entity, granting the rights. When the user of the right, property or information is resident in one country say India and pays royalties to the owner thereof who is resident in another country say the USA, the amount paid by the user is generally subject to withholding tax in India, the source country. The basic challenge, which is pending before courts relates the characterisation of the certain payments. While the taxpayer contends that the payment received is in lieu of services and not grant of rights, the Revenue Authorities contends otherwise. The most talked about controversy here relates to transmission of data through undersea cables, satellites etc. Other could be where the taxpayer contends that there is transfer of rights in perpetuity and hence the transaction qualifies a sale. The most talked about controversy here relates to usage of off the shelf software products.

The second leg of controversy relates to the treatment of the cost incurred in the hands of the Indian user entity. For the purposes of this article, we are limiting the discussion to the transfer pricing challenges, which arise when the transaction is between two related entities of the group.

Take a simple scenario, a manufacturing enterprise or an inventor may have incurred substantial sums on the development of the property generating the royalties. However, the work of research and testing involves considerable capital outlays and does not always yield successful results. The issue lies in determining an appropriate arm's length return for using such property, which is rather complex. The Revenue Authorities generally raise the challenge from a variety of perspectives, such as (a) why user entity per se has taken up the right; (b) what is the technology granted and how it has benefited the Indian entity; and (c) how to determine the arm's length price.

In this article, we have taken a deep dive into these controversies.

CONTROVERSIES DISSECTED

One of the typical situations giving rise to the transfer pricing controversy involves a Foreign Multinational Group licensing technology/know-how to its Indian affiliate and charging a bundled Royalty. The Indian affiliate would deploy the technology in the manufacturing process and; thereafter would undertake selling and distribution function selling goods under the brand name of the Foreign Multinational Group. In lieu of the rights granted, Indian affiliate would pay a Royalty charge, of say 5%, which will be computed on its net sales. The entities would document their understanding through a written agreement.

The Revenue Authorities generally makes the following assertions upon encountering the above situation:

(a)

The taxpayer has not been able to provide substantial evidence of any tangible benefit arising from the use of such rights and as to why it entered into such an arrangement;

(b)

The taxpayer have not been able to demonstrate that its profits have increased, by use of technology or brand name and no cost benefit analysis was furnished;

(c)

The taxpayer has used Regulatory guidelines to justify the royalty rate and such treatment lacks judicial approval;

(d)

The taxpayer has failed to produce contemporary data, justifying the rate of royalty payout.

With the aid of some or all the assertions, Revenue Authorities at times adjudicate that value of such royalty payment charge is NIL.

In subsequent paragraphs, we deal with some of the key propositions which could be used to defend and justify the royalty payout.

2.8 Amendments to section 9(1)(vi)

2.8.1 Amendments Explanations 4, 5 and 6 have been inserted in section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-4-1976 so as to clarify that—

(i) the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred (Explanation 4).

(ii) royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India (Explanation 5).

(iii) the expression 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret (Explanation 6).

2.8.2 Object

The objective of the amendments as explained in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2012 is as follows:

"II. Section 9(1)(vi) provides that any income payable by way of royalty in respect of any right, property or information is deemed to be accruing or arising in India. The term "royalty" has been defined in Explanation 2 which means consideration received or receivable for transfer of all or any right in respect of certain rights, property or information. Some judicial decisions have interpreted this definition in a manner which has raised doubts as to whether consideration for use of computer software is royalty or not; whether the right, property or information has to be used directly by the payer or is to be located in India or control or possession of it has to be with the payer. Similarly, doubts have been raised regarding the meaning of the term processed.

Considering the conflicting decisions of various courts in respect of income in nature of royalty and to restate the legislative intent, it is further proposed to amend the Income-tax Act in following manner:-

(i) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the consideration for use or right to use of computer software is royalty by clarifying that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information as mentioned in Explanation 2, includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

(ii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not

(a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.

(iii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the term "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.

These amendments will take effect retrospectively from 1st June, 1976 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 1977-78 and subsequent assessment years."

Whether the income from the supply contract can be treated as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi)

As already held above that the assessee did not have any business connection in India. It has also been held that the supply of equipment in question was in the nature of supply of goods. Therefore, this issue is to be examined keeping in view these findings. Moreover, another finding of fact is recorded by the Tribunal that the cellular operators did not acquire any of the copyrights referred to in section 14(b ) of the Copyright Act, 1957. [Para 54]

Once one proceeds on the basis of aforesaid factual findings, it is difficult to hold that payment made to the assessee was in the nature of royalty either under the Act or under the DTAA. It is apparent that what was sold by the assessee to the Indian customers was a GSM which consisted both of the hardware as well as the software, therefore, the Tribunal is right in holding that it was not permissible for the revenue to assess the same under two different articles. The software that was loaded on the hardware did not have any independent existence. The software supply is an integral part of the GSM mobile telephone system and is used by the cellular operator for providing the cellular services to its customers. There could not be any independent use of such software. The software is embodied in the system and the revenue accepts that it could not be used independently. This software merely facilitates the functioning of the equipment and is an integral part thereof. [Para 55]

A fortiorari when the assessee supplies the software which is incorporated on a CD, it has supplied tangible property and the payment made by the cellular operator for acquiring such property cannot be regarded as a payment by way of royalty. [Para 56]

It is also to be borne in mind that the supply contract cannot be separated into two viz., hardware and software. [Para 57]

No doubt, in an annexure to the supply contract the lump sum price is bifurcated in two components, viz., the consideration for the supply of the equipment and for the supply of the software. However, it was argued by the assessee that this separate specification of the hardware/software supply was necessary because of the differential customs duty payable. [Para 58]

Be as it may, in order to qualify as royalty payment, within the meaning of section 9(1)(vi) and particularly clause (v) of Expalanation - II thereto, it is necessary to establish that there is transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of any license) in respect of copy right of a literary, artistic or scientific work. Section 2(o ) of the Copyright Act makes it clear that a computer programme is to be regarded as a literary work. Thus, in order to treat the consideration paid by the cellular operator as royalty, it is to be established that the cellular operator, by making such payment, obtains all or any of the copyright rights of such literary work. In the presence case, this has not been established. It is not even the case of the revenue that any right contemplated under section 14 of the Copyright Act,1957 stood vested in this cellular operator as a consequence of the supply contract. Distinction has to be made between the acquisition of a 'copyright right' and a 'copyrighted article'. [Para 59]

Further, there is force in assessee's submission that even assuming the payment made by the cellular operator is regarded as a payment by way of royalty as defined in Explanation 2 below Section 9 (1) (vi), nevertheless, it can never be regarded as royalty within the meaning of the said term in article 13, para 3 of the DTAA. This is so because the definition in the DTAA is narrower than the definition in the Act. Article 13(3) brings within the ambit of the definition of royalty a payment made for the use of or the right to use a copyright of a literary work. Therefore, what is contemplated is a payment that is dependent upon user of the copyright and not a lump sum payment as is the position in the present case. [Para 60]

Thus, it has to be held payment received by the assessee was towards the title and GSM system of which software was an inseparable parts incapable of independent use and it was a contract for supply of goods, therefore, no part of the payment, therefor, can be classified as payment towards royalty. [Para 61]

11.1 Under section 9(1)(vi), income by way of royalty payable is deemed to accrue or arise in India subject to certain conditions. The term 'royalty' has been defined in Explanation 2 to this clause.

Section 9 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 so as to provide that the term 'royalty' shall include :

(a)

consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, but not including the amounts referred to section 44B.

(b)

consideration for rendering of any services in connection with the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

The amendment provides that 'royalty' shall not include amounts referred to in section 44BB. Section 44BB, inter alia, provides that in the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of supply of plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the exploration for and exploitation of mineral oils, 10% of the aggregate of the amounts which have been specified in the section shall be deemed to be profits and gains of the business. Thus, hire charges for the plant and machinery used for exploration, etc., of mineral oils shall not be treated as 'royalty' and shall continue to be taxed under section 44BB.

Following points need to be noted :

The amendment to section 9 brings it in line with the Double Tax Conventions (DTCs) entered into by India which provide that 'royalty' includes consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. These DTCs are based on the OECD Model Conventions 1963 and 1977. It may be noted, however, that the definition of 'royalties' in Article 12(2) of OECD Model was amended in 1992 by excluding payments for the use, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

A distinction must be made between royalties paid for the use of equipment and payments constituting consideration for the outright sale of equipment. In CIT v. Davy Ashmore India Ltd. [1991] 190 ITR 626, the Calcutta High Court has held that where there is an outright sale or purchase, the consideration is for the transfer of designs, secret formula, etc., and cannot be treated as royalty. Applying the same ratio, consideration for outright sale of industrial, commercial or scientific equipment cannot be treated as royalty.

Section 44D provides that no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C in computing the income by way of royalty or fees for technical services received from the Government or an Indian concern in pursuance of an agreement made by the foreign company with Government or with the Indian concern. For the purpose of section 44D, royalty has the same meaning as in Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi). Hence if any income by way of royalty is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed under any of sections 28 to 44C, and tax will have to be paid on gross amount. If any income by way of consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment or consideration for rendering of any services in such connection is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vi), then the same will attract the same rate of tax as applicable to 'royalty'.

'Equipment' includes anything used in equipping; furniture, outfit, warlike apparatus; necessaries for travelling, etc. (Oxford Dictionary). III. Royalty Contrary to the expectation that the retrospective amendment in respect of royalty will provide some finality, litigation on the issue has continued unabated. There is a sense of "déjà vu" inasmuch as different High Courts have once again taken differing views on taxability of income as 'royalty.'

In September 2012, in the case of DIT v. Nokia Networks OY [2013] 212 Taxman 68/[2012] 25 taxmann.com 225 the Delhi High Court held that payment for supply of software imbedded in hardware was not taxable as royalty under Article 13 of the India-Finland DTAA. Relying on its own ruling in DIT v. Ericsson A.B. [2012] 343 ITR 470/204 Taxman 192/16 taxmann.com 371, Delhi High Court rejected the arguments of the Revenue that the question of copyright and copyrighted article was not relevant for the taxability of software under the Act or the DTAA and that the 'right to use' simpliciter of software was a part of the copyright in the software, irrespective of whether a further right to make copies is granted. Delhi High Court observed that the language of the India-Finland DTAA differed from amended section 9(1)(vi) and retrospective amendment could not be read into the treaty.

In November 2013, the Madras High Court, in the case of Verizon Communications Singapore (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 70, ruled that the amount paid by Indian companies to a foreign company for dedicated broadband services constituted "royalty" and ought to be taxed in India under the Income-tax Act as well as the India Singapore treaty. Analyzing the technical aspects of providing bandwidth services in detail and interpreting the retrospective amendments to the definition of 'royalty' in section 9 made by Finance Act, 2012, the Madras High Court observed that the retrospective amendment had removed all doubts insofar as the expression 'use or right to use' was to be understood in the context of possession, control or location, thus approving that the term 'use or right to use' is of wide amplitude.

IBM and Sonata have now approached the Apex Court for determining whether packaged software can be taxed as royalty under DTAAs. It appears that only the verdict of the Supreme Court will put this debate to rest.

B. TRANSFER PRICING

Though transfer pricing is a relatively new area of law, we have all recently witnessed 2 high profile cases before the Bombay High Court that thrust the subject into limelight. Till a couple of years ago, only tax professionals dealing with international tax management/compliance of MNCs were concerned with the nuances of transfer pricing. However, there has been a noticeable change in this trend, with the print and electronic media reporting extensively on these cases. Suddenly, transfer pricing has become a topic of interest not only with most tax professionals but with the general public as well. The fact that transfer pricing has less to do with tax and more to do with market dynamics and economics definitely has a role to play in this development. But another, more important reason, for the increased interest in transfer pricing is the fact that most economies have started showing decreased tolerance to the practices adopted by MNCs for shifting profits to low tax jurisdictions, thereby depriving the "source countries" of their legitimate revenue. The vigour with which OECD is driving its Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) Action Plan and the frequency with which this problem is being discussed at international forums indicates the increasing concern of tax base erosion. Before I elaborate more on BEPS, I want to touch upon a few important issues that are currently in focus.

I. Vodafone II and Vodafone III before Bombay High Court

It seems that any litigation involving 'Vodafone' can never be a low-key affair. If foreign investors complained of flip flops on indirect share transfers in 2012, subjecting share issue transactions to transfer pricing provisions left them 'Shell Shocked' in 2013.

In a detailed judgment of 239 pages, the Bombay High Court cleared the air on some important procedural aspects in the realm of transfer pricing, including the powers of the AO, TPO and DRP. In this case popularly termed as "Vodafone II", the High Court clarified that the AO is not only bound by the TPO's decision in respect of ALP computation, but is also bound by the TPO's decision as regards the character of the transaction i.e. whether or not the transaction is an 'international transaction.' The High Court also held that the powers of the DRP are wide enough to consider all questions of fact/law raised before it. The DRP's power to 'confirm' a transfer pricing adjustment would also include the power 'not to confirm' the same, thereby empowering it to annul the variations as well.

■ The same conclusion follows in relation to the software licences. The record shows that the assessee retains all rights, title and interest in the software; the customer is granted only a restricted licence to use the software for its operations; and the contractual terms prohibit modification, merging, translation, decoding, decompilation, disassembly or reverse engineering. These restrictions, far from indicating any transfer of know-how, underscore the opposite: that the customer is not permitted to access, extract or replicate the underlying technology. There is no factual or legal basis, therefore, to hold that any industrial, commercial or scientific experience in developing the software has been transferred or imparted to the customer. The payment is for a limited right of use in a controlled manner, without enabling the customer to exploit the underlying intellectual creation independently. In treaty interpretation, one must be vigilant against expanding the concept of “royalty” beyond its intended bounds; otherwise, every specialised product or service would become royalty merely because it is delivered by an enterprise possessing expertise an outcome neither contemplated by article 12 nor supported by the jurisprudence. [Para 13]

■

As regards the ancillary services of training, implementation and support, the record itself shows that these services are ancillary and incidental and inextricably linked to the principal supply of data and software and are provided remotely from outside India. Such services involve the application of knowledge by the assessee to ensure effective use and functioning of the supplied product; they do not involve transfer of technical experience or making available any know-how enabling independent reproduction by the customer. The OECD Commentary itself draws a firm distinction between a know-how contract and a service contract, and clarifies that where the provider continues to perform the work himself using his expertise, the payment is not royalty. Therefore, these ancillary receipts also cannot be brought within the net of article 12(3) as royalty for information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience. [Para 14]

Even if the content is similar, a sale of tangible goods cannot be transmuted into royalty for “experience” merely because expertise was involved in producing such charts. If such logic were to be accepted, it would lead to an untenable proposition that every sale of goods manufactured or developed using skill or experience would become royalty, which would be a distortion of both treaty language and accepted principles of international taxation. Most DTAAs between India and other countries define 'royalties' to include payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment. If the specific DTAA between India and the country of which the foreign country is a resident includes 'payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' in its definition of royalty, then the income would be classified as royalty under the DTAA. In such a case, the income would be taxable in India at the rate specified in the DTAA, provided the foreign company is the beneficial owner and the income is not effectively connected to a PE in India. If the DTAA does not include such payments in its royalty definition (under the OECD Model), the income would be treated as business profits and taxable in India only if the foreign company has a PE in India and the profits are attributable to that PE.

8.5-11d Classification as FTS - Section 9(7)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(7)(b) defines 'fees for technical services' as any consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). Where the foreign company also provides the installation and training services for the capital goods, equipment, or tooling to the Indian manufacturer to use them, any fees paid by the Indian manufacturer for these services would squarely fall within the definition of FTS under section 9(7)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India.

Most DTAAs have a specific article on FTS (Fees for Included Services). These articles may include a 'make available' clause, meaning the services must not only be technical but also 'make available' technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to the recipient. If the foreign company is merely providing equipment and not imparting any technical knowledge or skills to the Indian manufacturer that enable the latter to apply the technology independently, the 'make available' test (if present in the DTAA) would not be met. In such a situation, the FTS will not be taxable in India. If the DTAA does not explicitly contain a 'make available' clause, then any service of a managerial, technical, or consultancy nature will be taxable as FTS.

The taxable income, taking these factors into account, will be as follows.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India, and the business income earned in India is connected to such PE, the tax liability in such a case shall be computed as per the ITA. If conditions are not fulfilled, the actual business income shall be computed as per the general provisions.

If the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the business income earned by him in India shall not be taxable in India. In such a situation, the presumptive scheme of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 will have no relevance.

If the specific DTAA between India and the country of which the foreign country is a resident includes 'payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' in its definition of royalty, then the income would be classified as royalty under the DTAA. In such a case, the income would be taxable in India at the rate specified in the DTAA, provided the foreign company is the beneficial owner and the income is not effectively connected to a PE in India. If the DTAA does not include such payments in its royalty definition (under the OECD Model), the income would be treated as business profits and taxable in India only if the foreign company has a PE in India and the profits are attributable to that PE.

8.5-11d Classification as FTS - Section 9(7)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(7)(b) defines 'fees for technical services' as any consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). Where the foreign company also provides the installation and training services for the capital goods, equipment, or tooling to the Indian manufacturer to use them, any fees paid by the Indian manufacturer for these services would squarely fall within the definition of FTS under section 9(7)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India.

Most DTAAs have a specific article on FTS (Fees for Included Services). These articles may include a 'make available' clause, meaning the services must not only be technical but also 'make available' technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to the recipient. If the foreign company is merely providing equipment and not imparting any technical knowledge or skills to the Indian manufacturer that enable the latter to apply the technology independently, the 'make available' test (if present in the DTAA) would not be met. In such a situation, the FTS will not be taxable in India. If the DTAA does not explicitly contain a 'make available' clause, then any service of a managerial, technical, or consultancy nature will be taxable as FTS.

8.5-11e Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on the two factors:

(a)

Whether the foreign company has a PE in India

(b)

Whether the income is such that the presumptive scheme as specified in Section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 applies (corresponding to Section 44BBD of the ITA 1961) (Business of providing services or technology in India, for the purposes of setting up an electronics manufacturing facility).

The taxable income, taking these factors into account, will be as follows.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India, and the business income earned in India is connected to such PE, the tax liability in such a case shall be computed as per the ITA. If the conditions of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 is fulfilled; the taxable business income shall be computed on a presumptive basis at the rate of 25% of the specified amount. If conditions are not fulfilled, the actual business income shall be computed as per the general provisions.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the business income earned by him in India shall not be taxable in India. In such a situation, the presumptive scheme of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 will have no relevance.

Besides these there are two other categories of software, these being: network software and language software. Till now, the Tribunals have been holding that packaged software being ‘goods’, there was no need for the importer to deduct tax at source and that the payment towards procurement of the packaged software cannot be considered as ‘royalty’. However, this latest decision from the Karnataka High Court would supersede such Tribunals’ decisions, at least, for importers in Karnataka. 2.2 The facts of the case, in brief: Certain importers of software licenses had taken a view that the payments made for software imports would not attract the provisions of section 195 of the Income-tax Act, necessitating the deduction of tax at source, since such payments would not constitute taxable income in the nature of royalty or scientific work, in the hands of the non-resident, in terms of section 9(1)(vi) read with the DTAA. The First and Second Appellate Authorities had upheld the importers’ contention that when the payments would be for acquiring a right to use a copyright and not the copyright itself it would not get treated as royalty payments in terms of the DTAAs and, hence, there was no need for deducting tax at source under section 195. The Tribunal had also upheld the importers’ contention that the import of software licenses would be in the nature of a transaction involving import of goods, in the light of the precedents set by the various Courts including the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the TCS case. The revenue contended that software is a ‘scientific work’ and payments for import of software would be covered under section 9(1)(vi) of the Act and that the importer cannot contend that the payment made by him would not constitute income in the hands of the non-resident recipient and that, the importer is duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195.

2.3 The gist of the judgment: In a sweeping judgment, which is perhaps the first judgment from a High Court on the contentious issue related to the applicability of section 195 on software imports, the Karnataka High Court has rejected, in toto, the decisions of the Bangalore Tribunal in various similar judgments and has held that the importer was duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195 for import of software licenses, based almost exclusively, on the Apex Court’s judgment in Transmission Corporation of AP Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 105 Taxman 742. The High Court’s judgment in leads to the premise that the obligation to deduct tax at source under section 195 has nothing to do, with the actual liability of the non-resident to tax under the provisions of the Act, including the quantum thereof. The importer could take recourse to the provisions of section 195(2) if he is of the view that only a part of the payment made by him would bear the character of income in the hands of the non-resident.

2.4 The implications arising out of this judgment: Due to this ruling of the Karnataka High Court, all overseas payments will now be subject to withholding tax, whether or not the income is taxable. Not only is this in dramatic contrast to previous High Court’s decisions, it is also a judgment that will lead to higher cost of business, increased uncertainty and may be even more litigation—at Least for a while.

The law itself as it reads, which is section 195, specifically says that it is a sum which is chargeable to tax under the Income-tax Act on which tax has to be deducted at source, if that payment, of course, is being made to a non-resident. Based on that, for example, the Rajasthan High Court in the SBI case has taken a view that if income is exempt under provisions of the Indian Income-tax Act, one does not need to withhold tax at source at all when the payment is being made to non-resident of such an exempt income.

But now, a judgment by the Karnataka High Court has turned this established principle.

•In terms of this judgment, the importer has only two options before him, vis-à-vis the payments to be effected to the non-resident, viz. either to deduct tax at source under section 195 or to make an application to the Department under section 195(2). In terms of the judgment, this principle would apply equally to import of goods or to import of services or for transactions involving import of goods and services as in the case of a works contract.

•It would look like that importer cannot get into issues related to the applicability of section 9(1) or to the provisions of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA) for purposes of discharging his liability under section 195. In other words, in terms of this judgment, the provisions of section 195 are quite draconian, requiring the resident payer to deduct tax at source without getting into issues related to the taxation of the receipts, in the hands of the non-resident.

'Blaze Advisor' software for its internal business purposes, subject to host of additional terms and limitations contemplated in the body of the said agreement. From a perusal of the agreement, it can safely be gathered that the assessee had made the remittance of USD 100,000 to Fair for grant of license to use its copyrighted software viz. 'Blaze Advisor' software for its internal business purposes. From a perusal of the agreement it is clean that the assessee was clearly divested of all its rights to either transfer, assign and sub-license the said software. There is a clear distinction between royalty paid on transfer of copyright right and consideration for copyrighted articles. The right to use of copyrighted article or product with the owner retaining his copyright, is not the same thing as transferring or assigning rights in relation to the copyright. Rather, for enjoyment of some or all the rights which the copyright owner has is necessary to invoke the royalty definition. In the above backdrop of a non-exclusive and non-transferable license enabling the use of a copyrighted product cannot be construed as an authority to enjoy any or all of the enumerated rights ingrained in article 12. Rather, where the purpose of the license or the transaction is only to restrict the use of the copyrighted product for internal business purpose of the licensee, it would not be legally correct to state that the copyright itself or right to use copyright has been transferred to any extent. Thus as the assessee had only been granted a non-exclusive and non-transferable license to use the copyrighted article i.e 'Blaze advisor' software by its AE which had retained with itself the copyrights of the same, the amount received by the licensor its AE from the assessee did not give rise to any royalty income within the meaning of article 12(3).

The remittance of USD 100,000 made by the assessee to Fair for grant of license to the assessee to use its copyrighted product viz. 'Blaze Advisor' software for its internal business purposes only could not be brought to tax as 'royalty' under article 12(3) of the India-USA DTAA. As no liability was cast upon the assessee to deduct tax at source at the time of making of the aforesaid remittance, hence the latter cannot be held as being an assessee in default within the meaning of section 201.

However, it is possible that the non-resident entity may have a business connection with the resident Indian entity. In such a case, the resident Indian entity could be treated as the Permanent Establishment of the non-resident entity. The tax treatment of the Permanent Establishment in such a case is under consideration in this circular. During the last decade or so, India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated enterprises of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision of services itself like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. The non-resident entity or the foreign company will be liable to tax in India only if the IT-enabled BPO unit in India constitutes its Permanent Establishment. The extent to which the profit of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board.

A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc. or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment become taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as are attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deduction expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if, instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm’s length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profits that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm’s length principle".

"Arm’s length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(iii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm’s length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.

The CBDT Circular No. 1/2004, dated 2nd January, 2004 is hereby withdrawn with immediate effect.

Sub-clauses (c) and (d) address enhanced involvement of agent in the business of a non-resident, leading to increased tax base. They agree with the concept of Permanent Establishment ("PE") and taxation of business income under accepted international taxation principles as laid down in the Model tax conventions issued by the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development ("OECD") as well as the United Nations ("UN"). An interesting question that arises is whether the clarification provided here goes beyond the scope of the provisions in the ITA. Section 9 which extends the scope of taxation laid down under section 5 of the ITA, states that "all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India6, or through or from any property in India, or through or from any asset or source of income in India, or through the transfer of a capital asset situate in India" would be deemed to accrue or arise in India. The most significant condition for extended scope of taxation is that there should be "business connection" in India. This term has not been defined in the ITA. However, it has been explained in various decisions by the Supreme Court of India. In the case of R. D. Aggarwal & Co.7 which was before Circular 23 was issued, the Apex Court held that there should be a real and intimate relation between trading activity carried on outside the taxable territories and trading activity carried on within the territories.

The ITA explains that if all the operations are not carried out in India then entire income will not be liable to taxation in India. Explanation 1( a) to section 9(1)(i) reads as follows :

"in the case of a business of which all the operations are not carried out in India, the income of the business deemed under this clause to accrue or arise in India shall be only such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India."

A combined reading of section 9(1)(i), the views expressed by the Supreme Court of India in the case of R. D. Aggarwal and the above Explanation, leads to the conclusion that the income of a non-resident will be liable to taxation in India only when the trading activity in India and the trading activity outside India, have real and intimate relationship. Further, only that income would be taxable in India which can be reasonably attributed to the operations carried out in India. In fact, the OECD subscribes to similar views.

OECD Model Tax Convention on PE and Transfer Pricing

It has been internationally accepted that the source country should not tax income of a foreign entity unless there is some longer economic relationship between the source country and the entity. This has been incorporated in the OECD Model tax treaty. Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of the Model states: "The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to that permanent establishment." When it comes to defining the term "permanent establishment" ("PE") Article 5 identifies the following categories – fixed PE, service PE and agency PE. So far as the first PE is concerned, broadly speaking, there is requirement of permanent relationship. Agency PE requires the agent to be dependent and some more conditions to be satisfied. Similarly, for service PE to exist, the services provided by a foreign entity should be over a sufficiently longer period and should satisfy certain conditions.

The authorized OECD approach on attribution of income to permanent establishments (July 2008) has led to an interplay between PE and the transfer pricing approaches. The authorized OECD approach rests on the foundation of Article 7(1) and Article 7(2) of the OECD Model Tax convention. As mentioned above, Article 7 (1) permits the host country to tax the "profits of the enterprise" but only so much as is "attributable to" a PE in the host country. Article 7(2) states that the profits to be attributed to the PE are the profits "it might be expected" to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a part.

Based on the above, the authorized OECD approach prescribes a two step approach for attributing profits to a PE. Step 1 is to hypothesize the PE as a "functionally separate entity" and Step 2 is to compute arm’s length remuneration as per the OECD transfer pricing guidelines.

Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 141/203 Taxman 477/[2012] 345 ITR 494 and Synopsis International Old Ltd. (supra). Overturning the decision in Samsung Electronics Company Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 has held that ownership of copyright in a work is different from the ownership of the physical material in which the copyrighted work may happen to be embodied. Where the core of a transaction is to authorize the end-user to have access to and make use of the "licensed" computer software product over which the licensee has no exclusive rights, no copyright is parted with. When we view the transaction of the assessee group under consideration in totality, it transpires that it has two components, viz., first, NV Bekaert SA paying for purchasing SAP software and installing them in its IT Infrastructure facility; and, second, various group companies paying to NV Bekaert SA for using the IT Infrastructure facility created by it. Whereas the first is a case of copyright royalty, the second is a case of industrial royalty. The ratio of the decision in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (supra) has application only on copyright royalty cases and not on industrial royalty cases as the Hon'ble Apex Court dealt only with copyright royalty. It is only that part of the overall transaction under which NV Bekaert SA purchased SAP and other software that would be governed by the decision of the Hon'ble Summit Court. The purchase price of such software will not constitute royalty in the hands of such vendors so as to require any deduction of tax at source by NV Bekaert SA, which acquired the copyrighted article having no right to make copies of the same. Howbeit, the transaction of the assessee is only of availing access to the IT Infrastructure facility set up by its AE, which is a payment of industrial royalty not ruled by the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. The DRP appears to have been swayed by the decision in Samsung (supra) without realizing that it was not applicable to the transaction of the assessee using the IT Infrastructure facility set up by N.V. Bekaert SA, which was, in fact, a royalty as a consideration for use of industrial or commercial equipment in terms of Explanation 2(iva) and (vi) read with Explanation 5 to section 9(1)(vi) of the Act and not a payment for use of any software simpliciter. The Pune Tribunal in Rieter Machine Works Ltd. v. ACIT (International Taxation) [2022] 134 taxmann.com 326 considered a case of Switzerland based non-resident who set up an I.T. Infrastructure facility (analogous to that of NV Bekaert SA in our case). Group entities across the world including its Indian entity, namely, Rieter India Private Ltd. (RIPL) (analogous to the assessee under consideration) had an access to that facility. The non-resident assessee offered a sum of Rs. 20.04 crore received from RIPL towards its share in the allocation of costs for granting access to its IT facility, described as IT Service charges, for taxation in India. However another sum of Rs. 3.88 crore received from RIPL, being share of the Indian entity in software license cost, was not offered for taxation on the ground that it was reimbursement of IT license costs incurred towards centrally purchasing software licenses and use by RIPL. The Tribunal observed that the software licenses were purchased for installation in the IT Infrastructure facility of the non-resident assessee and RIPL was given only access to that IT facility, similar to what has happened in the case under consideration. Vide its order dated 21-10-2021, which was duly confronted to both the sides during the course of hearing of the extant appeal, the Tribunal held Rs. 3.88 crore was not different from Rs. 20.04 crore and was hence chargeable to tax in India in the hands of the non-resident assessee. The facts of the instant case are on all fours with Rieter Machine Works Ltd. (supra) insofar as the taxability of the amount received by foreign entity from the Indian entity for allowing access to its IT Infrastructure facility, is concerned.

No 'sale' of packaged software - It may be noted that in case of branded (tailor made) software, there is no 'sale' of software as such as entire property in software is never passed on to buyer. Only right to use is transferred (sometimes for a limited period, which has to be renewed by paying further amount). There will be 'sale' of software only if source code and entire property in software is transferred to buyer. Payment for software is in nature of royalty - In CIT v. Sunray Computers (2012) 204 Taxman 1 = 16 taxmann.com 268 (Karn HC DB), it was held that payment for supply of software is in nature of royalty (and hence TDS is applicable) - same view in CIT v. Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (2011) 203 Taxman 477 = 16 taxmann.com 141 (Karn HC DB)

Excise duty and service tax where MRP is not required to be declared on package - In case of packaged software, where MRP is not required to be printed under Legal Metrology Act, excise duty would be payable on only cost of media, if assessee is registered under service tax provisions - Notification No. 14/2011-CE dated 1-3-2011 - parallel Notification No. 25/2011-Cus dated 1-3-2011 [On balance amount i.e. amount charged for transfer of right to use goods, service tax would be payable, though this is not specifically stated in the notification]

MRP is not required to be printed on following categories of software - (i) software on optical media supplied free of charge, for which right to use or license is purchased separately (ii) full pack - packaged software with limited validity, not for resale and generally imported for demonstrations or for OEMs (iii) up-grade fully pack - packaged software supplied free of charge under annual maintenance/subscription/software assurance contract and (iv) updates for packaged software - supplied free of charge under annual maintenance/subscription/software assurance contract etc. - In these cases, excise duty/CVD will be charged only on the value, excluding the value representing consideration for transfer of right to use such packaged/canned software. However, service tax under the category of ITSS would be levied on such portion subsequently - MF(DR) circular No. 15/2011-Cus dated 18-3-2011.

Splitting of media and right to use software - CBE&C has clarified that value of software can be split into software media and right to use software (i.e. IPR relating to software) as the notification itself envisages such splitting - MF(DR) Instruction No. 354/189/2009-TRU dated 4-11-2009 in respect of imported software but will equally apply to packaged software manufactured in India. This distinction is not relevant in case of packaged software, as in that case, excise duty is payable on basis of MRP, except where MRP is not required to be declared, as explained above.

SSI units can take benefit of the exemption - Since duty payable has to be determined after considering exemption notification, in my view, SSI units can avail the exemption of service tax, since in their case, 'appropriate duty of excise' is Nil in view of SSI exemption Notification.

Traders dealing in packaged or canned software - In my view, traders of such software will not be liable (Indeed they are even otherwise not liable as sale and purchase of goods cannot be subjected to service tax, but I understand that in some Commissionerates, traders are being asked to pay service tax on sale of packaged software).

Customised software - Customised software is subject to service tax - Para 6.4.5 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Really, if Vat is payable on entire value of goods, then value for purpose of service tax becomes Nil. However, most of software manufacturers are paying both Vat and service tax.

Implementation of ERP package is subject to service tax - In State of Karnataka v. IBM India (P) Ltd. (2015) 52 GST 1230 = 63 taxmann.com 316 (Karn HC DB), it has been held that activities of consultancy services and enterprise resource planning (ERP) software implementation services are subject to service tax. Decisions over-ruled in the budget 1. The Vodafone ruling:

The Supreme Court ("SC") in the case of Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. UOI [2012] 341 ITR 1 (SC) has held that sale of shares outside of India by a foreign company to another is not liable to tax in India.

The Bill has sought to negate most of the parameters applied by the SC and has proposed retrospective amendments to the definition of the terms "capital assets" and "transfer". Similarly, amendments have also been proposed in section 9 (1) (i) of the Act by inter-alia providing that an asset or any share or interest in a company or entity outside India shall be deemed to have situated in India if the share or interest derives, directly or indirectly, its value substantially from the assets located in India. These amendments have been proposed with retrospective effect from 01 April 1962.

Additionally, in a first of its kind, a validation clause has also been proposed to be inserted to validate any notice sent or taxes levied in respect of income accruing or arising, through or from transfer of a capital asset situated in India, in consequence of the transfer of shares of a company registered or incorporated outside India or in consequence of agreement or otherwise outside India. In terms thereof, such notices shall be deemed to have been validly made and such notice or levy of tax shall not be called in question on the ground that the tax was not chargeable or on any other ground.

2. Taxability of software as "royalty":

Different High Courts ("HC") had taken divergent views on the issue, while the Karnataka HC had taken a view against the tax payers (i.e. software payments were held to be taxable as "royalty"), the Delhi HC had in the case of DIT v. Ericsson A. B. [2012] 66 DTR 1 (Del) decided the issue in favour of the assessee.

The Bill proposes to bring within the ambit of the term "royalty" transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred. The amendment is sought to be made with retrospective effect from 01 June 1976.

3. The other "royalty" story:

a. The Bill also proposes to amend/expand the definition of the term "royalty" to cover within its transmission by satellite as a "process". This is sought to be done with retrospective effect from 01 June 1976 to negate the decision of the Delhi HC in the case of Asia Satellite Telecommunication Co. Ltd. v. DIT [2011] 332 ITR 340 (Del) and other decisions on similar lines.

b. Similarly, the Bill proposes to cover within the ambit of the term "royalty" any right, property or information whether or not these are:

i. in the possession or control of the payer;

ii. used directly by the payer;

iii. situated in India.

This is to dilute the decision of the Mumbai Bench of the ITAT in the case of Standard Chartered Bank v. DDIT [2011] 11 ITR (Trib) 721 which has inter-alia held that since the assessee had merely used the equipment and did not have the possession or control of the equipment with themselves nor did they themselves use the equipment, the payment cannot be taxed as "royalty".

The amendment is with effect from 01 June 1976.

4. The Transfer Pricing controversy put to rest:

a. Various Benches of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal ("ITAT") have held that the tolerance band of +/-5% provided for in Section 92C (2) of the Act is available as a standard deduction to the tax payers while computing the "Arm's Length Price" ('ALP'). The Bill proposes to settle the dispute against the tax payers by clarifying, with retrospective effect from 01 April 2002 that the tolerance band of +/- 5% is not to be taken as a standard deduction while computing the ALP.

b. The Karnataka HC in the case of GE India Technology Centre Pvt. Ltd. v. DRP and ACIT [2011] 338 ITR 416 (Kar) has held that the Dispute Resolution Panel ('DRP') cannot go beyond the proposed draft order and make enhancements on issues beyond the variations proposed in the draft order. The Bill proposes to enlarge the powers of DRP powers with retrospective effect from 01 April 2009, so to permit enhancement on any matter arising out of the assessment proceedings relating of the draft order notwithstanding that such matter was raised or not by the assessee.

5-6 Value of subsequent re-sale if payable to foreign supplier

If any part of proceeds of subsequent re-sale of imported goods is payable to seller, directly or indirectly, its cost is includible. (This may happen if a distributor/agent imports goods and once he sells these goods in India, part of sales proceeds may be payable to foreign seller). [Rule 10(1)(d) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007]. 5.5-7 Charges for reproduction of goods in India not to be added

Interpretative Note to rule 10(1)(c) of Customs Valuation Rules makes it clear that charges for right to reproduce the imported goods in India shall not be added.

Sometimes, master copy of software like Page Maker, Norton, Windows, Autocad are imported and are licensed to be reproduced in India by the foreign owner of these softwares. Charges for reproducing these softwares will not be added.

In Sony Music Entertainment P Ltd. v. CC 2005 (189) ELT 227 (CESTAT), assessee was paying royalty to their foreign holding company on CDs manufactured or sold in India. This royalty was not a condition for imports of CDs from foreign principal. It was held that the royalty cannot be added to value of imported CD from foreign principal - followed in CC v. Sony BMG Music Entertainment (I) P Ltd. (2007) 218 ELT 699 (CESTAT) [Departmental appeal admitted for hearing by SC on 21-4-2008 - (2010) 256 ELT A18]

However, the term 'reproduction' is a term of art and used in commercial sense. Right to reproduce is not for convenience of user but for the purpose of distribution. Thus, if importer imports software and pays licence fee with permission to use its copies at various branches, making additional copies for its own use at various branches does not amount to 'reproduction'. Right to use countrywide is not right to 'reproduce'. Thus, the whole licence fee is includible in assessable value - State Bank of India v. CC 2000 AIR SCW 125 = 115 ELT 597 (SC 3 member bench).

5.5-8 Other payments made to seller to be added

If buyer has made, directly or indirectly, any payment to seller as a condition of sale, such payments should be included for obvious reason that 'ordinary' selling price has been reduced due to such payment. [Rule 10(1)(e) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

The royalty, license fee or other payment for process is to be added even if the goods may be subjected to such process after importation of the goods - Explanation to rule 10(1)].

CONCEPT OF PERMANENT ESTABLISHMENT

5. The concept of PE was introduced into the Income-tax Act, 1961 as part of the statutory provisions of transfer pricing by the Finance Act, 2001. In section 92F(iii), the word ‘enterprise’ is defined to mean ‘a person including a PE of such person who is proposed to be engaged in any activity relating to the production’. The CBDT Circular No. 14 of 2001 has clarified that the term P.E. has not been defined in the Act, but its meaning may be understood with reference to the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) entered into by India. The article 5 of the DTAA1 4, which India enters into with other countries, lays down that ‘a permanent establishment means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on’. Thus, the intention was to rely upon the concept and definition of PE in the DTAA.

However, vide the Finance Act, 2002 the definition of PE was inserted in the Income-tax Act, 1961 vide section 92F (iiia) which states that the PE shall include a fixed place of business through which the business of the Multi National Enterprise (MNE) is wholly or partly carried on. The difference lies therein between the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the inclusive sense under the Income-tax Act as against the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the exhaustive sense under the DTAA. This analysis is important because it indicates the intention of the Parliament in adopting an inclusive definition of PE so as to cover all forms of PE inclusive of service PE, agency PE, software PE, Construction PE, etc.

In a ruling given by the Authority for Advance Rulings, India (‘AAR’), the AAR has held that a subsidiary may be regarded as a PE, if it does not have significant independent activities of its own.15 In another ruling, the AAR has held that if the agent does not have the authority to conclude contract, then he cannot constitute a PE16 . However, on the other hand, if the parent executes mass contracts made on standard forms without being scrutinized by it, then the agent may constitute a PE. The Supreme Court of India in DIT (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc.1 7 [2007] 162 Taxman 165 has gone a long way in demystifying the concept of permanent establishment in India.

The applicant is a company incorporated in Australia. It claims to be one of the leading providers of software services which help in virtualization, networking and application delivery. It also offers a range of application collaboration, firewall, networking and streaming solutions. In the year 2006, the applicant entered into a distribution agreement with 'I', an independent Indian company engaged in the business of distribution of computer software and hardware. Under the agreement, 'I' was appointed as a non-exclusive distributor of the products of the applicant in India. Some of the key products distributed under the agreement are Citrix XenApp, Citrix Access Gatway and Citrix Netscaler. According to the applicant, under agreement, the software products are purchased by the distributor from the applicant and sold by the distributor. With respect to the hardware products, the applicant shifted the products directly to the distributor which in turn supplied these products to re-sellers and end-user customers. But, for the software product, Citrix XenApp, while sale and collection is made through the distributor, no physical delivery of the product is made to the distributor. On the basis of the demand of the customers for Citrix XenApp, the distributor places orders of purchase with the applicant and makes payment for the same to the applicant. The applicant then directly transmits a 'key' to the end-user customer who is required to download the XenApp software. On receipt of the key, the end-user customer downloads the software from the server of the applicant.
