THE DOCUMENTATION PROCESS

NEED FOR DOCUMENTATION

4. Transfer pricing calculation produces at least two consequences. First, it puts national tax jurisdictions under stress because it is an income-shifting system that allows MNEs to maximize their after-tax profits by channelling their taxable income to low tax jurisdictions. Second, it provides a substantial advantage to MNEs in comparison with non-multinational firms because only the former can use that strategy.1 0

Tax jurisdictions are constantly challenged to ensure that MNEs do not take undue advantage of their exposure vis-a-vis a localized operator. The only way to guarantee that a MNE is playing by the rules is through proper assessment of its cross-border transactions. That is possible through a detailed study of the company’s functions, assets, and risks that are distributed across tax jurisdictions because those three factors will ulti- mately determine where the profit should be taxed. Thus, there is a need for detailed documentation providing not only the details of the related-party cross-border transaction, but also a logical justification of the prices charged for the transaction.

4.1 ARM’S LENGTH PRINCIPLE - That brings one to the concept of arm’s length principle, which simply means replicating an open market where transactions occur between unrelated entities. It is the principle or international standard that OECD member countries have agreed should be used for determining transfer prices for tax purposes. As mentioned in the OECD guidelines:

Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention : where ‘conditions are made or imposed between the two enterprises in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enterprises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly.’

The arm’s length principle implies that the profits of an MNE should follow where the company has the bulk of its functions, assets, and risks. That is the basic principle, a common underlying concept that most tax authorities across jurisdictions tend to comply with and incorporate as the basis of their transfer pricing principles. A tax authority in any jurisdiction would correctly expect to see a corresponding share of the profit.

The arm’s length principle is equally applicable whether one is dealing with the transfer of tangible goods, intangibles, or services between related parties. The facts and circumstances of each case and the nature of the related-party transactions that are being considered, however, dictate the nuances of application of the principle. While there may be significant variations in the expectations of tax authorities on the documentation requirements, which are usually determined based on each jurisdiction’s tax legislation, some fundamentals do remain the same. For instance, one of the best ways to prove that royalties paid for the transfer of an intangible are at arm’s length is to find comparable arm’s length agreements in the wider marketplace. Also, for a transfer of value added services, it is always preferable to find comparable service transactions between unrelated third parties to prove that the charges paid for the services rendered are at arm’s length. From our experience in the field of transfer pricing documentation for various industries (software, automobile, lumber, rubber, and so on) and for the various types of transactions, it is advisable to use the assistance from experts in the field while preparing documentation to be presented to the tax authorities.

The assessee company has entered into agreements with ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia for supply of standard software products, which in turn, are to be sold in India to the customers of the assessee company mainly, Banks and Financial Institutions. The software transmitted to the assessee company is installed on a server with identifying location and machine No. of the customer. As per the terms of agreements, the assessee company do not have any exclusive right to distribute the software products. It obtains orders on its own account for customers in India and thereafter places orders with non-resident companies. When the products are delivered to the assessee, it sells the products to the customers in India. The non-resident companies raise invoices on the assessee company and in turn, the assessee company raises separate invoices on the end users. It is to be seen that the orders are placed by customers and banks in India with the assessee company on a need based arrangement. The supply of the products are made by the non-resident companies only after approving the technicality of the software module and other necessary particulars. The software products are delivered to the assessee on a CD/any other media specified in the invoices. It is seen that the assessee does not have ownership in the copyright supplied by the non-resident companies. It is also to be seen that the assessee does not have any right to make copies of software or use the software anywhere else. The software is carefully marked for that particular customer to whom the assessee has sold the software product. From the above features, it is clear that the relationship subsisted between the assessee company and the non-resident companies was on a principal-to-principal basis. The risk of the failure of the software product is borne by the assessee company. The assessee company does not have any right to make changes in the software supplied by ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. The assessee company is permitted to make only nominal/cosmetic modifications for the purpose of installing the software and running the software product in the system of customers. The software transferred by the non-resident companies is a standard software. [Para 48]

The services rendered by the assessee in installing the software products in the system of its customers are in the nature of making the software compatible to the environment of the individual customers. The assessee company never becomes the owner of the software. The intellectual property in the software products always remains with the ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. [Para 49]

The decisions cited by the counsel appearing for the assessee support the above stated position of the case. In the decisions of Dassault Systems K.K. [2010] 322 ITR 125/188 Taxman 223 (AAR - New Delhi), CIT v. Dynamic Vertical Software India (P.) Ltd. [2011] 332 ITR 222/201 Taxman 78 (Mag.)/12 taxmann.com 431 (Delhi), DIT v. Ericsson A.B. [2012] 343 ITR 470/204 Taxman 192/[2011] 16 taxmann.com 371 (Delhi), the courts have held that where the assessee is purchasing software from the vendor and selling the same further in Indian market, the consideration paid for such purchase could not be termed as "royalty". It is held that in order to constitute royalty, what is contemplated, is a payment that is depending on user of copyright and not a lump sum paid for the acquisition of copyrighted article. [Para 50]

In the present appeals also, what has been purchased by the assessee from ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia was only copyrighted articles and not copyright, proper. Within the meaning of Indian Copyright Act, 1957, a copyright is an exclusive right to reproduce software including storage of the same in electronic machines with exclusive right to sell it. In the present case, the assessee does not have ownership of the software and does not have right to reproduce the said software. It is in fact only procuring copyrighted software product meant for a particular customer in India. The technical role of the assessee is limited in installing and running the software product in the system of customers in India. Therefore, the assessee is right in its contention that the payments made by the assessee company in the previous year relevant to the assessment years under appeal to non-resident companies are only purchase consideration for procuring copyrighted software products. They were not in the nature of Royalty. [Para 51]

Introduction

Technology has always been at the cutting edge of the significant transformation that is taking place in the market place today. Mobile technology, analytics, cloud computing and wearables have emerged as new forms of technology, and even several traditional companies have started to add capabilities in these areas to cater to the growing customer preferences. In this digital revolution, leading the pack is the e-commerce segment, which is driving rapid growth of domestic IT-ITeS industry and is attracting unprecedented levels of global interest, funding and talent. Owing to such rapid revolution and growth, India ranks third in start-ups formed in the technology industry globally.

Keeping in pace with the growth in this industry, the controversies surrounding taxation of digital transactions are also ever on the rise. Governments and tax administrators of many countries are constantly evaluating the tax implications arising on operations of such entities, since transactions of the e-commerce players raises several contentious tax issues due to absence of national boundaries, physical presence of goods and non-requirement of physical delivery. In India, there are innumerable tax issues faced by the technology industry and in the ensuing paragraphs we have discussed the populist ones.

1. Withholding tax issues on cross border payments involving software

Transactions in the technology industry such as payments for purchase or usage of software, payments for online advertising, app stores, cloud computing are under the tax radar. Such transactions could involve:

-

Transfer of rights in a property (such as right to alter or reproduce work or issue copies of the work);

-

Few transactions could involve payment for services such as access / subscription to databases, standardised applications, e-library, online games, music, news etc.; and

-

Certain transactions could be a combination of both transfer of property rights and services. For e.g. customised software or configurable computing resources such as networks, servers, storage, applications along with services made available to the users through the internet.

The taxation and the related withholding tax implications on such payments to non-residents would be based on the characterisation of such income (business income or royalty or fees for technical services) under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("the Act") read with the beneficial provisions of the tax treaty. Non-resident tax payers in several instances were seeking to characterise their income from such transactions as business income and offer the same to tax in India only where such income was attributable to a permanent establishment ("PE") in India. Hence, in order to curb such mischief, in the garb of a clarification, the Government brought in a retrospective amendment in the Act to widen the scope of definition of "Royalty". The amended definition of "Royalty" seeks to include transfer of any right to use a software including the granting of a license, irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred. This amendment significantly targets transactions involving payments for shrink-wrap or embedded software.

The issue of taxation of cross border software licensing transactions including payments towards access to databases, online applications etc. have been a significant bone of contention between the Indian Revenue authorities and the tax payers over the last decade.

Some of the key illustrative factors considered relevant by the Courts for determining the characterisation of income are listed below:

Nature of rights granted to the payee - Whether rights in the property is transferred or mere right of usage of property is conferred;

Nature of software - Customised vis-à-vis standardised software;

Whether the payment is towards the use or right to use a copyrighted article or a copyright in the article.

Degree of possession and control of the server / database / application;

Recourse to the service provider for the further requirement of any services;

Whether any specific configuration is carried out for the payee?

Whether any information is made available to the payee and right of further commercial exploitation is conferred on the payee?

Whether the payment is made for right other that right in the intellectual property?

Determination of taxability of transactions should be based on a holistic evaluation of the intention of the parties involved and the primary purpose for which the payment is being made. Issues on taxability of software payments along with taxation aspects of e-commerce transactions were extensively researched and opined upon by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development ("OECD") - Technical Advisory Group almost two decades back. However, India differed on most of the views of the OECD on this issue and currently maintains an enhanced observer status to the OECD. The views expressed by India are in variance with most of the developed countries on characterisation of income on software payments. The current action plans initiated by the OECD under the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting ("BEPS") also do not deal with such issues adding to the woes of the technology industry players.

Under the same clause, the risk passed in India. A reading of sections 26 and 40 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 shows that the passing of the title and the passing of the risk need not be simultaneous they can be effected at different points of time. Under section 40, it is open to the parties to agree that even where the property in the goods has passed, the seller may undertake the risk of deterioration in the goods necessarily incident to the course of transit. In view of section 40 of 1930 Act, though the title to the GSM equipment passed in USA, the risk continued to remain with the assessee (seller) and the risk passed to the cellular operator only on delivery in India. Therefore, the result was that merely because the risk passed in India, it could not be said that the sale took place in India. Therefore, no income could be said to have arisen in India. [Para 231]

The further finding that there was a virtual projection of the assessee in India through the office of MINL also remained though because of the deeming provision of article 5.3 it was to be held that the office of the Indian company could not be considered as the permanent establishment of the assessee. Those facts, though they were insufficient to hold, because of the deeming provisions of article 5.3 of the DTAA that there was a permanent establishment in India, they were sufficient to hold that there was business connection in India through which income could be deemed to accrue to the assessee. Those facts did not get obliterated just because of the deeming provision relating to permanent establishment. Moreover, there was no such deeming provision in the case of business connection in section 9(1)(i) to the effect that those activities are not sufficient to constitute a business connection. These payments, could not be viewed as payments for right to use the equipment. The assessee was entitled to certain services, during rendition of which even if certain equipment were to be used, but that by itself did not result in any use of or right to use the equipment by the assessee. The service may involve use of equipment but that does not vest right in the assessee to use the equipment. Even if a part of consideration can be said to be on account of use of equipment by breaking down all the components of economic activity for which consideration is paid, it is neither practicable, nor permissible, to assign monetary value to each of the segment of this economic activity and consider that amount in isolation, for the purpose of deciding character of that amount. Similarly, even if the payment is to be considered as payment for use of software, as is the settled legal position as on now, unless there is no transfer of copyright, there cannot be any occasion to hold it as royalty. In any event, so far as the transaction between the assessee and the BT Canada is concerned, it is simply in the nature of reimbursement of expenses incurred by BT Canada, on behalf of the assessee, and it has no income element so far as BT Canada is concerned. Status of BPO entity

8. The BPO entity in India carrying on the outsourcing activities for a non-resident company, may be its branch or subsidiary company or an independent company.

A branch connotes a physical presence of the foreign enterprise in India. It is an office with an independent administration. Where a non-resident has an office in India and employs staff to carry on its business, it is its branch. A branch office is not regarded as a separate legal entity. Its profits are the profits of a company owning the branch office. It is different from a subsidiary which has a legal entity of its own - CIT v. Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. [1987] 165 ITR 416 (Cal.)—and which is regarded as a domestic company in the country where it is established. The subsidiary company may be a branch office of a foreign establishment under certain circumstances. If it is engaged in transactions with or on behalf of the foreign enterprise as an agent of the parent company in circumstances pointing out to a trading in a host country, it can be said to be performing functions on behalf of that enterprise in the same way as any could do - Fire Stone Tyre and Rubber Co. Ltd. v. Lewellin 37 TC 111. To that extent the subsidiary is the branch office of the foreign enterprise, in spite of it having independent and own legal status.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)] Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.

Transfer pricing calculation produces at least two conse quences: Firstly, it puts national tax jurisdictions under stress because it is an income-shifting system that allows multination als to maximize their after-tax profits by channelling their taxable income to low tax jurisdictions. Secondly, it provides a substantial advantage to multinationals in comparison with non-multinational firms because only the former can use this strate gy.10

Tax jurisdictions are thus constantly challenged to ensure that MNEs do not take undue advantage of their exposure vis-a-vis a localized operator. The only way to guarantee that an MNE is playing by the rule is through proper assessment of their cross-border transactions. This is possible through a detailed study of the company’s functions, assets and risks that are distributed across tax jurisdictions, as these three factors will ultimately determine where the profit should be taxed. Thus the need for a detailed documentation providing not only the details of the related party cross-border transaction, but also a logical justi fication of the prices charged for the transaction.

ARM’S LEGNTH PRINCIPLE

5. This brings us to the concept of arm’s length principle, which simply means replicating the working of an open market where transactions occur between unrelated entities. It is the princi ple or international standard that the OECD member countries have agreed should be used for determining transfer prices for tax purposes. As mentioned in the OECD Guidelines:

It is set forth in Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention as follows: where "conditions are made or imposed between the two enterprises in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enter prises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly".

The arm’s length principle implies that the profits of an MNE should follow where the company has the bulk of its functions, assets and risks. This is the basic principle, a common underly ing concept that most tax authorities across jurisdictions tend to comply with and incorporate as the basis of their transfer pricing principles. A tax authority in any jurisdiction would correctly expect to see a corresponding share of the profit.

The accrual must be real taking into account the actuality of the situation. Whether an accrual has taken place or not must, in appropriate cases, be judged on the principles of real income theory. After accrual, non-charging of tax on the same because of certain conduct based on the ipse dixit of a particular assessee cannot be accepted. What has really accrued to the assessee has to be found out and what has accrued must be considered from the point of the real income taking the probability and the improbability of realisation in a realistic manner and dovetailing of these factors together but once the accrual takes place, on the conduct of the parties subsequent to the year of closing, an income which has accrued cannot be made ‘income’.

The doctrine of real income comes in for application in two types of cases :

◆ Where there is surrender of income before it has accrued

◆ Where there is diversion of income through overriding title

6.15-4g INCOME - SURRENDERED BEFORE ACCRUAL - Income given up or foregone by an assessee on the basis of bilateral agreements or under the provisions of statutes but before its accrual, is not chargeable notwithstanding the fact that entries in respect of it have been made in his books of account which are maintained on a mercantile basis. ‘Hypothetical income’ is the income of the assessee which he could have had under the original agreement which was subsequently varied in the course of the current year reducing the quantum before its accrual and once it has accrued, it ceases to be hypothetical income.1 The real profits of a businessman could not obviously include the amount surrendered by him by way of rebate under statutory compulsion. It is as if he has received only the original amount minus the amount to be surrendered. The amount surrendered is not part of the profits at all.2 Income surrendered because of contract is not likewise included.3

6.15-4h INCOME - DIVERTED AT SOURCE - Receipts which are impressed with an obligation to be applied in a particular manner, may not form part of the trading receipts of an assessee. If the obligation is in the nature of a charge on the source (i.e., the profit-earning apparatus of the assessee), the income is stated to be diverted at source and when the assessee receives the amount, he does so on behalf of somebody else. What has got to be considered is what is the income of the assessee and when that question arises what has got to be considered is the real income and not any artificial income. For purposes of ascertaining that real income, every part of that income which may seem to be the income, if in fact it is not his income, if that part has been diverted and never constituted his real income, has got to be excluded. Real income is what remains after deducting the amount which may be said to have been diverted and, which never constituted the real income of the assessee and such amounts will have to be excluded from the consideration before the real income of the assessee is reached.1

When we say that the effect of the overriding title diverts income at source, it does not mean to suggest that the sale proceeds or the gross receipts also belong to the title holder, and the recipient of the proceeds or receipt is his agent. The dealings in the transaction, resulting in the sale, are done by the concerned person with the other parties not as an agent of the person who would ultimately be the beneficiary of income but as one has a right to claim it before the amount of income becomes the income of that person.

2.1-1 Differences between the pre-amendment Explanation 2A and the post amendment Explanation 2A

Differences between the pre-amendment Explanation 2A and the post amendment Explanation 2A are as follows:— Explanation 2A(a) refers to "transaction in respect of any goods, services or property carried out by a non-resident with any person in India". Should the transaction be "in India" or the person with whom the non-resident is transacting should be "in India"? It appears that the person (counterparty) has to be in India. The transaction may or may not be in India. Likewise, the non-resident need not be in India.

The counterparty has to be in "India" which term has been defined in section 2(25A) as follows:

"India" means the territory of India as referred to in article 1 of the Constitution, its territorial waters, seabed and subsoil underlying such waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone or any other maritime zone as referred to in the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 (80 of 1976), and the air space above its territory and territorial waters.

The definition is very wide and read literally, Explanation 2A would cover even transactions between a non-resident airlines and a passenger in an aeroplane flying over India! It could be argued, however, that in the context, the wide meaning is not adopted.

It is pertinent to note that mere SEP does not constitute business connection; it is the SEP of a non-resident "in India" that constitutes business connection (the opening line of Explanation 2A). Now, the first proviso to Explanation 2A states that transaction or activities specified in the Explanation shall constitute SEP in India, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business "in India" or not or whether he renders services "in India" or not etc. Thus, the proviso by using the expression "in India", appears to constitute an SEP of a non-resident in India as used in the opening lines in Explanation 2A, and as contained in clauses (a) and (b) of Explanation 2A and hence, there is a business connection even if the non-resident is not in India.

Since the words "through digital means" are deleted in the amended definition, there could be an SEP if there is a specified business activity or interaction with prescribed number of users in India whether through digital or other means.

Unlike trade in goods, services do not cross the border or pass the frontier and, therefore, hard to regulate at that point. A ‘service’ is an intangible product and can be supplied easily by using information technology such as calls, fax and e-mail. The important characteristics of services are:—

(a) Services are process.

(b)Transaction in services may require personal contact between providers and consumers.

(c)Some services may have to be regulated.

Where ‘services’ itself moves without the provider or recipient having to travel to another country is referred to in terms as ‘Cross Border Provision of Services’5; whereas when the recipient of the service or ‘consumers’ moves to the country where service provider is established is known as ‘Consumption abroad’ or ‘Movement of consumer’6. Lastly, when the business itself moves to the country where services are to be provided it is considered to be commercial presence which is commonly referred as Permanent Establishment.

OUTSOURCING SERVICES IN INDIA

3. Of late, the outsourcing industry around the world has been confronted with the contentious question of whether outsourced services provided by companies — particularly by captive service providers/manufacturers — would lead to a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident service recipient to come into existence under the terms of the relevant tax treaty. India has been a major beneficiary in the outsourcing boom, and, hence, if Indian tax authorities were to hold that such activities are tantamount to a PE, the global profits attributable to the PE would be taxable in India at the rate of 42.23 per cent7. Further, the availability of a tax credit in the home jurisdiction for such tax paid in India would be uncertain, potentially leading to double taxation and wiping out the economic advantage of outsourcing to India. On the other hand, if no PE exists, no profits can be subjected to Indian corporate tax.

In India, tax liability is based on the structure of the outsourcing contract and the scope of activities being undertaken. The generally preferred models, like third-party service providers, captive centres set up as wholly owned subsidiaries or outsourcing to transition partners on a BOT basis are taxed differently under Indian tax laws. Companies establishing captive facilities and BOT arrangements have to consider issues relating to transfer pricing and permanent establishment.

2.2-1a-2 MEANING OF TERM 'SOURCE' - The term 'source' has been explained by the Supreme Court as follows: "Source in relation to an income has been construed to be where the transaction of sale takes place and not where the item of value, which was the subject of the transaction, was acquired or derived from. HTIL and Vodafone are offshore companies and since the sale took place outside India, applying the source test, the source is also outside India, unless legislation ropes in such transactions." [Vodafone International Holdings B. V. v. UOI [2012] 6 SCC 6131]

Thus, source is where the transaction of sale has taken place. If the specified activity has taken place outside India, it may be argued that the source is not in India within the meaning of section 9(1)(i).

In CIT v. Havells India Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 476/208 Taxman 114 (Delhi), the Court had to interpret section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 which provides that fees for technical services do not accrue or arise in India to the extent they are paid by a resident for utilizing the services for making or earning any income from any "source" outside India. It observed as follows:

"Section 9(1)(vii)(b) contemplates a source located outside India. It is difficult to conceptualise the place/situs of the person who make payment for the export sales as the source located outside India from which assessee earned profits. The export contracts obviously are concluded in India and the assessee's products are sent outside India under such contracts. The manufacturing activity is located in India. The source of income is created at the moment when the export contracts are concluded in India. Thereafter the goods are exported in pursuance of the contract and the export proceeds are sent by the importer and are received in India. The importer of the assessee's products is no doubt situated outside India, but he cannot be regarded as a source of income. The receipt of the sale proceeds emanate from him from outside India. He is, therefore, only the source of the monies received. The income component of the monies or the export receipts is located or situated only in India. We are making a distinction between the source of the income and the source of the receipt of the monies. In order to fall within the second exception provided in Section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Act, the source of the income, and not the receipt, should be situated outside India. That condition is not satisfied in the present case."

Thus, the Court held that export sales proceeds received from goods manufactured and exported from India do not constitute a "source" outside India but is a source in India. Similarly, for the non-resident who sells the goods from outside India, it could be argued that it constitutes a source in the country from which the sale is made and not in India where the customer is situated.

In this regard, the Tribunal has provided some judicial guidance with reference to the relevant sections, which can be helpful in interpreting and applying SDT.

There have been two cases in the year 2012 which emphasize that the concepts of 'arm's length price' and 'ordinary profit' are different. In the case of Visual Graphics Computing Services (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 52 SOT 172/ 21 taxmann.com 145 (URO), Chennai Tribunal held that the concepts of 'arm's length price' and 'ordinary profit' are different and any excess profit over arm's length profit cannot be the basis for denial of tax holiday deduction by the tax authorities under Section 10A of the Act. In this case, the TPO accepted the transactions to be at arm's length and stated that profit reported by the taxpayer were above the arm's length profit. The Assessing Officer (AO) held that the excess profit worked out in the context of TP was not entitled for deduction under Section 10A of the Act. The Tribunal ruled that the anti-avoidance provisions contained in Chapter X of the Act are a separate code enacted for the specific purpose of computing income from international transactions having regard to the ALP. Any adjustment that the AO would like to make with reference to the income would have to be made independent of the order of TPO. Thus, Tribunal held that ALP cannot be used to determine 'ordinary profits' for the purpose of Section 10A(7) of the Act.

Similarly in the case of Weston Knowledge Systems Solutions (India) (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2012] 52 SOT 120/23 taxmann.com 215 (URO), Hyderabad Tribunal confirmed that 'ordinary profits' and 'arm's length price' are two different concepts. In this case, the taxpayer claimed a tax holiday under Section 10A of the Act. For the services rendered to its AE, the taxpayer maintained TP documentation, based on which the AO contended that the margin of the taxpayer being higher than the average margin of the comparables, tantamounts to 'more than the ordinary profits'. Tribunal placed reliance on the Chennai Tribunal ruling in the case of Tweezerman (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Addl.CIT [2010] 133 TTJ 308, which ruled that provisions of Section 80-IA(10) of the Act do not give an arbitrary power to the AO to determine the profits of the taxpayer. The phrase 'more than ordinary profits' referred in section 80-IA(10) of the Act is different from 'ALP'.

There have also been several other rulings which may have implications relevant for domestic transfer pricing.

In the case of Durga Rice Gen Mills. Chandigarh Tribunal held that provisions of section 40A(2) cannot be applied for making addition for the difference in value of sales at which the goods are actually sold and the value, which in the opinion of the AO is correct.

Another ruling which could have an impact on domestic transfer pricing in India is CIT v. Schmetz India (P.) Ltd. [2012] 211 Taxman 59/26 taxmann.com 336 (Mag.), wherein a division bench of Bombay High Court held that extraordinary profits cannot lead to the conclusion that this is an arrangement between the parties. This would penalize efficient functioning. The Revenue had not been able to show that these findings of fact were perverse or arbitrary. Thus, High Court held that the reworking of the profits by the AO was not proper.

The above rulings may provide the taxpayer some guidance on interpreting and implementing SDT which came into the purview of TP effective financial year (FY) 2012-13.

Royalty payouts

Since the inception of TP regulations in India, royalty payout has probably been the most litigated issue between the taxpayers and the Revenue authorities. In the year 2012, interesting aspects came to light in the form of judicial pronoun-cements. But most importantly, the case of CIT v. EKL Appliances Ltd. [2012] 209 Taxman 200/24 taxmann.com 199, adjudicated upon by the Delhi High Court, brought to light certain principles which may prove to be very useful for the taxpayer.

In the case EKL Appliances Ltd. (supra), the Delhi High Court (HC) ruled that the tax department cannot dictate to the taxpayer whether or not to incur an expenditure. ALP of royalty expenditure is not to be linked with profit/income resulting therefrom. Entity level losses are therefore not a valid ground to disallow royalty expenditure.

3.4-3 Purchase of goods in India for export [Section 9(8)(c)(ii)(A) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961 provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export. In the corresponding section 9(9)(c)(ii) of the ITA 2025, the words used are "purchase of goods in India for the purposes of export out of India".

On a strict literal interpretation, the addition of "out of India" might seem redundant, since "export" universally means sending goods out of the country. However, the expression "export out of India" would primarily serve to explicitly remove any remote ambiguity. It could prevent an interpretation where "export" might be construed to include movement to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) within India (which is treated as foreign territory for certain purposes but is geographically within India) or other domestic transfers that are deemed exports for other regulatory purposes but do not involve physical exit from India's customs territory. It would clarify that the exemption applies only when goods physically leave the Indian customs territory.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

However, this argument is bound to fail in view of the very specific provisions under service tax laws. The Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infotech Software Dealers Association has held that transaction in relation to canned/off-the-shelf software can be service in case the developer of software retains the copyright while right to use of software is given to the subscriber. The scenario has become grave for the dealers who prior to introduction of service tax were charging only sales tax on the value of software. Now in view of the specific category under service tax, they need to charge both sales tax and service tax. Since the sales tax and service tax are indirect taxes and to avoid litigation, the dealers tend to charge both the taxes and it is only the end - consumer who has to suffer in view of multiplicity of taxes.

As regards the customized/uncanned software, the contract for development of such software perhaps at the best may be viewed as a service contract. The customized software means software developed for a specific customer to meet his specific requirements. The software industry prior to the introduction of new category of taxable service in the name of 'Information Technology Software Service' was at an advantageous position, as no indirect taxes were applicable on the development of customized software treating it as a service contract. However, the advantageous position got diluted after the introduction of new category as above, as now development of customized software attracts service tax. The dilution has further been deepened after the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. in which it has been held that even customized software may qualify as goods.

The sales tax authorities after taking recourse to the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court are issuing notices demanding tax on the transaction involving development of software. The judgment has opened a Pandora's Box of litigations in relation to customized/uncanned software.

Another area of litigation concerning software is supply of software through electronic downloads. In such a scenario, service tax gets attracted in view of the specific language of the taxable service under the category of 'Information Technology Software Service'. However, whether sales tax is also payable is another point where litigation surrounds the software industry. The Hon'ble Karnataka High Court recently in the case of Sasken Communication Technologies Ltd. has observed that intellectual property once put on a medium becomes goods and when transferred is leviable to sales tax. After this judgment, the industry players can hope that the sales tax authorities do not litigate on this issue.

The menace of double taxation is detrimental to the interests of users of goods/services as it results into high procurement costs, especially in those cases where credit of input taxes paid cannot be taken by the users. The domestic users only take a hit as the exporters of software generally enjoy the tax free status and, accordingly, no taxes are charged on the value of goods/services exported from India. Presently, the sales tax (local VAT) rate for software is either at 4% or at 5% and service tax rate is at 10%, which can significantly enhance the costs of procurements in case software suffers double taxation, specifically in cases where the credit of input taxes is not available either in full or in part.

Though the laws on sales tax and service tax are on the statute books for good number of years now, yet the provisions of these laws need alignment, which seems to be an uphill task in view of the fact that the Governments desire to garner more and more revenue and sometimes it happens by introducing provisions which put the taxpayer in a situation where he has no alternative but to resort to litigation.

2.2 Issues regarding Classification - Another controversy that surrounds the software revolves around its classification, especially in those cases where the software is not embedded in the hardware and is procured separately from the vendor of the hardware. The problem is generally faced by the importers of telecom equipments.

At present, the rate of customs duty on telecom equipments is generally at around 15% and on software it is at around 10% in case it is imported say on CD. Due to the difference in the rate of customs duty, the customs authorities always litigate on the genuineness of the imports and try to include the value of software in the value of hardware and, accordingly, make the value of software suffer higher rate of customs duty. This particular issue of telecom industry is yet to test the scrutiny of judiciary but apparently, both hardware and software are classifiable into different customs tariff classifications and different customs duty structure is also justifiable.

2.3 Issues regarding Withholding Tax - Another issue that hovers around software is whether the payments remitted by a resident to a non-resident for software can be said to be one for use of copyright or can be categorised as one for copyrighted article. The issue has over a period of time been interpreted differently by the Appellate Tribunals across India. In case, the amount is categorised as royalty, the Indian entity making the payment is required to do withholding of tax under section 195 of the Income-tax Act.

The Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Novel Inc. v. Dy. DIT [2011] 16 taxmann.com 186 has held that payments made by the Indian distributors to a non-resident for procuring rights to further sell the software to customers in India would not amount to royalty.

CASE STUDY 3: Transfer of Bundled Intellectual Property – Web-based business model

3.1 Introduction - The traditional notion of software has been a company hiring engineers who sit in a building writing code to create a software program used for a specific purpose and such program once developed is sent to customers in the tangible form of CD’s or DVD’s. This model equated well with the assembly line manufacturing process and an age-old model of tangible products.

However, the above is not how a majority of software is developed nowadays; the Internet has brought forth new business model – both business to business (B2B) & business to consumer (B2C) models.

Today there exists "web" companies which are valued at billions of dollars whose "crown jewels" are usually the intangible intellectual property they own or their patented business models or their proprietary technology web-service platforms. Examples of such web companies are Google, Facebook, eBay5 2 etc.

3.2 A simple web-based business model - In this case study we take a web-based business model related to the online advertising market (also called SEM – Search Engine Marketing), one of the fastest growing markets in the world. This is similar to the case study presented in Elizabeth King’s case study on Replication of Internet-Based Business Model52.

Search engines like Google5 3 derive most of their income from such markets which allow advertisers to bid on keywords in an auction-model on their technology platforms; when users search for the keywords which have been bid upon they are shown text ads sorted in the descending order of their bid. Such a market gave rise to a host of web companies who provide service to advertisers to efficiently and optimally bid on millions of companies – they are essentially providing SEM solutions to online advertisers.

We consider a USA company, USCo, which provides SEM i.e. Search Engine Marketing solutions using its unique and patented algorithmic techniques for efficient and optimal bidding; in simple terms the company takes control of advertisers online campaigns of its clients and bids on keywords in the online advertisement marketplaces offered by search engines like Google Adwords54 . USCo’s clients are typically two-fold: companies who wants to advertise online to boost traffic to its website and sales of its products & services, advertising agencies who provide full-service to their clients and provide both offline (TV, newspapers etc.) & online advertising solutions for clients.

USCo has a successful and established business model and handles over $500 million in advertising spend on the various search engines. Parts of USCo’s business model are patented. Further, USCo has developed proprietary software for its internal usage – to process, analyze & model the huge amount of data it churns daily. USCo has also developed online marketing & solicitation tools which it uses to market to, obtain, test and sign-up clients.

Now an Indian company, lets call it IndCo, wants to replicate USCo’s business model in India. Towards this the top management gets training in USCo and on doing so provides the USCo’s business model of online advertising solutions to clients & ad agencies in India.

To summarize:

1.USCo transfers the intellectual property of its proprietary software modified to suit local conditions.

2.USCo also provides the right to use of its marketing and solicitation online tools to IndCo, again these pages have to be modified slightly for local conditions.

3.USCo will perform routine service, maintenance and upgrades on the proprietary software given to IndCo.

4.USCo will provide legal and financial planning and advisory services to IndCo.

5.IndCo has been issued the rights to use USCo’s trademark and name in the Indian market.

3.3 International taxation issues - The above model is akin to a business format franchise 70. The key question is what are the arm’s length services fees payable by IndCo to USCo?

The resale and cost-plus methods presuppose a particular division of labour that is not characteristic of the USCo and IndCo. The profit-comparison methods would require quasi-comparable companies in the same startup stage and would probably yield no residual profits to USCo.

If the Indian data centre's role is limited to managing data centre infrastructure and is not involved in concluding contracts or securing orders in India for the foreign company's services to overseas users, then the DAPE risk may not arise. However, if the Indian entity facilitates the foreign company's contracts with overseas or Indian users in any significant way from India, it may result in a DAPE. 8.7-11c Classification as royalty - Section 9(6)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of royalty to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. The classification of data centre services as 'royalty' has been a subject of judicial scrutiny. Indian courts, such as the Mumbai ITAT in Rackspace US, Inc. v. DCIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92, have held that income from cloud hosting and ancillary services was neither royalty nor Fees for Technical Services (FTS). The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

8.7-11d Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on whether the foreign company has a PE in India.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India and the business income earned in India is connected to that PE, the tax liability shall be computed in accordance with the ITA.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the foreign company does not have a PE in India, its business income earned in India shall not be taxable in India.

8.7-12 Transaction with associated enterprises

Where an Indian entity provides data centre services to its associated enterprise (a foreign company), it may opt for the safe harbour framework under the transfer pricing provisions. If the Indian entity earns an operating profit margin of at least 15% of operating expenses from such international transactions, the transaction price will be deemed to be at arm's length, and no transfer pricing adjustment will be required. [see Para 12.2-2b]

8.7-13 Comprehensive illustration

There are five parties in the transaction relating to the data centre: SCloud Pte. Ltd. (a Singapore-based cloud management platform), DC Ltd. (an Indian data centre), RS India Ltd. (an Indian reseller), OTT Pvt. Ltd. (the Indian end user) and OS Inc. (the Singapore-based end user).

The details of the transaction between the parties are as follows:

DC enters into an agreement with SCloud to provide 50 servers, 10TB storage, power, cooling, and facility services for Rs. 7,00,000 per month. DC owns and operates all physical equipment, while SCloud has only API access to manage virtual resources and no ownership or physical control.

SCloud enters into a reseller agreement with RS, offering managed cloud services (including the DC infrastructure, SCloud proprietary management platform, orchestration software, 24/7 monitoring, technical support, and analytics) for Rs. 13,50,000 per month.

SCloud enters into a cloud service agreement with OS, under which OS offers managed cloud services for USD 50,000 per month.

Indian subsidiary may make payment to foreign parent company for (a) use of its brand name of parent company or (b) obtaining technical know-how or (c) royalty for using Intellectual property of parent company (like patent, design, trade mark or copyright).

As per residuary rule 3 of Place of Provision of Service Rules, the place of provision of a service shall be the location of the service receiver.

Branch office in India

9. If branch of liaison office is opened in India, issue of service tax arises.

Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 states that an establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

Thus, the branch office or liaison office in India would require service tax registration and would be liable to pay service tax if any service is provided from its branch office.

Maintenance of branch outside India

10. Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012 reads as follows - An establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

This Explanation has been given to definition of 'service'. In fact, this Explanation has nothing to do with definition of 'service' and is at a wrong place.

However, this Explanation is creating lot of difficulties (may be mainly because it has been placed at a wrong place). This Explanation is being interpreted to mean that HO in India and branch outside India are two different 'persons'. Hence, if the HO in India remits money to maintain branch outside India, it will be treated as 'import of service' i.e. branch outside India is providing service to Head Office in India.

Really, 'shall be treated as establishment of different persons' does not mean 'shall be treated as two different persons'.

Thus, Branch/office in India and branch/office of same business entity outside India will be treated as different 'establishments' and not 'different persons'.

A branch received service from its other branch outside India will not be subject to service tax under reverse charge mechanism as 'import of service', as they are not different persons.

Similarly, a branch in India cannot 'export' service to its branch outside India.

In KPIT Cummins v. CCE [2014] 43 GST 266/[2013] 38 taxmann.com 340 (Mum. - CESTAT), assessee was remitting money from India for maintaining various establishments outside India. A prima facie view has been held that when service is provided outside India and consumed outside India, no service tax is leviable in India. Further, the branches of assessee outside India were providing services from out of India and were getting payments outside India. Local taxes in that country were paid. It was held that it cannot be said that foreign branches have provided services on behalf of assessee and assessee cannot be held liable under Business Auxiliary Services under reverse charge. In any case, it would be export of service and not taxable.

Conclusion

A foreign company establishing manufacturing unit in India must prepare and plan for various service tax issues that are likely to arise. Otherwise, it is likely to be taken by surprise by some unexpected demands of service tax.

5. Income from cloud hosting and its ancillary services neither royalty nor FTS : ITAT

Racksapce US, Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92 (Mum. - Trib.)

The assessee was a tax resident of the USA. Assessee earned income from cloud services, including cloud hosting and other supporting and ancillary services provided to Indian Customers. The assessee filed the return of income and the notes stating that the cloud hosting services were not taxable as 'royalties' under Article 12 of the India-US tax treaty.

The Mumbai ITAT held that the agreement between the assessee and its customer was for providing hosting and other ancillary services to the customer and not for the use of or leasing of any equipment.

The Data Centre and the Infrastructure therein were used to provide these services belonging to the assessee. The customers do not have physical control or possession over the servers, and right to operate and manage this infrastructure or servers vested solely with the assessee. The agreement was to provide simpliciter hosting services and not give the underlying equipment on hire or lease. Considering the difference in the ostensible compensation structures across different categories of manufacturers, it becomes pertinent for MNEs to clearly identify the functional characterization as well as the compensation structure at the outset, i.e., even before the Indian Taxpayer begins the actual manufacturing activity. Adopting a particular characterization initially without thinking through the entire life cycle of the proposed manufacturing operation could be fraught with significant transfer pricing and tax costs. For instance, an Indian manufacturer set up as a full-fledged entrepreneurial manufacturer could be rightfully expected to incur losses during the initial period of set up. However, as a part of its manufacturing operations, it may develop valuable intangibles, and may achieve significant economies of scale. Therefore, the start up losses would need to be balanced with an expectation of, or at least, a probability of extraordinary profits going forward. Now, if the MNE group wishes to re-characterize the manufacturer as a contract manufacturer going forward, the group may be faced with significant business restructuring related implications, and associated tax costs.

Payment of Royalties and Technology Fees to Foreign Affiliates

Typically, the Indian manufacturer would tend to rely primarily on the technical know-how, technical assistance and training provided by their foreign affiliates for its manufacturing operations, for a significant period of operations.

Further, one or more foreign affiliates could invest continuously and substantially in research and development activities which benefit, the Indian manufacturer, who is completely dependent on the affiliates for the technology required for the manufacturing operations.

The royalty and fee arrangements need to be carefully constructed. The arrangements must reflect the commercial reality of the underlying transaction, and must correspond to what independent parties are likely to agree in arm's length dealings.

From a documentation perspective, it is necessary to elaborately document the precise nature of the intangible and/or the technology support received from the foreign affiliate. The valuation of the intangible (if and to the extent possible), use of the intangible in the value chain, significance of the intangible etc., should also be thoroughly evaluated and documented. The benefits derived by the Indian manufacturer from use of the intangible, including process improvement, quality improvement, cost savings, etc. should also be documented, and if possible, even quantified.

The arm's length nature of these payments has been disputed by the Indian revenue authorities in several cases by questioning the commercial expediency and the quantum of benefit derived by the Indian entity. In cases where Indian taxpayers have been unable to substantiate the benefits received by them, the revenue authorities have been determining the arm's length price for such payments as NIL. This approach of the authorities has also been upheld in few cases where the taxpayer was not able to substantiate the rationale or benefits from the royalty payments6.

Further, the royalty/fee arrangements need to be evaluated regularly to confirm that they continue being relevant from an arm's length perspective, for the period for which royalties/fees are being paid. For instance, assume that a certain technology was provided to the Indian manufacturer in year 1 and a royalty was charged for use of the technology. Further, assume that this technology became obsolete in Year 10, or that it started becoming freely available (say, due to expiration of the underlying patent or otherwise) starting Year 10. The MNE group must re-examine if in these circumstances, whether any royalty indeed ought to be paid by the Indian manufacturer, starting Year 10 under arm's length circumstances.

Another aspect to be considered here is that in a case where the Indian manufacturer is able to generate some intangibles (for instance, improved designs or processes) as a part of its manufacturing process, and the said intangible is then provided to other manufacturing units of the MNE group, in arm's length circumstances, the Indian manufacturer could also be entitled to a remuneration for allowing the use of intangibles developed by it.

Imports from Foreign Affiliates

Machinery and equipments needed for a new manufacturing facility could be imported from abroad. Especially in cases where an existing manufacturing plant is being relocated to India, a vast majority of the machinery and equipments could be imported from overseas affiliates. These can either be used or new machinery/equipments. The Indian transfer pricing regulations provide for determination of arm's length price of such capital purchases also.

The machinery and equipments imported from foreign affiliates need to be valued by a valuation expert. Especially in cases of used machinery, the written down value of the machinery in the books of the foreign affiliate may not necessarily be the correct indication of the arms length price of the machinery. The arm's length price of such machinery needs to be determined based on the current commercial valuation of the machinery, considering options, if available, in the market for similar machinery. Quotations from independent third parties could also serve as useful guides for approximating the arm's length price of the machinery. In any case, a balance needs to be maintained between the valuation requirements under the transfer pricing regulations and Customs regulations. Any imbalance in valuation/pricing could lead to additional tax cost under either set of applicable regulations.

Similarly, in the initial period, the Indian manufacturer might not be able to localize its raw material requirements, and consequently, it may be dependent on its foreign affiliates for its raw material requirements. Again, the pricing policy for such raw materials needs to balance the requirements under Transfer Pricing and Customs Regulations.

Navigating the landscape of valuation for the imports

In the complex world of imports, businesses often consider the value of the physical goods to be paramount. However, they sometimes overlook that beyond the physical cargo lies something less visible yet crucial — the royalty/license fee payments. Royalties arise from licensing agreements which grant the importer rights inter alia to use manufacturing know-how, brand names, or software embedded within imported goods.

As the nature of contracts pertaining to imports/exports and associated license fee/royalty has evolved, the Customs valuation has also come a long way. Once upon a time, a physical shipment was all that customs authorities cared about for determining its value and imposition duties. Today's imports bundle licensed software, technology, trademarks, and other rights, making valuation of such shipments more complicated. While the goods themselves represent the tangible aspect for customs valuation, the accompanied intangible rights and their payments may significantly contribute to the overall value of the import transaction. This evolution sets the stage for courts to demystify when license fee/royalty should be included in the transaction value of the imported goods.

The recent judgement by CESTAT, New Delhi in the judgment of HCL Technologies Ltd. and SAP India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication) [Final Order No. 51379-51462 of 2025 dated 29-9-2025] bring these complexities to the forefront. It deals with critical questions regarding includability of license fee in the value of the imported goods, specifically in the context of delivery of software through physical and electronic media.

Under the Lens: CESTAT's approach in the case of HCL Technologies Ltd.

Facts at a Glance

HCL Technologies Ltd. ('HCL') entered into an End-User License Agreement ('EULA') with SAP India Private Limited ('SAP India') to obtain non-exclusive and perpetual license to use propriety software, documentation and other information of SAP India. As per terms of the EULA, the software was to be delivered electronically. In the year 2006, SAP India raised substantial invoices on HCL for payment of license fee relating to rights provided under the EULA.

During the same time, HCL received some imported CDs containing SAP Software via courier, wherein a nominal value was declared under the courier bill of entry, for customs purposes. Perhaps, this is what caught the eye of the Customs Department – A CD with a software... only for pocket change?

An investigation was initiated against inter alia HCL for such imports. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Customs Department rejected the declared value of the CDs under Rule 10A of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 ('CVR') [now Rule 14 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] and sought to include the license fee in the valuation of imported CDs in terms of Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR.

The allegation of the Customs Department was that unless the license fee is paid, the software on the CD cannot be accessed or used; thereby, making the license fee integral to the transaction value of the imported CDs.

Tribunal's Verdict: Four Conditions for Royalty Inclusion in Customs Valuation

The Tribunal determined that for inclusion of royalties to the value of the imported goods, the following four key conditions under Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR needed to be satisfied:

1.

The license fee must relate to the imported goods;

2.

The fee must be payable directly or indirectly by the importer at the time of import;

3.

The license fee must be a condition of sale of the goods; and

4.

The fee must not already be included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods.

Guided by these conditions, the Tribunal took a closer look at the terms of the EULA entered between HCL&SAP India, and made the following findings:

The license fee was not related to the physical import of the CDs; rather, it was related to the intangible right to use the software in India. The EULA had itself provided electronic delivery as the mode of delivery of the software. Thus, the license fee was for usage of software rights and not for the import of physical CDs themselves.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import.

The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively. This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.
